name: Medical Biology and Genetics
description: Complete study manual · 15 practical class topics

topics.title: The microscope and the rules of working with it. Preparing temporary slides. Viruses. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, their structure and differences

goals.text: To teach the student the tasks of biology and the main properties of life, the cell theory, the structure of the light and electron microscope and the rules of working with them, the technique of preparing a temporary slide, and the structure and medical importance of the non-cellular (viruses) and cellular (prokaryotic and eukaryotic) forms of life.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the main properties of life and its levels of organization;
the main statements of the cell theory and the methods of studying the cell;
the mechanical, optical and illuminating parts of the light microscope and the types of microscopes;
the structure and reproduction of viruses and bacteriophages and the diseases they cause;
the main differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: set up the microscope and examine a slide under the low-power and high-power objective;
calculate the total magnification;
prepare a temporary slide (onion skin epidermis);
recognize and correct mistakes made while working with the microscope.

sections.title: 1. Biology and the main properties of life

blocks.text: **Biology** (Greek *bios* — life, *logos* — science) is the science that studies all manifestations of life: the structure, function, development and origin of organisms and their relationships with each other and with the environment. The term was introduced independently by J.B. Lamarck and G. Treviranus at the beginning of the XIX century. **Medical biology** studies the human body as a biological object and is the foundation for histology, physiology, biochemistry, microbiology, pathology and the clinical sciences.

Biology uses **observation, description, comparison, experiment, the historical method, modeling** and **statistical** methods. Living nature differs from non-living nature by the following set of properties:

blocks.title: Table 1.1. The main properties of life
head: Property
Meaning
rows: Based on proteins and nucleic acids; rich in the organogenic elements C, H, O, N
Homeostasis — keeping the internal environment constant
Constant replacement of the component parts
Passing traits to the next generation and producing new traits
Responding to external and internal stimuli
The organism consists of separate parts but works as a single system

blocks.text: Levels of organization of life

items: **Molecular-genetic** — nucleic acids and proteins; storing and transmitting hereditary information.
**Cellular** — the cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life.
**Tissue and organ** — groups of specialized cells in multicellular organisms.
**Organism (ontogenetic)** — the whole individual and its development.
**Population-species** — a group of freely interbreeding individuals of a species; the elementary unit of evolution.
**Biogeocenotic and biosphere** — exchange of matter and energy between organisms and the environment.

parts.text: Order of the levels: **“My Cat Takes Only Pure Biscuits”** — Molecule, Cell, Tissue, Organism, Population, Biosphere.

blocks.text: Stages in the development of biology

Knowledge of living nature has accumulated since ancient times: people first divided plants and animals into useful, poisonous and disease-causing groups. As data on the diversity of organisms grew, it led to the conclusion that they share a common origin. This matters for medicine: if all life has one origin, the **universal biological laws** of the whole organic world also apply to the human being as a biological object.

blocks.text: **The biosocial nature of humans.** The human being is at the same time a biological species (*Homo sapiens*) and a social being. Human structure, reproduction, heredity, development and ageing obey general biological laws, but social factors such as lifestyle, work, diet and ecological conditions change how these laws show themselves. For example, a hereditary predisposition (diabetes mellitus, hypertension) turns into disease with an unhealthy lifestyle.

parts.text: For a physician, biology is the theoretical foundation of medicine: cell biology explains pathology, genetics explains the diagnosis of hereditary diseases and genetic counselling, the laws of ontogenesis explain congenital defects and teratogenesis, and parasitology explains the diagnosis and prevention of parasitic diseases.

sections.title: 2. The cell theory and methods of studying the cell

blocks.text: The cell was first seen in 1665 by the English scientist **R. Hooke** in a section of cork; he called it a “cell”. **A. Leeuwenhoek** observed unicellular organisms, erythrocytes and spermatozoa; **R. Brown** discovered the nucleus in 1831. In 1838–1839 **M. Schleiden** and **T. Schwann** created the cell theory, and in 1858 **R. Virchow** added the statement “Every cell comes only from a cell” (*Omnis cellula e cellula*).
Main statements of the modern cell theory

items: The cell is the elementary unit of structure, function and development of life.
The cells of all organisms are similar (homologous) in structure, chemical composition and life processes.
Cells reproduce only by division of a mother cell.
In a multicellular organism cells unite into tissues and organs and form an integrated system.
The cells of an organism are totipotent — all cells contain the same genetic information, but different genes are active in them (differentiation).

blocks.text: Important contributions to cell theory were made by **M. Malpighi** and **N. Grew** (cellular structure of plants), **J. Purkinje** (described protoplasm in 1830), **W. Flemming** (described mitosis in 1879) and **A. Weismann** (showed meiosis in germ-cell formation in 1887). After this it was confirmed that a cell consists of three parts — **the plasma membrane (or cell wall), the cytoplasm and the nucleus**.
Advantages of cellular organisation for the organism

items: Division of the body into small units increases the total surface area and speeds up metabolism.
Dead or pathologically changed cells are replaced by new ones (regeneration).
The cell stores hereditary information, doubles it (reduplication) and passes it to the next generations.
The cell stores energy, transports it and converts it into work.
In multicellular organisms the division of functions between cells (specialisation) makes evolution possible.

parts.text: In his work “Cellular Pathology”, published in 1858, R. Virchow showed that disease is the result of changes in cells. This idea founded **pathological anatomy**; modern biopsy, cytological examination (for example, the cervical smear — the Papanicolaou test) and tumour diagnosis rest on this principle.

blocks.title: Table 1.3. Methods of studying the cell
head: Method
Principle and use
rows: Viewing stained and unstained slides; resolving power ≈ 0.2 µm
Ultrastructure of organelles; resolving power ≈ 0.1–1 nm
Detecting substances in the cell (DNA, glycogen, enzymes) by color reactions
Following the path of radioactively labeled substances in the cell
Separating organelles according to their density
Growing cells outside the organism (virology, karyotype analysis)
Nuclear transfer and injection of substances into a cell with a micromanipulator

blocks.text: The light microscope consists of **mechanical**, **optical** and **illuminating** parts (Figure 1.1). The mechanical part holds all the parts together, moves the slide and adjusts the focus; the optical part magnifies the image; the illuminating part directs the light onto the slide.

blocks.label: Figure 1.1
blocks.caption: A teaching light microscope: 1 — eyepiece (ocular); 2 — body tube; 3 — revolving nosepiece; 4 — objective; 5 — stage; 6 — condenser (with diaphragm); 7 — mirror; 8 — coarse adjustment knob; 9 — fine adjustment knob; 10 — arm; 11 — base (Wikimedia Commons photograph, numbers added).

blocks.title: Table 1.4. Parts of the light microscope
head: Part
Components
Function
rows: Base, arm, body tube, revolving nosepiece, stage (with clips), coarse and fine adjustment knobs
Holds the optical parts, positions the slide, brings the image into focus
Magnifies the image of the object
Mirror (or lamp), condenser, iris diaphragm, light filter
Collects light, directs it onto the slide and controls its intensity

blocks.text: **Total magnification** = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification. For example, with a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective the object is magnified 400 times. The ×90 objective is an **immersion** objective: a drop of **cedar (immersion) oil**, whose refractive index is close to that of glass, is placed between the slide and the objective.

The quality of a microscope is determined not by its magnification but by its **resolving power** — the smallest distance at which two points are still seen as separate. In the light microscope it is about half the wavelength of light (≈ 0.2 µm); therefore small structures such as ribosomes and membranes are visible only in the electron microscope.

blocks.title: Table 1.5. Types of microscopes and microscopy
head: Type
Feature
Use
rows: Turns differences in optical density into light-dark contrast
The object appears bright on a dark background
Birefringent structures are visible in polarized light
An electron beam passes through an ultrathin section
Electrons reflected from the surface give a three-dimensional image
Surfaces of cells and tissues, surface of parasites

blocks.text: Units of measurement in microscopy and the size of objects

Cells and their parts are measured in **micrometres** (1 µm = 10^−3^ mm) and **nanometres** (1 nm = 10^−3^ µm = 10^−9^ m). The resolving power of the human eye is ≈ 0,1 mm, of the light microscope ≈ 0,2 µm and of the electron microscope ≈ 0,1–1 nm. So for each object in the table below one can predict which instrument is needed.

blocks.title: Table 1.6. Size of biological objects
head: Object
Approximate size
Means of viewing
rows: Diameter of the DNA double helix

parts.text: “**Thousand — thousand — thousand**”: 1 mm = 1000 µm, 1 µm = 1000 nm. Cells are measured in micrometres; viruses and parts of organelles in nanometres.

sections.title: 4. Rules of working with the microscope

items: Lift the microscope holding the arm with the right hand and the base with the left; place it 3–5 cm from the edge of the table with the arm facing you.
Turn the nosepiece to put the **low-power objective (×8 or ×10)** in the center until it clicks.

Raise the condenser and open the diaphragm. Looking into the eyepiece, turn the mirror until the field of view is evenly lit (with artificial light use the flat side of the mirror, with daylight — the concave side).
Put the slide on the stage with the coverslip facing up, fix it with the clips and bring the area to be studied under the objective.

Looking from the side, lower the objective with the coarse adjustment knob to 0.5 cm above the slide; then, looking into the eyepiece, turn the knob **away from yourself** (raising the tube) until a clear image appears.

Bring the area of interest to the center of the field and switch the nosepiece to the **high-power objective (×40)**; sharpen the image only with the **fine adjustment knob** (turning it no more than half a turn).
After work put the low-power objective in place, remove the slide, wipe the microscope with a soft cloth and put it in its case.

parts.text: The **coarse adjustment knob** must not be used with the high-power objective: its working distance is about 0.6 mm, so it touches the slide, breaks the coverslip and damages the lens. Do not wipe lenses with your fingers or with paper.

blocks.text: **Drawing rule:** the slide is viewed with the left eye while both eyes stay open; the drawing is made with the right hand in an album with a simple pencil, the parts are named with pointer lines, and the name of the slide and the magnification are written under the drawing.
Working with the immersion objective (×90)

items: First view the preparation with the low-power and then the high-power objective and bring the area of interest to the centre of the field.
Turn the revolver to move the objective aside and put one drop of immersion (cedar) oil on that spot of the preparation.
Looking from the side, carefully lower the immersion objective until it dips into the oil drop.
Raise the condenser to the top position and open the diaphragm fully — immersion needs a lot of light.
Looking into the eyepiece, focus the image with the micrometer screw only.
After work, wipe the oil off the objective and the preparation at once with a soft cloth moistened with benzine or xylene.

blocks.title: Table 1.7. Typical problems when working with the microscope
head: Problem
Probable cause
Correction
rows: The field of view is dark
The objective has not clicked into place; diaphragm closed; condenser lowered
Set the revolver, open the diaphragm, raise the condenser, adjust the mirror
The image is blurred, like a “fog”
Dirty lens or eyepiece; preparation placed upside down
Wipe the lens with a special cloth; the coverslip must face upwards
Half of the field is lit
The objective is not turned fully into place
Turn the revolver until it clicks
Spots that move in the field
Rotate the eyepiece; if the spot also turns, clean the eyepiece
No image is found at high power
The object was not centred; focusing was done with the coarse screw
Return to low power, centre the object, then use the fine screw

blocks.text: A **temporary slide** is prepared in a drop of water, glycerol or saline for viewing during one class; it dries quickly and cannot be stored for long. A **permanent slide** is prepared by fixing the tissue, dehydrating it, embedding it in paraffin, cutting it on a microtome into sections 5–7 µm thick, staining it (for example, with hematoxylin and eosin) and mounting it under Canada balsam; it can be kept for many years.
Preparing a temporary slide of onion skin epidermis

items: Place 1 drop of water in the middle of a clean glass slide with a pipette.
With forceps peel a thin, transparent film of epidermis from the inner concave surface of an onion scale.
Spread the film in the drop, making sure it does not fold.
Touch the drop with the coverslip held at an angle of 45° and lower it slowly — this way no air bubbles remain.

Remove the excess water with filter paper; if needed, put a drop of iodine solution at the edge of the coverslip and draw it under with filter paper from the opposite side (the nucleus stains yellow-brown).
Examine the slide first under low power and then under high power, and draw the cell wall, cytoplasm, nucleus and vacuole.

parts.text: Round “cells” with a thick black rim on a slide are often **air bubbles**: when the focus knob is turned, their black rim widens and narrows, while a real cell shows an internal structure (the nucleus).

blocks.text: Stages of making a permanent preparation

items: **Fixation** — preserving cell structures close to their living state in formalin, alcohol or Carnoy's fluid.
**Washing** — rinsing the fixative out with water.
**Dehydration** — removing water in alcohols of increasing strength (70°, 80°, 96°, absolute).
**Clearing** — making the tissue transparent in xylene or chloroform.
**Embedding** — immersing in melted paraffin to form a solid block.
**Sectioning** — cutting sections 5–7 µm thick on a microtome.
**Staining** — removing the paraffin and staining the section (haematoxylin-eosin).
**Mounting** — covering the section with a coverslip over a drop of Canada balsam.

blocks.text: Temporary preparation of human buccal epithelium

items: Gently scrape the inner surface of the cheek with a sterile spatula or toothpick.
Smear the material into one drop of physiological saline on a slide.
Add one drop of methylene blue (or iodine) solution and cover with a coverslip.
At low and high power, observe and draw the flat, polygonal cells and the round nucleus in their centre.

blocks.title: Table 1.8. Stains used for microscopic preparations
head: Stain
What it stains (colour)
rows: Blood cells, malaria plasmodium — nucleus red, cytoplasm blue
DNA — crimson-violet (a cytochemical reaction specific to DNA)

sections.title: 6. The non-cellular form of life — viruses and bacteriophages

blocks.text: Viruses were discovered in 1892 by the Russian scientist **D.I. Ivanovsky** while studying tobacco mosaic disease. Viruses are **obligate intracellular parasites** 20–300 nm in size that reproduce only inside living cells. Outside the cell (as a virion) they show no properties of life, but after entering a cell they carry out their own genetic program; that is why they are regarded as a form between living and non-living nature.

blocks.label: Figure 1.2
blocks.caption: Viruses of various shapes: herpes virus (icosahedral capsid and envelope), influenza virus (helical nucleocapsid and envelope), tobacco mosaic virus (helical symmetry) and a bacteriophage (complex symmetry) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Structure of a virus

items: **Nucleic acid** (the genome) — either DNA or RNA (never both); single- or double-stranded.
**Capsid** — the protein coat surrounding the nucleic acid; built of capsomeres. Nucleic acid + capsid = **nucleocapsid**.
**Envelope** (supercapsid) — in complex viruses, a lipoprotein membrane taken from the host cell membrane, carrying glycoprotein “spikes” (influenza, HIV, herpes).
Some viruses carry enzymes: for example, HIV has **reverse transcriptase**, which makes a DNA copy of RNA.

blocks.label: Figure 1.3
blocks.caption: Structure of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV): lipid envelope with glycoprotein “spikes”, protein coat (capsid), RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Viruses exist in two forms: the **extracellular (resting) form** — the virion, which shows no signs of life; and the **intracellular (reproducing) form** — the virus–cell complex. By structure, **simple viruses** (only nucleic acid and a protein capsid) and **complex viruses** (with an additional lipoprotein envelope, carbohydrates and enzymes) are distinguished.

blocks.title: Table 1.9. Groups of viruses by genome
head: Group
Examples
rows: Smallpox, herpesviruses (herpes simplex, chickenpox, Epstein–Barr), adenoviruses, papillomaviruses

blocks.text: Reproduction of a virus in the cell

items: **Adsorption** — the virus binds to a specific receptor on the cell surface.
**Entry** — by endocytosis or membrane fusion; a bacteriophage injects only its nucleic acid.
**Uncoating** — the capsid breaks down and the genome is released.
**Synthesis** — viral nucleic acid and proteins are made using the cell’s machinery.
**Assembly** — new virions are formed.
**Release** — by lysis of the cell or by budding.

blocks.text: **Bacteriophages** (phages) are viruses that parasitize bacteria; they were discovered in 1917 by F. d’Hérelle. A phage consists of a head (DNA inside an icosahedral capsid), a tail (a contractile sheath and an inner tube), a base plate and tail fibers (Figure 1.4). **Virulent** phages lyse the bacterium; **temperate** phages insert their DNA into the bacterial chromosome (a prophage), produce lysogeny and carry genes in transduction. Phages are used to treat intestinal infections (phage therapy) and to type bacteria.

blocks.label: Figure 1.4
blocks.caption: Structure of a bacteriophage: head (DNA inside the capsid), tail, base plate and tail fibers; on the right — phages attached to the surface of a bacterium as seen in the electron microscope (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 1.5
blocks.caption: Reproduction cycle of a bacteriophage in a bacterial cell: adsorption and injection of DNA, synthesis of phage DNA and proteins, assembly of new phages and lysis of the bacterium (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 1.10. Lytic and lysogenic cycles
head: Feature
Lytic cycle
Lysogenic cycle
rows: Lyses in 20–40 minutes, releasing up to 100–200 new phages
Survives and passes the prophage to its progeny
Phage therapy, phage typing of bacteria
Transduction; appearance of new properties (for example, the diphtheria toxin gene is carried by a prophage)

blocks.title: Table 1.11. Important viral diseases of humans
head: Disease
Agent (genome)
Main site affected
Route of transmission

parts.text: Antibiotics do not act on viruses because viruses have no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism of their own. The main measures against viral infections are **vaccination** and **antiviral drugs** acting on the stages of viral reproduction (for example, reverse transcriptase inhibitors in HIV infection).

blocks.text: Hypotheses on the origin of viruses

items: **Regressive hypothesis** — viruses arose by simplification (degeneration) of microorganisms that turned to a parasitic way of life.
**Organelle hypothesis** — viruses originated from cell organelles or autonomous genetic elements (episomes, plasmids).
**“Escaped genes” hypothesis** — viruses are fragments of normal genes that broke away from the cell and gained the ability to multiply on their own.

blocks.text: Prions and viroids

There are infectious agents even simpler than viruses. **Prions** are misfolded **protein** particles without any nucleic acid; they convert the normal prion protein into a pathological form like themselves (S. Prusiner, 1982). Prions cause fatal brain diseases such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, kuru and “mad cow disease” (spongiform encephalopathy); they resist boiling, alcohol and ultraviolet light. **Viroids** are small circular RNA molecules of 250–400 nucleotides with no protein coat; they cause disease mainly in plants (T. Diener, 1971).

parts.text: Prions are not destroyed by ordinary sterilisation regimens, so neurosurgical instruments are decontaminated by enhanced methods (prolonged autoclaving at 134 °C, alkaline solutions) or disposable instruments are used.

blocks.text: Cellular organisms are divided into two groups. **Prokaryotes** (*pro* — before, *karyon* — nucleus) are bacteria and archaea without a formed nucleus. **Eukaryotes** are the cells of fungi, plants, animals and humans that have a true nucleus.

A **bacterial cell** is 0.5–5 µm in size. It consists of a cell wall (peptidoglycan — murein), sometimes a capsule, the cytoplasmic membrane and its folds — **mesosomes**, cytoplasm, **70S ribosomes**, a **nucleoid** (a single circular DNA molecule) and **plasmids** (additional small circular DNA). Most have flagella and pili (fimbriae). By shape, cocci, rods (bacilli), vibrios and spirilla are distinguished. Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**; under favorable conditions they divide every 20–30 minutes. Under unfavorable conditions some of them form **spores**.

blocks.label: Figure 1.6
blocks.caption: Structure of a bacterial cell. Left — a model based on electron microscopy, right — an electron micrograph of the bacterium *Salmonella*: 1 — flagellum; 2 — cell wall; 3 — cytoplasmic membrane; 4 — nucleoid; 5 — plasmid; 6 — mesosome; 7 — cytoplasm; 8 — ribosomes (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Bacteria have no true sexual reproduction, but **exchange of genetic information** (parasexual processes) does occur. Through these processes, for example, antibiotic-resistance genes spread rapidly:

items: **Conjugation** — two bacteria connect by a cytoplasmic bridge (sex pilus) and transfer a plasmid or part of the chromosome.
**Transformation** — a bacterium takes up a free DNA fragment from the environment (F. Griffith, 1928, pneumococcus experiment).
**Transduction** — a DNA fragment is carried from one bacterium to another by a bacteriophage.

blocks.text: A **spore** is a resting form produced under unfavourable conditions (drought, high temperature): a thick, multilayered coat forms around the chromosome and the rest of the cell dies. Spores remain viable for decades, survive boiling and are killed only in an autoclave (120 °C, under pressure). By their relation to oxygen, bacteria are **aerobic**, **anaerobic** (the agents of tetanus and gas gangrene) or **facultatively anaerobic** (*E. coli*).

**Mycoplasmas** are the smallest free-living prokaryotes, 0.1–0.3 µm in size, without a cell wall; their shape is variable and they are not sensitive to penicillin (they cause pneumonia and urogenital infections).

head: Feature
Prokaryotes
Eukaryotes
rows: Absent; DNA lies in the cytoplasm (nucleoid)
One circular DNA without histones; plasmids
Several linear chromosomes, DNA bound to histones

parts.text: The presence of circular DNA and 70S ribosomes in mitochondria and plastids shows that they originated from ancient prokaryotes (**symbiogenesis theory**).

blocks.title: Table 1.13. Important diseases caused by bacteria
head: Disease
Agent
Route of transmission
rows: Raw milk, meat, contact with animals

blocks.text: Most scientists consider that eukaryotic cells arose from prokaryotes. Two main theories explain the origin of the eukaryotic cell and its organelles.

**Invagination theory** — internal membrane systems, the nuclear envelope, the ER and other membrane organelles formed as a result of the inward folding (invagination) of the prokaryotic cell membrane. This theory explains well why the nuclear envelope and the ER form one membrane system.

**Symbiosis (endosymbiosis) theory** (L. Margulis, 1967) — a large anaerobic cell living by fermentation engulfed aerobic bacteria by phagocytosis but did not digest them; this mutually beneficial coexistence became hereditary. The aerobic bacteria became **mitochondria** (their ancestors are purple bacteria), and photosynthetic cyanobacteria became **chloroplasts**.
Evidence supporting the symbiosis theory

items: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have **two membranes**; the composition of the inner membrane resembles the bacterial membrane.
They contain histone-free **circular DNA** and their own genes.
They have **70S ribosomes** like those of bacteria; some antibiotics that act on bacteria (chloramphenicol) also stop protein synthesis in mitochondria.
They multiply independently of the cell by **binary fission**.
Mitochondrial rRNA is close to that of purple bacteria, and chloroplast rRNA to that of cyanobacteria.

blocks.text: By comparing the nucleotide sequences of ribosomal RNA, C. Woese (1977) divided all cellular organisms into three domains — **Bacteria (eubacteria)**, **Archaea (archaebacteria)** and **Eukaryotes**. Because their genetic code is the same, the hypothesis of a common ancestor — the **progenote** — was put forward.

parts.text: Mitochondria are passed only through the mother (with the cytoplasm of the egg), so diseases caused by mitochondrial DNA mutations (for example, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy) are transmitted only from the mother to all her children. The ototoxic effect of some antibiotics acting on bacterial ribosomes (aminoglycosides) is also linked to the similarity of mitochondrial ribosomes to bacterial ones.

skills.title: Skill: examining a slide under the low-power and high-power objective

items: Place the microscope correctly and put the low-power objective into working position.
Raise the condenser, open the diaphragm and light the field of view with the mirror.
Put the slide on the stage with the coverslip facing up and fix it.
Looking from the side, lower the objective with the coarse knob to 0.5 cm.
Looking into the eyepiece, raise the tube and find a clear image.
Bring the area of interest to the center and switch the nosepiece to the ×40 objective.
Adjust the sharpness only with the fine adjustment knob.
Calculate the total magnification and draw the picture in the album.

skills.title: Skill: preparing and staining a temporary slide

items: Put 1 drop of water on a glass slide.
Separate the object (onion epidermis) and spread it in the drop.
Lower the coverslip slowly at an angle of 45°.
Remove the excess water with filter paper.
Put the stain (iodine solution) at the edge of the coverslip and draw it under with filter paper from the opposite side.
Examine the slide under the microscope and identify the parts of the cell.

skills.title: Skill: preparing and staining a human buccal epithelium smear

items: Put 1 drop of physiological saline on a slide.
Take a gentle scraping from the inner surface of the cheek with a sterile spatula and smear it into the drop.
Add 1 drop of methylene blue and wait 1–2 minutes.
Lower the coverslip at a 45° angle and remove excess fluid with filter paper.
Find a group of cells at low power and look at a single cell at high power.
Draw the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus and write the magnification; put the used spatula into disinfectant solution.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A student saw the slide well under the low-power objective, then switched the nosepiece to the high-power objective, but the image disappeared.
cases.ask: What are the possible causes, and how should they be corrected?
cases.answer: Causes: (1) the area of interest was not brought to the center of the field — the field of the high-power objective is much narrower; (2) the slide is upside down (coverslip facing down), so the high-power objective cannot reach focus; (3) there is not enough light — with the high-power objective the diaphragm must be opened and the condenser raised; (4) the objective was not turned until it clicked into place. Correction: return to the low-power objective, center the area, place the slide correctly, increase the light and adjust only with the fine knob.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A student broke the coverslip while working with the high-power objective.
cases.ask: What mistake was made?
cases.answer: The sharpness under the high-power objective was adjusted with the coarse knob: the working distance of this objective is very small (≈ 0.6 mm), so with the coarse knob the tube drops sharply and the objective hits the slide. The slide may also have been placed upside down. The correct way is to use only the fine adjustment knob with the high-power objective and to bring the objective close to the slide while looking from the side.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a light microscope slide, cells were seen whose flattened nucleus was pressed to the edge of the cell and whose cytoplasm consisted of one large cavity.
cases.ask: What cell could this be? Why is the nucleus pushed to the edge?
cases.answer: This could be a fat cell (adipocyte) or a mature plant cell with a large central vacuole. In an adipocyte almost all the cytoplasm is occupied by a single large fat droplet; in a plant cell, by the central vacuole filled with cell sap. In both cases the large inclusion or vacuole presses the nucleus and the cytoplasm against the cell wall (to the periphery).

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A student tried to look at bacteria with a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective, but they looked like tiny dots and the student could not make out their structure.
cases.ask: What magnification is needed and how can it be achieved?
cases.answer: With the ×40 objective the total magnification is 10 × 40 = 400 times — not enough for a bacterium (0,5–5 µm). Bacteria are examined with the **immersion objective** (×90): total magnification 10 × 90 = 900 times. For this, a drop of immersion oil is put on the preparation, the objective is dipped into the oil, the condenser is raised and the diaphragm fully opened, and focusing is done only with the fine screw. Because the oil has the same refractive index as glass, light rays are not scattered and the resolving power increases.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: A patient came to the doctor with symptoms of a cold (fever, blocked nose, cough) and demanded an antibiotic. Examination showed an acute respiratory viral infection.
cases.ask: Will an antibiotic be effective here? Justify your answer by the structure of viruses and bacteria.
cases.answer: No. Antibiotics act on structures typical of bacteria — the cell wall (peptidoglycan), 70S ribosomes and bacterial enzymes. Viruses have no cell wall, no ribosomes and no independent metabolism: they use the machinery of the host cell. So an antibiotic does not act on a virus; instead it disturbs the normal microflora and selects resistant bacteria. An antibiotic is prescribed only when a bacterial complication (for example, bacterial pneumonia) develops.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: In a hospital, resistance to an antibiotic appeared in one strain of *E. coli*. A few weeks later the same resistance was found in another species of intestinal bacteria (*Klebsiella*).
cases.ask: How could the resistance gene have passed from one species to another?
cases.answer: Resistance genes are often located on **plasmids**. A plasmid passes between bacteria by **conjugation** (through the sex pilus), even between different species. The gene can also pass by **transduction** (with a bacteriophage) or **transformation** (uptake of free DNA from the environment). This is why unjustified use of antibiotics leads to rapid spread of resistant strains.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Work with the microscope always starts with the **low-power objective**; with the high-power objective only the **fine adjustment knob** is used.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Structure of a virus “from inside out”: **Genome → Capsid → Envelope** (“GCE — Get Coat, Envelope”).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The 70S ribosomes and peptidoglycan wall of bacteria are the targets of antibiotics; because human cells lack them, antibiotics act selectively — and they do not act on viruses.

topics.title: Ultrastructure of eukaryotic cells. Fine structure of the cell membrane and the entry of substances into the cell

goals.text: To teach the student the chemical composition of the eukaryotic cell, the ultrastructure and functions of the general and special organelles and of inclusions, the structure of the nucleus and chromosomes, the structural model of the biological membrane and the mechanisms of transport of substances across it, and the medical importance of solutions.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the elemental and molecular composition of the cell and the role of water and organic substances;
the structure and functions of membrane-bound and non-membrane organelles;
the parts of the nucleus and the structure of chromatin and of the metaphase chromosome;
the fluid mosaic model of the membrane;
the mechanisms of passive and active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis;
the effect of hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions on the cell.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify organelles on electron micrographs and diagrams;
observe and explain plasmolysis and deplasmolysis, hemolysis and crenation of erythrocytes under the microscope;
classify chromosomes by the position of the centromere.

sections.title: 1. General structure and chemical composition of the eukaryotic cell

blocks.text: Eukaryotes include unicellular protozoa, fungi, plants and animals. A eukaryotic cell has three main parts: the **plasma membrane** (cell envelope), the **cytoplasm** (hyaloplasm, organelles and inclusions) and the **nucleus**. Human cells range in size from 7–8 µm (erythrocyte) to 150 µm (egg cell), and their shape depends on their function: spherical, flat, cuboidal, prismatic, stellate, with processes (neuron).

blocks.text: **Water** makes up 70–80 % of the cell mass. It is the universal solvent, the medium and a participant of chemical reactions (hydrolysis), a regulator of heat and a means of transporting substances. **Mineral salts** in the form of ions are needed for the membrane potential (K^+^, Na^+^, Cl^−^), buffering (HPO~4~^2−^, HCO~3~^−^), blood clotting and muscle contraction (Ca^2+^).

blocks.text: Proteins are **simple** (made only of amino acids: albumins, globulins) and **complex** (protein + non-protein part: glycoproteins, lipoproteins, nucleoproteins, chromoproteins such as hemoglobin). Disruption of the natural structure of a protein is called **denaturation**.

blocks.text: **Enzymes** are biological catalysts; they speed up a reaction by lowering its activation energy and are not used up themselves. An enzyme binds its substrate through the **active site** with high specificity according to the “lock and key” principle. Enzyme activity depends on temperature (optimum in humans ≈ 37 °C), pH (pepsin — pH 1,5–2, trypsin — pH 8) and inhibitors. Many enzymes need **cofactors** — metal ions or **coenzymes** formed from vitamins.

**ATP (adenosine triphosphate)** is the universal energy “currency” of the cell. When its **high-energy (macroergic) bonds** between phosphate residues are hydrolysed in the reaction ATP → ADP + P~i~, ≈ 40 kJ/mol of energy is released. ATP is formed mainly by oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria and partly in glycolysis; it is used for biosynthesis, active transport, muscle contraction and conduction of nerve impulses.

sections.title: 2. The plasma membrane: structure and functions

blocks.text: The cell envelope consists of the **plasmalemma** (the main part) and the **glycocalyx** on its outer surface (carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids). In plant cells there is a cellulose cell wall outside the plasmalemma.

In the electron microscope the membrane appears as a three-layered (dark–light–dark) structure 7.5–10 nm thick and is called the **universal elementary biological membrane**. According to the modern **fluid mosaic model** (S. Singer and G. Nicolson, 1972), the basis of the membrane is a **phospholipid bilayer**: the hydrophilic “heads” face outward and the hydrophobic “tails” face inward. **Integral** (fully embedded, spanning the membrane), **semi-integral** and **peripheral** (lying on the surface) proteins are arranged in the lipid layer like a mosaic and can move laterally (Figure 2.1). Cholesterol regulates the fluidity of the membrane.

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: Structure of the plasma membrane (fluid mosaic model): phospholipid bilayer, integral and peripheral proteins, cholesterol, carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins (glycocalyx) and cytoskeletal filaments (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Main functions of the plasmalemma

items: **Barrier** — separates the internal environment of the cell from the external one;
**Transport** — passes substances selectively;
**Receptor** — recognizes hormones, mediators and antigens (glycocalyx);
**Intercellular communication** — forms contacts (desmosomes, tight and gap junctions);
**Enzymatic** — membrane-bound enzymes (for example, in the intestinal epithelium);
**Electrogenic** — creates the membrane potential and conducts the nerve impulse.

blocks.text: Intercellular junctions

In multicellular organisms cells are joined by special junctions and form tissues. The free surface of epithelial cells carries **microvilli** (which increase the absorptive surface) and **cilia**, while the lateral surfaces carry the following junctions:

parts.text: When autoantibodies against desmosome proteins form, epidermal cells separate from each other and blisters appear on the skin (**pemphigus vulgaris**). Loss of intercellular junctions helps tumour cells to detach and spread to other organs (**metastasis**).

sections.title: 3. Transport of substances across the membrane

blocks.text: The **sodium-potassium pump** (Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase) removes 3 Na^+^ ions from the cell and brings 2 K^+^ ions into it for each ATP molecule (Figure 2.2). As a result there is much K^+^ inside the cell and much Na^+^ outside; this is the basis of the **resting membrane potential**, of maintaining cell volume and of secondary active transport. Up to one third of the energy used by the body goes into the work of this pump.

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: Active transport: the sodium-potassium pump. Using the energy of ATP, Na^+^ ions are pumped out of the cell and K^+^ ions into the cell (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Ion channels** are pores formed by transmembrane proteins that selectively let certain ions through. They are **voltage-gated** (Na^+^, K^+^, Ca^2+^ channels in nerve and muscle cells) or **ligand-gated** (opening when a mediator binds — the acetylcholine receptor). Water molecules pass slowly through the lipid layer; most water passes quickly through special protein channels — **aquaporins** (in the kidney tubules under the action of antidiuretic hormone).

Because of the Na^+^/K^+^ pump and channels, the inside of the cell is negatively charged relative to the outside — the **resting membrane potential** (≈ −70 mV in neurons) is formed. This potential underlies the nerve impulse, muscle contraction and secondary active transport (absorption of glucose and amino acids together with Na^+^ by **symport**).

parts.text: Cardiac glycosides (digoxin) partly block the Na^+^/K^+^ pump: Na^+^ and, through it, Ca^2+^ rise in myocardial cells and the heart contracts more strongly; an overdose causes arrhythmia. A mutation of the gene for the chloride channel protein (CFTR) thickens the secretions of glands — **cystic fibrosis**.

parts.text: Solutions given intravenously are mainly **isotonic** (0.9 % NaCl, 5 % glucose). **Hypertonic** solutions (10 % NaCl) are used to clean purulent wounds (they draw water from the wound) and magnesium sulfate as a laxative, while **hypotonic** solutions are used with caution in some states of dehydration.

blocks.text: Types of endocytosis

items: **Phagocytosis** (“cell eating”) — large particles (bacteria, cell debris) are engulfed by pseudopodia and a phagosome forms; typical of neutrophils and macrophages (I.I. Mechnikov, 1882).
**Pinocytosis** (“cell drinking”) — fluid and dissolved substances are taken up in small vesicles.

**Receptor-mediated endocytosis** — the substance binds to a specific membrane receptor, then a pit and vesicle coated with the protein **clathrin** form (for example, uptake of low-density lipoproteins — cholesterol, and of transferrin — iron).
**Transcytosis** — a substance is taken up on one side of the cell and released on the other (capillary endothelium, passage of maternal antibodies across the placenta).

parts.text: In a hereditary defect of the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor gene, cholesterol is not taken up by cells and accumulates in the blood — **familial hypercholesterolaemia** (autosomal dominant): atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction develop at a young age.

blocks.text: The **cytoplasm** is the part of the cell between the plasmalemma and the nucleus. It consists of the **hyaloplasm** (cytosol — a colloidal solution rich in proteins, enzymes and ions), **organelles** (permanent structures with a definite function) and **inclusions** (temporary structures). Organelles are **general** (in all cells) and **special** (in some specialized cells); general organelles are in turn divided into membrane-bound and non-membrane groups.

blocks.label: Figure 2.3
blocks.caption: Endoplasmic reticulum: rough (ribosome-studded) and smooth ER connected with the nuclear envelope (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 2.4

blocks.text: The path of a secretory protein in the cell

items: Protein synthesis begins on a free ribosome; a signal sequence attaches the ribosome to the membrane of the **rough ER**.
The polypeptide passes into the ER lumen, where it folds and glycosylation begins.
Transport vesicles carry the protein to the **cis face of the Golgi complex**.
In the Golgi cisternae the protein is modified (its carbohydrate part is completed, it is phosphorylated) and sorted.
Secretory granules, lysosomes or membrane vesicles bud off from the **trans face**.
The secretory granule fuses with the plasmalemma and releases its product by **exocytosis** (for example, insulin and enzymes in the pancreas).

blocks.text: Types of lysosomes

items: **Primary lysosomes** — newly budded vesicles from the Golgi complex with inactive enzymes.
**Secondary lysosomes (phagolysosomes)** — formed by fusion of a primary lysosome with a phagosome or pinocytic vesicle; digestion takes place here.
**Autophagosomes** — digest the cell's own worn-out organelles (autophagy).
**Residual bodies** — vesicles holding undigested remnants; lipofuscin (“ageing pigment”) accumulates in them.

blocks.text: If the lysosome membrane ruptures, the enzymes leak into the cytoplasm and digest the cell itself (**autolysis**); this is why lysosomes are also called the “suicide bags of the cell”. **Peroxisomes** use the enzyme catalase to break toxic hydrogen peroxide (H~2~O~2~) down into water and oxygen and oxidise very-long-chain fatty acids; they are especially numerous in liver and kidney cells.

blocks.label: Figure 2.5
blocks.caption: Structure of the mitochondrion: electron micrograph (top) and diagram — outer and inner membranes, cristae, matrix and intermembrane space (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The **mitochondrion** is a double-membrane organelle; its outer membrane is smooth, and the inner membrane forms **cristae**. The cristae carry the respiratory-chain enzymes and the **ATP synthase** complex (“mushroom-shaped” bodies). The inner space — the **matrix** — contains the Krebs-cycle enzymes, circular mitochondrial DNA (37 genes in humans) and 70S ribosomes. Cells with high energy needs (cardiomyocytes, the midpiece of the sperm, kidney tubule epithelium) have many mitochondria with dense cristae.

parts.text: In hereditary deficiency of lysosomal enzymes, undigested substances accumulate in lysosomes — **lysosomal storage diseases** (Gaucher, Tay-Sachs, glycogenosis type II). Mitochondria are passed on only through the mother, so mutations of mitochondrial DNA are inherited only from the mother.

blocks.label: Figure 2.6
blocks.caption: Structure of the ribosome: the large and small subunits and their union into a complete ribosome (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Ribosomal subunits are assembled from rRNA and proteins in the **nucleolus** and leave for the cytoplasm through the nuclear pores. They join only during protein synthesis; several ribosomes attached to one mRNA are called a **polyribosome (polysome)**. **Free ribosomes** make proteins for the cell itself (hyaloplasm proteins), while **ribosomes bound to the ER** make export, membrane and lysosomal proteins. Because the 70S ribosomes of bacteria differ from the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes, many antibiotics (tetracycline, erythromycin, streptomycin) stop only bacterial protein synthesis.

blocks.label: Figure 2.7
blocks.caption: The cell centre (centrosome): two centrioles, their structure of microtubules (9 triplets) and a cross-section on an electron micrograph (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The **cytoskeleton** is a network of protein filaments in the cytoplasm; it keeps the shape of the cell, positions organelles and provides movement of the cell and within it. **Microtubules** are built of tubulin dimers and grow from the centrosome; the “motor” proteins **kinesin** and **dynein** carry vesicles along them (for example, in the axon of a neuron). **Microfilaments** (actin) together with myosin form cell contraction, the support of microvilli and the contractile ring in cytokinesis. **Intermediate filaments** are the strongest filaments, and each tissue has its own protein: keratin in epithelium, vimentin in connective tissue, desmin in muscle, neurofilaments in neurons and lamins under the nucleus.

parts.text: **Colchicine** stops tubulin polymerisation and destroys the spindle — mitosis is arrested in metaphase; that is why it is used in karyotyping to “freeze” chromosomes in metaphase. **Vincristine, vinblastine** (which destroy the spindle) and **paclitaxel** (which over-stabilises microtubules) work on the same principle and are used as anticancer drugs.

blocks.text: **Special organelles:** cilia and flagella (axoneme — 9 peripheral pairs + 2 central microtubules, “9 + 2”), myofibrils (contraction in muscle cells), neurofibrils (in neurons), tonofibrils (in epithelium), microvilli (increase the absorptive surface of the intestinal epithelium).

parts.text: In a hereditary defect of the ciliary protein dynein (**Kartagener syndrome**) clearance of the airways is impaired (chronic bronchitis, sinusitis), spermatozoa are immotile (infertility), and reversed position of the organs is often seen.

blocks.text: **Inclusions** are structures that appear and disappear as a result of cell activity: **trophic** (glycogen, fat droplets, protein granules), **secretory** (secretory granules), **excretory** (substances to be removed), **pigment** (melanin, hemoglobin, lipofuscin — the “aging pigment”).

The **nucleus** is the center that stores hereditary information and controls the activity of the cell. The interphase nucleus consists of (Figure 2.8): the **nuclear envelope** (karyolemma — two membranes, the perinuclear space and **nuclear pores**; the outer membrane continues into the ER), the **karyoplasm** (nuclear sap), **chromatin** and the **nucleolus** (where rRNA is synthesized and ribosomal subunits are assembled). Cells without a nucleus (mature erythrocytes) do not divide and do not live long.

blocks.label: Figure 2.8
blocks.caption: Structure of the nucleus: nuclear envelope and pores, chromatin, nucleolus, rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Chromatin** is a complex of DNA and histone proteins. Its densely staining, inactive part is called **heterochromatin**, and its lightly staining, active (transcribed) part — **euchromatin**. DNA winds around histones to form **nucleosomes** and then coils step by step, turning into compact **chromosomes** during mitosis.

**Nuclear pores** are complex protein assemblies in the nuclear envelope (diameter ≈ 120 nm); through them mRNA, tRNA and ribosomal subunits leave for the cytoplasm, while histones, polymerases and other proteins enter the nucleus. Active cells have many pores. Under the inner nuclear membrane lies the **lamina** — a network of lamin proteins that keeps the shape of the nucleus and anchors chromatin.

blocks.label: Figure 2.9
blocks.caption: Levels of supercoiling of the DNA molecule: DNA double helix → nucleosomes wound on histones → chromatin fibres → metaphase chromosome (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 2.11. Levels of chromatin coiling (compaction)
head: Level
Diameter
Shortening relative to DNA

blocks.text: A **nucleosome** is a protein core of 8 histone molecules (2 each of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4) with a 146 base-pair stretch of DNA wound ≈ 1,7 times around it. The **linker DNA** between nucleosomes (15–100 base pairs) binds histone H1, which packs the nucleosomes even more tightly. **Constitutive heterochromatin** (around centromeres and telomeres) is always condensed in all cells, while **facultative heterochromatin** condenses only in some cells — for example, in the somatic cells of women one X chromosome becomes the **Barr body** (sex chromatin).

A **metaphase chromosome** consists of two **chromatids** joined at the primary constriction — the **centromere**. The centromere divides the chromosome into two **arms**; the ends of the arms are **telomeres**. Some chromosomes have a secondary constriction and a **satellite**.

blocks.text: Rules of chromosomes

items: **Constancy of number** — the number of chromosomes in the somatic cells of each species is constant (2n = 46 in humans).
**Pairing** — in somatic cells chromosomes form homologous pairs (23 pairs in humans).
**Individuality** — each pair differs from the others in size, shape and gene content.
**Continuity** — each chromosome arises only from a chromosome by replication.

blocks.text: The **karyotype** is the set of features of the diploid chromosome complement typical of a species: number, size and shape. The human karyotype consists of 44 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes: 46,XX in women and 46,XY in men. A graphic representation of the karyotype (homologous pairs ordered by size and centromere position) is called an **idiogram**. Chromosome numbers differ between species: 2n = 8 in Drosophila, 2n = 14 in the pea, 2n = 48 in the chimpanzee and 2n = 78 in the dog.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Blood taken from a patient was placed in a solution. In the slide prepared from it, the blood cells had a shrunken (crenated) shape.
cases.ask: Explain the situation.
cases.answer: The blood was placed in a hypertonic solution (NaCl concentration above 0.9 %). According to the law of osmosis, water moves from the less concentrated medium (inside the erythrocyte) to the more concentrated medium (the outer solution); the cell volume decreases and it shrinks — plasmolysis (in erythrocytes — crenation). That is why large volumes of hypertonic solutions must not be given intravenously.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Blood taken from a patient was placed in a solution. In the slide, the blood cells were swollen and burst.
cases.ask: Explain the situation.
cases.answer: The blood was placed in a hypotonic solution (for example, distilled water). Water enters the erythrocyte, the cell swells, the membrane stretches and bursts, and hemoglobin escapes — hemolysis. Therefore isotonic (0.9 %) NaCl, not distilled water, is used to dilute drug solutions.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: An electron micrograph of liver cells showed marked enlargement and increase of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. The patient had been taking barbiturates for a long time.
cases.ask: What is this change related to?
cases.answer: The enzymes that detoxify drugs and poisons (the cytochrome P450 system) are located in the membranes of the smooth ER. With long-term intake of barbiturates these enzymes are induced, and the smooth ER that contains them enlarges as well. As a result drugs are broken down faster — tolerance to the drug develops.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A 6-month-old child is behind in motor development and startles excessively at sounds. A “cherry-red spot” is found on the retina. The parents are healthy and come from an Ashkenazi Jewish community.
cases.ask: Which organelle is dysfunctional and how is the disease inherited?
cases.answer: This is **Tay–Sachs disease** — a lysosomal storage disease. The enzyme **hexosaminidase A** is missing in lysosomes, so GM~2~ ganglioside is not broken down, accumulates in the lysosomes of neurons and kills them. The disease is inherited as **autosomal recessive**: the healthy parents are heterozygous carriers (Aa × Aa), and each child has a 25 % chance of being affected. Carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis are done in genetic counselling.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: In a cytogenetics laboratory, colchicine was added to a lymphocyte culture at the end of incubation for karyotyping.
cases.ask: Why is colchicine added and which cell structure does it act on?
cases.answer: Colchicine stops the formation of **microtubules** (tubulin polymerisation) and destroys the **spindle**. As a result the chromatids cannot separate to the poles and cells are arrested in **metaphase**. In metaphase the chromosomes are most coiled, short and thick, so it is easy to count them and determine their shape and centromere position — this is why the karyotype is studied on the metaphase plate.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: In a patient treated for heart failure, an overdose of digoxin caused a disturbance of heart rhythm.
cases.ask: Which membrane transport system does digoxin act on? How do you explain the rhythm disturbance?
cases.answer: Digoxin inhibits **Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase** (the sodium-potassium pump). Normally the pump uses 1 ATP to move 3 Na^+^ out and 2 K^+^ in. When the pump is partly blocked, Na^+^ rises inside the cell, Na^+^/Ca^2+^ exchange slows and Ca^2+^ increases in the cell — the heart contracts more strongly (therapeutic effect). With an overdose, Ca^2+^ and ion balance are disturbed too much, the membrane potential changes, and extrasystoles and other arrhythmias appear.

topics.title: The mitotic and life cycle of cells. Cell proliferation. Meiotic division of the cell. Pathology of mitosis and meiosis

goals.text: To teach the student the life cycle and mitotic cycle of the cell, the periods of interphase, the changes in chromosome set and DNA content in the phases of mitosis and meiosis, other forms of division, the types of asexual and sexual reproduction and the medical consequences of division errors.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of life cycle and mitotic cycle, the periods of interphase (G~1~, S, G~2~) and the checkpoints;
the groups of tissues according to the rate of cell renewal;
the phases of mitosis and the chromosome set (n) and DNA content (c) in them;
meiotic divisions I and II and the importance of crossing over and reduction;
the concepts of amitosis, endomitosis and polyteny;
the forms of asexual and sexual reproduction.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the phases of mitosis on a slide of onion root tip;
write the genetic formula of the cell (n, c) for each phase;
explain the link between errors of meiosis and chromosomal diseases.

sections.title: 1. The life cycle and mitotic cycle of the cell

blocks.text: The **life cycle** is the period from the moment a cell appears by division until it divides itself or dies. It includes growth, differentiation, performance of a specialized function and aging. The **mitotic (cell) cycle** is the period of preparation for division (interphase) and of division (mitosis); it occurs only in dividing cells (Figure 3.1).

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: Stages of the cell cycle: interphase (G~1~ — growth, S — DNA replication, G~2~ — preparation for division) and mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) followed by cytokinesis (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 3.1. Periods of interphase
head: Period
Main processes
Genetic formula
rows: The cell grows; RNA, proteins and organelles are synthesized; enzymes for the S period accumulate
DNA replication, synthesis of histones; each chromosome becomes two-chromatid; centrioles duplicate
Tubulin for the spindle and ATP accumulate; DNA errors are checked
The cell leaves the cycle and performs a specialized function

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Replication of a chromosome: in the S period a one-chromatid chromosome is doubled and becomes a duplicated chromosome of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere; at division they separate again (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **The G~0~ period (resting period)** is the state of cells that have left the mitotic cycle, do not divide but perform their function. For example, liver cells are normally in G~0~, but if part of the liver is removed they return to the cycle and divide. Neurons and cardiomyocytes, however, hardly ever leave G~0~. In human cells the mitotic cycle lasts on average 18–24 hours; of this, mitosis takes ≈ 1 hour and the rest is interphase.

Interphase may be **autosynthetic** (the cell prepares to divide) or **heterosynthetic** (the cell makes products for the organism and performs a specialized task). The cycle is controlled at **checkpoints** (G~1~/S, G~2~/M and the metaphase checkpoint) through cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases; if DNA is damaged, the **p53** protein stops the cycle or starts apoptosis.

blocks.title: Table 3.2. Groups of tissues according to the rate of cell renewal
head: Group
Feature
Examples
rows: Do not divide or divide very rarely after birth
Usually in G~0~; return to division after injury
Cells of the liver, kidney, salivary glands
Cells constantly die and are replaced from stem cells
Skin and intestinal epithelium, blood cells, spermatogenic epithelium

blocks.text: **Mitosis** (indirect division) is the main way somatic cells divide; it produces two daughter cells genetically identical to the mother cell. Mitosis consists of four phases and is followed by division of the cytoplasm — **cytokinesis**.

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Phases of mitosis
head: Phase
Processes
Genetic formula
rows: Chromosomes coil and become visible; the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear; centrioles move to the poles, the spindle forms
Spindle fibers attach to the kinetochores, chromosomes move toward the equator
Chromosomes lie in the equatorial plane and form the **metaphase plate**; they are most condensed — the best time to study the karyotype
Centromeres divide, chromatids (daughter chromosomes) are pulled to opposite poles
Chromosomes uncoil at the poles, the nuclear envelope and nucleolus re-form; cytokinesis

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Formation of the spindle in metaphase: centrioles at the poles, astral rays and spindle fibers radiating from them, and chromosomes at the equator (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In an animal cell cytokinesis proceeds by a **cleavage furrow** (contraction of an actin-myosin ring), and in a plant cell by formation of a **phragmoplast** and a cell plate in the middle of the cell. Higher plants have no centrioles, but a spindle still forms (without astral rays — “anastral” mitosis).

parts.text: Order of the phases: **“PMAT — Please Make A Team”**: chromosomes **P**ack (coil), **M**eet in the middle, **A**part they go, **T**wo nuclei form.

blocks.text: Biological and medical importance of mitosis

items: Ensures equal distribution of hereditary information to daughter cells and constancy of the karyotype;
Underlies growth of the organism and renewal and regeneration of tissues;
Is the cytological basis of asexual reproduction.
Failure of mitotic control leads to **tumors**; many anticancer drugs (colchicine, vincristine, taxanes) stop mitosis by acting on the spindle.

sections.title: 3. Other forms of division and pathology of mitosis

blocks.title: Table 3.4. Forms of division that differ from mitosis
head: Form
Essence
Where it occurs
rows: The nucleus divides by constriction, no chromosomes or spindle form; hereditary material is divided unequally
Aging and inflamed tissues, tumors, the macronucleus of ciliates
Chromosomes double without breakdown of the nuclear envelope, no cytokinesis — a **polyploid** cell
Chromatids replicate many times but do not separate — **giant (polytene) chromosomes**

blocks.label: Figure 3.4
blocks.caption: Amitosis: successive stages (1–5) of direct division of the nucleus by constriction; no chromosomes or spindle are formed (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Pathology of mitosis** includes unequal separation of chromosomes to the poles (**nondisjunction**), tripolar or multipolar mitoses, lagging of chromosomes at the equator, and loss of the spindle under colchicine (**C-mitosis**). In somatic cells such errors cause **mosaicism** (two or more cell lines with different karyotypes in one organism) and **aneuploidy** in tumor cells.

blocks.title: Table 3.5. Types of mitotic pathology
head: Group
Forms
rows: Arrest of the cell in prophase; disturbed coiling and uncoiling; fragmentation of chromosomes; “bridges” between chromosomes in anaphase; premature separation of chromatids; damage to the kinetochore
Prolonged metaphase; disordered arrangement of chromosomes at the equator; three-group, hollow and multipolar metaphase; asymmetric and monocentric mitoses; K-mitosis (colchicine mitosis)
Premature division; delay or complete absence of cytotomy (multinucleate, polyploid cells)

blocks.title: Table 3.6. Differences between apoptosis and necrosis
head: Feature
Apoptosis
Necrosis
rows: Physiological programme or DNA damage (p53 and caspases are activated)
Strong injurious factor: ischaemia, burns, poison
A group of cells, an area of tissue
Chromatin condensation, DNA breaks into fragments
Apoptotic bodies are engulfed by macrophages without inflammation
Cell contents leak out and inflammation develops

parts.text: **Apoptosis** is programmed cell death: the cell shrinks, chromatin condenses and fragments, the cell breaks into apoptotic bodies and is phagocytosed without inflammation. It is important in embryogenesis (removal of the tissue between the fingers) and in eliminating damaged and tumor cells; its weakening leads to tumors and its excess to neurodegenerative diseases.

blocks.text: **Proliferation** is the multiplication of cells by division; it underlies growth, tissue renewal and regeneration. In a multicellular organism cells divide only when there is a “permission” signal: proliferation is controlled by the balance of **stimulators** and **inhibitors**.

blocks.title: Table 3.7. Factors regulating proliferation
head: Stimulators
Inhibitors
rows: Growth factors: epidermal (EGF), platelet-derived (PDGF), fibroblast growth factor, erythropoietin
Chalones — substances produced by a tissue itself that stop its division
Hormones: growth hormone, insulin, oestrogens (uterine endometrium)
Glucocorticoids, tumour necrosis factor, transforming growth factor β (TGF-β)
Injury to and partial removal of a tissue (liver regeneration)
**Contact inhibition** — cells stop dividing once they touch each other and form a monolayer
Activity of cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDK)
Tumour-suppressor proteins: p53, retinoblastoma protein (Rb), p21

blocks.text: Genes for proteins that stimulate division are called **proto-oncogenes**. If they become permanently active **oncogenes** through mutation, chromosome rearrangement or viral action, the cell divides uncontrollably. When both alleles of the division-stopping **tumour-suppressor genes** (p53 — the “guardian of the genome”, Rb) are disabled, a tumour develops. Therefore a **tumour** is a disease of the genes that control the cell cycle.

**Telomeres and the Hayflick limit.** At each replication the chromosome ends (telomeres made of TTAGGG repeats) shorten a little. Therefore normal somatic cells in culture divide only 50–60 times (the **Hayflick limit**, 1961) and then age. In germ, stem and tumour cells the enzyme **telomerase** restores telomeres, so they can divide without limit.

blocks.title: Table 3.8. Potency of stem cells
head: Type
What cells it can form
Example
rows: The whole organism and extra-embryonic organs (placenta)
All cells of the three germ layers
Inner cell mass of the blastocyst (embryonic stem cells)
Several cell types of one tissue system
Haematopoietic stem cell of the bone marrow
Spermatogonia, basal cells of the epidermis

parts.text: Rapidly renewing tissues (bone marrow, intestinal epithelium, hair follicles, spermatogenic epithelium) are the most sensitive to **radiation and cytostatic drugs**, which act on dividing cells. This is why chemotherapy causes anaemia, leucopenia, diarrhoea, hair loss and infertility. Transplantation of bone-marrow stem cells is used to treat leukaemias.

blocks.text: **Meiosis** is the division that occurs during maturation of sex cells (gametes) and halves the number of chromosomes. After a single DNA replication there are **two divisions** in a row (meiosis I and meiosis II), and four haploid (n) cells are formed from one diploid (2n) cell (Figure 3.5).

blocks.label: Figure 3.5
blocks.caption: Stages of meiotic division: meiosis I (prophase I, metaphase I, anaphase I, telophase I) and meiosis II (prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II, telophase II) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Meiosis I — the reductional division

blocks.title: Table 3.9. Stages of prophase I
head: Stage
Process
rows: Chromosomes appear as thin long threads
Chromosomes thicken; segments are exchanged between chromatids of homologous chromosomes — **crossing over**
Homologs begin to move apart, chiasmata (crossing points) become visible; human oocytes stop at this stage (dictyotene) for years
Chromosomes are maximally condensed, the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear

items: **Metaphase I** — bivalents lie at the equator (the homologs of each pair face opposite poles) — 2n4c.

**Anaphase I** — not chromatids but **whole homologous chromosomes** (each with two chromatids) are pulled to the poles; the separation of each pair is independent of the other pairs — 1n2c at each pole.
**Telophase I** — two cells form in which the chromosome number is haploid but each chromosome has two chromatids (n2c).

blocks.text: **Interkinesis** is the short period between meiosis I and II; there is **no** DNA replication in it.
Meiosis II — the equational division

Meiosis II proceeds like mitosis: in metaphase II chromosomes lie at the equator, in anaphase II centromeres divide and chromatids move to the poles. As a result four haploid cells (1n1c) are formed. It differs from mitosis in that the chromosome number is haploid and there is no DNA synthesis before the division.

blocks.title: Table 3.10. Comparison of mitosis and meiosis
head: Feature
Mitosis
Meiosis
rows: Different from each other and from the mother cell
Constancy of chromosome number over generations, combinative variability

parts.text: Meiosis has **three sources** of genetic diversity: (1) crossing over; (2) independent assortment of homologous pairs in metaphase I — more than 2^23^ combinations in humans; (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilization. That is why brothers and sisters (except identical twins) are never completely alike.

**Nondisjunction** of chromosomes in meiosis produces disomic (n + 1) and nullisomic (n − 1) gametes. When they fuse with a normal gamete, **trisomy** (Down — 47,XX,+21; Klinefelter — 47,XXY) or **monosomy** (Shereshevsky-Turner — 45,X) develops. The risk of nondisjunction rises with maternal age because oocytes remain arrested in diplotene for many years.

blocks.text: Biological significance of meiosis

items: Halves the chromosome number in gametes — fertilisation restores the diploid set and the karyotype stays constant over generations.
Is a source of **combinative variability** through crossing over and independent assortment of homologues.
Forms the cytological basis of Mendel's laws (segregation and independent assortment).
Errors of meiosis (non-disjunction) are the main cause of chromosomal diseases.

blocks.title: Table 3.11. Number of chromosomes and amount of DNA at the stages of human meiosis
head: Stage
Formula
Number of chromosomes
Number of chromatids
rows: Prophase I, metaphase I (after DNA replication)

blocks.text: **Asexual reproduction** involves one parent, takes place without gametes and is based on mitosis; the offspring is a genetic copy (**clone**) of the parent. In **sexual reproduction** gametes from two parents fuse; the genetic diversity of the offspring increases, which ensures adaptation to a changing environment.

blocks.title: Table 3.12. Forms of reproduction
head: Form
Types
Examples
rows: Simple binary fission, multiple fission (schizogony), budding, sporulation
Vegetative reproduction (fragmentation, budding), by spores, polyembryony
Hydra, tapeworm larval stage (echinococcus), identical twins
Conjugation (exchange of genetic information), copulation (fusion of gametes)
Fertilization with gametes; parthenogenesis (development from an unfertilized egg), hermaphroditism

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The genetic material of a group of cells was studied and found to be 2n2c. After division, some cells had a DNA content of 2c and others 1c.
cases.ask: By what method did these cells divide?
cases.answer: Formation of 2c daughter cells is typical of mitosis: a 2n2c cell becomes 2n4c in the S period and after mitosis gives two 2n2c cells. Cells with 1c are formed after the second division of meiosis (1n1c). Thus some of the cells in the group divided by mitosis and others by meiosis (gametogenesis).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Under the action of a harmful factor, spindle fibers did not form in a cell.
cases.ask: Which processes are disturbed, and what is the result?
cases.answer: Without spindle fibers, chromosomes cannot gather on the metaphase plate and are not distributed to the poles in anaphase; mitosis stops in metaphase (C-mitosis). If the cell then re-forms the nuclear envelope, a polyploid (4n) cell with a doubled chromosome number appears. This principle is used with colchicine in karyotype analysis and to obtain polyploid plants, and with vincristine to treat tumors.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Sex cells were found to contain more chromosomes than normal.
cases.ask: Which periods of meiosis may have been disturbed, and what is the consequence?
cases.answer: The cause is nondisjunction of a pair of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I (n + 1 and n − 1 gametes) or nondisjunction of sister chromatids in anaphase II. When a disomic (n + 1) gamete fuses with a normal gamete, trisomy (47 chromosomes) results: for pair 21 — Down syndrome, XXY — Klinefelter syndrome. A nullisomic gamete gives monosomy (45,X — Shereshevsky-Turner syndrome).

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: On an onion root-tip preparation 500 cells were counted: 440 in interphase, 30 in prophase, 10 in metaphase, 8 in anaphase and 12 in telophase.
cases.ask: Calculate the mitotic index. Which phase lasts the longest?
cases.answer: Cells in mitosis: 30 + 10 + 8 + 12 = 60. Mitotic index = 60 / 500 = 0,12 (or 12 %, that is 120 ‰). The duration of a phase is proportional to the number of cells in it: of the phases of mitosis the longest is **prophase** (30 cells) and the shortest is **anaphase** (8). Over the whole cycle the longest period is **interphase** (440 cells, 88 %).

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: A patient receiving chemotherapy for leukaemia developed hair loss, mouth ulcers, diarrhoea and a fall in white blood cells.
cases.ask: Why are exactly these tissues damaged?
cases.answer: Cytostatic drugs act on dividing cells (on DNA synthesis or the spindle). They damage not only tumour cells but also **renewing cell populations**: hair follicles, mouth and intestinal epithelium and the blood-forming cells of the bone marrow. Static populations such as neurons and cardiomyocytes are hardly damaged. Breaks between treatment courses let the stem cells recover.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A child with retinoblastoma (a tumour of the retina) developed tumours in both eyes at an early age. The father also had this disease in childhood.
cases.ask: Explain this from the point of view of tumour-suppressor genes.
cases.answer: **RB1** is a tumour-suppressor gene: its protein (Rb) holds back the passage of the cell from G~1~ to S. For a tumour to develop, **both alleles** of the gene must be disabled (A. Knudson's “two-hit” hypothesis). In the hereditary form the child receives one mutant allele from the father (the first “hit” is present in all cells); if the second allele is damaged by chance in one retinal cell, a tumour develops — this is why the tumour is early, multifocal and bilateral. The predisposition is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

Exchange of segments between homologous chromatids in pachytene

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Mitosis — **one division, two identical diploid cells**; meiosis — **two divisions, four different haploid cells**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Stages of prophase I: **“Lazy Zebras Pace Down Daily”** — Leptotene, Zygotene (pairing), Pachytene (crossing over), Diplotene, Diakinesis.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Nondisjunction in meiosis is the main cause of trisomies and monosomies (Down, Klinefelter, Turner); failure of mitotic control leads to tumors.

goals.text: To teach the student the basic concepts and methods of genetics, G. Mendel’s laws and their cytological basis, the types of interaction of allelic and non-allelic genes, the inheritance of blood groups in humans and the method of solving genetic problems.
By the end of the class the student should know:

Mendel’s three laws and the hypothesis of gamete purity;
