blocks.text: **Genetics** is the science of the laws of heredity and variability of organisms. Its founder is the Czech scientist **G. Mendel**, who announced the laws of inheritance in 1865 on the basis of his experiments with peas. These laws were rediscovered in 1900 by H. de Vries, C. Correns and E. Tschermak; the term “genetics” was introduced by W. Bateson in 1906. Later stages: T. Morgan’s chromosome theory, the DNA model of J. Watson and F. Crick (1953), the discovery of the genetic code, genetic engineering and the reading of the human genome (2003).

blocks.title: Table 4.1. Basic terms of genetics
head: Term
Definition
rows: A segment of DNA that determines the structure of a particular protein or RNA; the unit of heredity
The position of a gene on a chromosome
Genes located at the same loci of homologous chromosomes and determining different states of one trait (A and a)
A trait that appears (prevails) in the heterozygote — written with a capital letter (A)
A trait that appears only in the homozygote (aa) — written with a small letter
An organism with identical alleles (AA or aa); forms one kind of gamete
An organism with different alleles (Aa); forms two kinds of gametes
The sum of the genes of an organism
The sum of all traits formed under the influence of the genotype and environment
Offspring obtained by crossing genetically different parents

blocks.text: **Rules of notation:** P — parents, ♀ — female, ♂ — male, × — cross, G — gametes, F~1~, F~2~ — first and second generation hybrids. The female organism is written first. In human genetics the marriage of parents is also shown with “×”.

The main conditions of the **hybridological method** used by Mendel: pure lines (homozygotes) were chosen, clearly contrasting alternative traits were observed, and each generation was analyzed separately and quantitatively (statistically).

sections.title: 2. Monohybrid cross. Mendel’s first and second laws

blocks.text: A **monohybrid cross** is a cross of organisms that differ in one pair of alternative traits. When Mendel crossed yellow-seeded (AA) and green-seeded (aa) peas, all plants in F~1~ had yellow seeds (Aa); when F~1~ plants were crossed with each other, yellow and green seeds appeared in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio (Figure 4.1).

blocks.title: Table 4.2. Pea traits studied in Mendel's experiments and the F~2~ results
head: Trait
Dominant
Recessive
Numbers in F~2~ (ratio)

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: Mendel’s first and second laws shown in a Punnett square: crossing yellow (AA) and green (aa) peas, uniformity of F~1~ and segregation in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

items: **Mendel’s first law (law of uniformity of first-generation hybrids):** when two homozygous organisms differing in alternative traits are crossed, F~1~ hybrids are uniform in genotype and phenotype.

**Mendel’s second law (law of segregation):** when F~1~ heterozygotes are crossed with each other, traits segregate in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio by phenotype and 1 : 2 : 1 by genotype (1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa).

blocks.text: **Hypothesis of gamete purity:** in a hybrid organism allelic genes do not blend; each gamete receives **only one allele** of the pair. Its **cytological basis** is the separation of homologous chromosomes (and the alleles on them) into different gametes in anaphase I of meiosis.

A **test cross** is crossing an organism with a dominant phenotype with a recessive homozygote (aa) to determine its genotype. If all offspring show the dominant trait, the organism tested is homozygous (AA); if segregation in a 1 : 1 ratio occurs, it is heterozygous (Aa).

parts.text: Problem-solving algorithm: (1) denote the traits with letters; (2) write the genotypes of the parents; (3) determine the gametes of each (each gamete carries one allele of each gene); (4) draw the Punnett square; (5) calculate the genotype and phenotype ratio or the probability (%).

blocks.text: Probability rules in genetics problems

items: **Product rule** — the probability that two independent events occur together equals the product of their probabilities. For example, from the marriage Aa × Aa the probability that **two** children are both aa is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

**Sum rule** — the probability that one of mutually exclusive events occurs equals the sum of their probabilities. For example, from Aa × Aa the probability of a child with the dominant phenotype is AA (1/4) + Aa (2/4) = 3/4.
Each new pregnancy is an **independent event**: whether previous children were affected or healthy does not change the probability for the next child.
A healthy person with the dominant phenotype who has an affected (recessive) sibling is heterozygous with probability **2/3** (he cannot be aa; of the remaining AA : 2 Aa).

blocks.text: Lethal genes and distortion of the segregation ratio

Segregation in F~2~ is not always 3 : 1. Some genes in the homozygous state kill the organism during embryonic life or soon after birth — they are called **lethal genes**. For example, when black-brown foxes are crossed together, the offspring segregate not 3 : 1 but **2 : 1**, because dominant homozygotes (AA) die as embryos and only Aa and aa are born. A similar situation is seen in **Karakul sheep** (AA lambs for the brown colour gene die soon because their gastrointestinal tract is underdeveloped) and in yellow mice.

In humans the **brachydactyly** (short fingers) gene shows short fingers in heterozygotes, while homozygous embryos die. Homozygotes for the **sickle-cell anaemia** gene (HbS HbS) die early from severe anaemia, while heterozygotes are almost healthy and **resistant to malaria**. That is why the HbS and **thalassaemia** genes are common in regions where malaria is widespread (Africa, the Mediterranean) — an example of **balanced polymorphism**.

**Multiple allelism** is the presence of more than two alleles at one locus in a population, though each organism carries only two of them. In humans the **ABO blood groups** are determined by the alleles I^0^, I^A^ and I^B^: I^A^ and I^B^ are dominant over I^0^ and codominant with each other.

blocks.title: Table 4.4. Genotypes of blood groups in the ABO system
head: Blood group
Antigen on erythrocytes
Antibody in plasma
Genotype

blocks.text: The **Rhesus factor** is determined by one main gene: Rh-positive (D — dominant) and Rh-negative (dd). If an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus, **Rh incompatibility** (hemolytic disease of the newborn) may develop in the second and later pregnancies.

**Mechanism of rhesus conflict:** in the first pregnancy of an Rh-negative (dd) mother, the red cells of an Rh-positive (Dd) fetus pass into the mother's blood mainly during delivery, and **anti-D antibodies** form in her. In the next pregnancy these IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the fetal red cells: haemolytic anaemia, jaundice and, in severe cases, **hydrops fetalis** develop. Prevention is to give the Rh-negative mother **anti-D immunoglobulin** within 72 hours after delivery (or abortion, miscarriage). If the father is dd there is no conflict; if the father is Dd, the probability that the fetus is Rh-positive is 50 %.

Other blood-group systems are also inherited codominantly. The **MN system** has the alleles L^M^ and L^N^: L^M^L^M^ — group M, L^N^L^N^ — group N, L^M^L^N^ — group MN (both antigens present). ABO incompatibility between mother and fetus (mother group I (0), fetus group II (A) or III (B)) can also cause haemolytic disease of the fetus, but it is usually mild.

parts.text: Blood group genetics is used in forensic medicine to **exclude** paternity: for example, a mother with group I (0) cannot have a child with group IV (AB). But blood groups **cannot prove** paternity — DNA analysis is needed for that. In the **Bombay phenomenon**, under the action of an epistatic recessive gene (hh), a person carrying the I^A^ or I^B^ gene appears to be group I (0).

sections.title: 4. Di- and polyhybrid crosses. Mendel’s third law

blocks.text: A **dihybrid cross** is a cross of organisms that differ in two pairs of alternative traits. When Mendel crossed yellow smooth (AABB) and green wrinkled (aabb) peas, all F~1~ were yellow smooth (AaBb). The F~1~ hybrid forms 4 kinds of gametes (AB, Ab, aB, ab), and in F~2~ there are 16 combinations, 9 genotypes and 4 phenotypes in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio (Figure 4.2).

blocks.label: Figure 4.2
blocks.caption: Mendel’s third law (independent inheritance of traits) in a Punnett square: 16 combinations and the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio in the cross AaBb × AaBb; the letters under each genotype show the phenotype — D dominant, R recessive — for the first and second trait (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Mendel’s third law (law of independent inheritance):** in a dihybrid cross, segregation for each pair of traits proceeds in a 3 : 1 ratio independently of the other pair, and genes combine in all possible combinations. The law holds only if the genes are located **on different pairs of chromosomes**. Its cytological basis is the independent separation of homologous pairs in metaphase I.
Independent assortment can be proved by a **test cross**: in the cross AaBb × aabb four phenotypes appear in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.

blocks.text: **Pleiotropy** is the effect of one gene on several traits. For example, in **Marfan syndrome** a mutation of the gene for the connective tissue protein fibrillin causes long “spider fingers”, dislocation of the lens and aortic aneurysm together; the **phenylketonuria** gene causes intellectual disability, light skin and hair and a peculiar odor of the urine.

Pleiotropy is **primary** or **secondary**. In primary pleiotropy one altered gene affects several tissues at the same time: for example, in **Hartnup disease** absorption of the amino acid tryptophan is impaired in both the intestine and the kidney tubules. In secondary pleiotropy the first trait sets off a chain of further traits: in sickle-cell anaemia, change of haemoglobin → change of red-cell shape → their sticking together and breakdown → anaemia and damage to the heart, kidneys and brain.

The terms “penetrance” and “expressivity” were introduced in 1927 by N.V. Timofeev-Resovsky. Penetrance is expressed as a percentage: for example, the penetrance of the retinoblastoma gene is ≈ 90 %, which means 10 % of gene carriers do not develop a tumour but pass the gene to their children. An example of expressivity: in polydactyly the extra finger may be on one hand only or on all four limbs.

parts.text: If the ratio adds up to **16**, a dihybrid cross (two genes) is involved: 9 + 7, 13 + 3, 12 + 3 + 1, 9 + 3 + 4, 15 + 1 are all “merged” variants of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

The expression of a gene is described by **penetrance** (the percentage of gene carriers in whom the trait appears) and **expressivity** (the degree to which the trait is expressed). For example, the polydactyly gene has incomplete penetrance.

blocks.text: In the examples below the solution algorithm (notation → parental genotypes → gametes → Punnett square → ratio or probability) is applied step by step.
Example 1. Incomplete dominance

**Problem:** in humans cystinuria is inherited as incomplete dominance: aa — healthy, Aa — excess cystine in urine, AA — cystine kidney stones. Both parents have excess cystine in urine (Aa). What conditions are possible in their children? **Solution:** P: Aa × Aa; G: A, a and A, a; F~1~: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. So 25 % of children have kidney stones (AA), 50 % have excess cystine in urine (Aa) and 25 % are healthy (aa). In incomplete dominance the genotype and phenotype ratios are the same (1 : 2 : 1).
Example 2. Disputed paternity by blood groups

**Problem:** the mother has group II (A), the child group I (0). Two men deny paternity: the first has group IV (AB), the second group III (B). Which of them could be the child's father? **Solution:** the child is I^0^I^0^ — one I^0^ came from the mother (so the mother is I^A^I^0^), the other from the father. A man with group IV (AB) (I^A^I^B^) cannot give the I^0^ allele — he cannot be the father. A man with group III (B) **may** be the father if he is I^B^I^0^ (but this does not prove paternity).
Example 3. Dihybrid cross (human)

**Problem:** polydactyly (P) and brown eyes over blue (B) are dominant; the genes are on different chromosomes. The father is heterozygous for both traits (PpBb) and the mother is five-fingered and blue-eyed (ppbb). What is the probability of a five-fingered blue-eyed child? **Solution:** this is a test cross: the father's gametes are PB, Pb, pB, pb (1/4 each), the mother's gamete is pb. F~1~: PpBb, Ppbb, ppBb, ppbb — 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. The probability of a five-fingered blue-eyed (ppbb) child is 1/4 = 25 %. The product rule gives the same: pp (1/2) × bb (1/2) = 1/4.
Example 4. Complementarity (congenital deafness)

**Problem:** normal hearing needs two non-allelic dominant genes — D (development of the cochlea) and E (development of the auditory nerve). Can deaf parents (DDee × ddEE) have hearing children? **Solution:** the father's gamete is De and the mother's is dE; all children are DdEe — **hearing**, because both dominant genes came together. If two DdEe people marry, hearing (D_E_) and deaf children appear in F~2~ in a ratio of 9 : 7.
Example 5. Polygeny (skin colour)

**Problem:** skin colour is determined by two pairs of polymeric genes: A~1~A~1~A~2~A~2~ — black, a~1~a~1~a~2~a~2~ — white; the more dominant alleles, the darker the skin. How is skin colour distributed among the children of two mulattoes (A~1~a~1~A~2~a~2~)? **Solution:** each parent forms 4 kinds of gametes; F~2~ has 16 combinations. By the number of dominant alleles: 4 (black) — 1/16, 3 (dark mulatto) — 4/16, 2 (medium mulatto) — 6/16, 1 (light mulatto) — 4/16, 0 (white) — 1/16. The ratio is 1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1.
Example 6. A lethal gene

**Problem:** in mice yellow colour (A) is dominant over grey (a), and the AA genotype dies in the embryo. Two yellow mice were crossed and 12 live mice were obtained. How many are yellow? **Solution:** P: Aa × Aa; F~1~: 1 AA (dies) : 2 Aa (yellow) : 1 aa (grey). Among the living, yellow : grey = 2 : 1, that is 2/3 of 12 — 8 yellow and 4 grey.

parts.text: If a problem says “an affected child was born to healthy parents”, the disease is **recessive** and both parents are heterozygous. If it says “a healthy child was born to affected parents”, the disease is **dominant** and both parents are heterozygous.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In humans curly hair (A) is dominant over straight hair (a). A heterozygous curly-haired man married a straight-haired woman.
cases.ask: What genotypes and phenotypes are possible in the children? What is the probability of a straight-haired child?
cases.answer: P: ♀ aa × ♂ Aa. The woman’s gamete is a; the man’s are A and a. F~1~: Aa (curly) and aa (straight) in a 1 : 1 ratio. Thus the probability of a straight-haired child is 50 % (this is an example of a test cross).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Wilson disease (disorder of copper metabolism) is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. One parent is ill; the other is healthy and has healthy parents, but this parent’s brother has Wilson disease.
cases.ask: Determine the probability of an affected child in this family.
cases.answer: The affected parent is aa. The healthy parent comes from healthy parents who have an affected son, so their parents are Aa × Aa, and the healthy parent, being unaffected, is AA (1/3) or Aa (2/3). If he or she is Aa, the probability of an affected child in the marriage aa × Aa is 1/2. Overall probability: 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3 (≈ 33 %). If the healthy partner is known to be heterozygous — 50 %, if homozygous — 0 %.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In humans brown eyes (A) are dominant over blue eyes (a), and nearsightedness — myopia (B) over normal vision (b). A blue-eyed myopic woman married a brown-eyed man with normal vision, and a blue-eyed child with normal vision was born.
cases.ask: Determine the genotypes of the parents and the probability of a brown-eyed myopic child in this family.
cases.answer: The child is aabb, so each parent gave the a and b alleles: the woman is aaBb, the man Aabb. Gametes: woman — aB, ab; man — Ab, ab. Children: AaBb (brown-eyed myopic), Aabb (brown-eyed normal), aaBb (blue-eyed myopic), aabb (blue-eyed normal) — each 1/4. The probability of a brown-eyed myopic child is 25 %.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: An Rh-negative (dd) woman married an Rh-positive man. Their first child was born Rh-positive and healthy; no prophylaxis was given to the mother after delivery. In the second pregnancy signs of haemolytic disease were found in the fetus.
cases.ask: Why was the second fetus affected? What could the man's genotype be and what prophylaxis was needed?
cases.answer: During the first delivery the red cells of the Rh-positive fetus passed into the mother's blood and **anti-D antibodies** formed (sensitisation). In the second pregnancy the IgG antibodies crossed the placenta and destroyed the red cells of the Rh-positive fetus. The man may be DD or Dd: if DD, all children are Rh-positive (Dd); if Dd, each child is Rh-positive with 50 % probability. Giving **anti-D immunoglobulin** within 72 hours after the first delivery would have quickly removed the fetal red cells, and no antibodies would have formed in the mother.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: Both parents have short fingers (brachydactyly). Of their children, 2 have brachydactyly and 1 has normal fingers. The doctor found that an earlier pregnancy with a fetus with “extremely short fingers and skeletal defects” had ended in early miscarriage.
cases.ask: How is brachydactyly inherited? What are the parents' genotypes? Explain the ratio.
cases.answer: Brachydactyly is an **autosomal dominant** trait that is **lethal** in the homozygous state. The birth of a normal child to affected parents shows that both are heterozygous: Bb × Bb. The offspring should be 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, but BB fetuses die with severe skeletal defects (the miscarried fetus). So among liveborn children brachydactylous (Bb) : normal (bb) = 2 : 1. In each further pregnancy the risk is: 25 % — fetal loss, 50 % — a child with brachydactyly, 25 % — a healthy child.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A blue-eyed woman with blood group I (0) married a brown-eyed man with blood group IV (AB). The man's mother was blue-eyed.
cases.ask: What phenotypes are possible in the children? Find the probability of a blue-eyed child with blood group III (B).
cases.answer: Because the man's mother was blue-eyed, he is heterozygous for eye colour: Aa I^A^I^B^. The woman is aa I^0^I^0^. Eye colour: Aa × aa → 1/2 brown, 1/2 blue. Blood group: I^A^I^B^ × I^0^I^0^ → 1/2 I^A^I^0^ (group II), 1/2 I^B^I^0^ (group III). The children have four phenotypes with equal probability: brown-eyed II, brown-eyed III, blue-eyed II, blue-eyed III. The probability of a blue-eyed child with group III (B) is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 = 25 %. There will be no children with group I (0) or IV (AB).

topics.title: The chromosome theory of heredity. T.H. Morgan. Linked inheritance of genes, crossing over. Sex-linked inheritance of traits

goals.text: To teach the student T. Morgan’s chromosome theory of heredity, complete and incomplete linkage of genes, crossing over and the determination of distances between genes, genetic maps, the genetic determination of sex and the inheritance of X- and Y-linked traits.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the main statements of the chromosome theory of heredity;
the concepts of linkage group and complete and incomplete linkage;
the frequency of crossing over and the concept of the morganid;
the types of sex determination (XY, XO, ZW) and the genetic basis of sex development in humans;
the features of X-linked dominant and recessive and Y-linked (holandric) inheritance.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: solve problems on linked genes and calculate the distance between genes;
determine the order of three genes on a chromosome from the distances between them;
solve problems on sex-linked traits (color blindness, hemophilia).

blocks.text: Mendel’s third law holds only for genes on different chromosomes. The number of genes is much greater than the number of chromosomes (in humans there are about 20 thousand protein-coding genes on 46 chromosomes), so each chromosome carries many genes. The American geneticist **T.H. Morgan** and his students (A. Sturtevant, C. Bridges, H. Muller) carried out experiments on the fruit fly (*Drosophila melanogaster*) in 1910–1916 and created the **chromosome theory of heredity**.

parts.text: Drosophila is a convenient object for genetic research: it is easy to breed, one generation takes 10–12 days, it has many offspring, varied traits and few chromosomes (2n = 8).

blocks.text: Main statements of the chromosome theory

items: Genes are located on chromosomes; each chromosome carries particular genes.
Genes are arranged linearly on a chromosome in a definite order; each gene has its own locus.

Genes on one chromosome form a **linkage group** and are inherited together; the number of linkage groups equals the haploid number of chromosomes (in humans 23 in women and 24 in men — X and Y separately).
Genes are exchanged between homologous chromosomes by crossing over; its frequency is directly proportional to the distance between the genes.
The karyotype of each species is specific and constant.

blocks.text: The chromosome theory was founded by **W. Sutton** and **T. Boveri** (1902–1903): they showed that the behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis exactly matches the distribution of Mendel's “hereditary factors”. C. Bridges proved that genes lie on chromosomes using non-disjunction of the sex chromosomes, and in 1931 C. Stern (in Drosophila) and H. Creighton and B. McClintock (in maize) proved the cytological basis of crossing over by showing that chromosome segments are exchanged together with the traits.

Morgan crossed gray-bodied long-winged (BBVV) and black-bodied short-winged (bbvv) Drosophila and obtained gray long-winged flies (BbVv) in F~1~. When he then crossed an F~1~ male with a recessive female (bbvv) (a test cross), not the 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 expected by Mendel appeared, but only the two parental phenotypes in a 1 : 1 ratio (Figure 5.1). Hence the B and V genes lie on one chromosome and are inherited **completely linked**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: Completely linked inheritance of the body color and wing length genes in Drosophila: B — gray body, b — black body, V — normal wings, v — short (vestigial) wings (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: If an F~1~ **female** is used for the test cross, then besides the parental-type flies a small number (8.5 % each) of new combinations appear — gray short-winged and black long-winged (**crossover**, recombinant) flies: 41.5 % : 41.5 % : 8.5 % : 8.5 %. This is **incomplete linkage**, and its cause is crossing over during meiosis in the female Drosophila (there is no crossing over in the male Drosophila).

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Incomplete linkage in Drosophila: when an F~1~ female (BbVv) is crossed with a recessive male (bbvv), crossing over gives 83 % parental-type and 17 % recombinant flies (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: There is no crossing over in Drosophila males, so a test cross with an F~1~ male shows **complete linkage**, while a test cross with an F~1~ female shows **incomplete linkage**. In humans crossing over occurs in both sexes, somewhat more often in women. Crossing-over frequency is influenced by age, temperature, ionising radiation, some chemicals and the closeness of the gene to the centromere (crossing over is rare near the centromere).

parts.text: Notation of linked genes: alleles on one chromosome are written on one side of the fraction line — **AB/ab** (cis position, dominant alleles on one chromosome) or **Ab/aB** (trans position, dominant alleles on different chromosomes).

blocks.text: **Crossing over** is the exchange of equal segments between chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I of meiosis (pachytene) (Figure 5.3). It breaks linkage groups, creates new combinations of genes and is a source of combinative variability.

blocks.label: Figure 5.3
blocks.caption: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes: I — before crossing over; II — crossing over; III — recombinant chromatids after crossing over (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The **distance between genes** is measured by the frequency of crossing over: **1 % crossing over = 1 morganid (centimorgan, cM)**. The recombination frequency (rf) is calculated as follows:
rf (%) = (number of crossover individuals / total number of offspring) × 100

For example, in the experiment above crossover flies make up 8.5 % + 8.5 % = 17 %, so the distance between the B and V genes is 17 morganids. The greater the distance, the more crossing over occurs; but the frequency of crossing over does not exceed 50 % (at 50 % the genes appear to be inherited independently).

A **genetic map** is a diagram of the order of genes on a chromosome and the relative distances between them. Knowing the distances between three genes, their order can be determined: the largest distance lies between the outer genes and equals the sum of the other two distances (Figure 5.4).

blocks.label: Figure 5.4
blocks.caption: Constructing a gene map: 1.5 % crossing over between A and B, 3.5 % between B and C, 5.0 % between C and D; the distance A–D equals 10.0 % (numbers are the percentage of crossing over between genes) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: A complete map of the human genome has now been made: **genetic (recombination)** maps are built by studying crossing over in families, and **physical** maps by hybridization, FISH and DNA sequencing. They are used to find the genes of hereditary diseases and in prenatal diagnosis.
Double crossing over and interference

Between genes lying farther apart, crossing over can occur at two points at the same time — **double crossing over**. The outer genes then return to the parental arrangement and the recombination is “hidden”, so the distance between distant genes comes out slightly less than the sum of the short distances. One crossover reduces the chance of another nearby — this is called **interference**. Its degree is assessed by the **coefficient of coincidence**: observed percentage of double crossovers / theoretically expected percentage (the product of the A–B and B–C frequencies).

The first human linkage groups found were: on chromosome 1 the **Rh factor** gene and the **elliptocytosis** gene (oval red cells); on chromosome 9 the **ABO** blood-group gene and the **nail–patella syndrome** gene. Such linkage makes it possible to predict, from one trait, the transmission of another (a disease gene) in a family — this is the basis of indirect DNA diagnosis.

Sex is the set of traits that ensure the reproductive function of an organism; it is determined by the **sex chromosomes** (heterochromosomes). The other chromosomes are called **autosomes**. The human karyotype: in women 44 autosomes + XX (46,XX), in men 44 autosomes + XY (46,XY). The sex with identical sex chromosomes is **homogametic** (one kind of gamete), and the sex with different ones is **heterogametic**.

Female

blocks.label: Figure 5.5
blocks.caption: Chromosomal sex determination in Drosophila: the homogametic female (XX) forms one kind of gamete and the heterogametic male (XY) forms two kinds; at fertilisation female and male zygotes arise in a 1 : 1 ratio (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In humans sex is determined **at fertilization**: if an X-bearing sperm fertilizes the egg, a girl (XX) is born, and if a Y-bearing sperm does, a boy (XY); the theoretical ratio is 1 : 1. Male development is determined by the **SRY gene** on the Y chromosome (the testis-determining factor). That is why a person with the karyotype 47,XXY has a male phenotype and a person with 45,X a female phenotype.

parts.text: Disorders of sexual differentiation: 46,XX male syndrome when the SRY gene has moved to the X chromosome; female phenotype in a person with the 46,XY karyotype in androgen receptor deficiency (**testicular feminization syndrome**). In such cases the karyotype and sex chromatin are examined to determine sex.

blocks.text: **Dosage compensation (M. Lyon hypothesis, 1961).** Although women have two X chromosomes and men only one, the amount of X-gene products is almost equal in the two sexes. The reason is that early in embryonic development (about day 16) one of the X chromosomes in female cells is **randomly** inactivated and becomes the **Barr body**, and this state passes to daughter cells. As a result the female body is a **mosaic** for X genes: for example, in a woman heterozygous for the colour-vision gene, normal and colour-blind areas alternate in the retina; tortoiseshell (three-coloured) cats are almost always female.

Traits determined by genes located on the sex chromosomes are called **sex-linked** traits. In males the genes on the X chromosome are unpaired (**hemizygous**), so even a recessive allele is always expressed in a male.

Hemophilia A and B, color blindness, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, G6PD deficiency
Women are affected 2 times more often than men; all daughters of an affected father are affected, his sons are healthy
Vitamin D–resistant rickets (hypophosphatemia), dark enamel of the teeth
Only in males, passed from father to all sons
Hypertrichosis of the ear pinna, webbing between the toes, some forms of azoospermia

blocks.text: In the example of **color blindness**: X^D^ — normal vision, X^d^ — color blindness. In a marriage of a carrier woman (X^D^X^d^) and a healthy man (X^D^Y), all daughters have normal vision (50 % of them carriers) and 50 % of the sons are color-blind. **Hemophilia** is inherited in the same way; its spread among the descendants of Queen Victoria of Great Britain is a famous example.

blocks.label: Figure 5.6
blocks.caption: Inheritance of haemophilia: from the marriage of a carrier woman (X^H^X^h^) and a healthy man (X^H^Y), a healthy daughter, a healthy son, a carrier daughter and a son with haemophilia may be born (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: **Haemophilia A** (deficiency of clotting factor VIII) and **haemophilia B** (factor IX) are X-linked recessive diseases: prolonged bleeding even after minor injury and bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) are typical. A famous historical example is the descendants of Queen Victoria (European royal families). **Duchenne muscular dystrophy** (dystrophin gene) begins in boys at 3–5 years with progressive muscle weakness. In **glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency**, some drugs (primaquine, sulphonamides) or eating broad beans cause a haemolytic crisis.

blocks.text: **Sex-limited (sex-influenced) traits** are determined by genes on autosomes but are expressed only in one sex or differently in the two sexes (under the influence of sex hormones): male-pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia) — dominant in men and recessive in women; development of the mammary glands, beard growth, pitch of the voice.

parts.text: An X-linked recessive disease is **never passed from father to son**, because a son receives the Y chromosome from his father. The carrier of an affected son is always the mother.

sections.title: 6. Worked examples on linked and sex-linked inheritance

blocks.text: Example 1. Predicting offspring from crossing-over frequency

**Problem:** genes A and B lie on one chromosome 20 cM apart. An AB/ab (cis) female was crossed with an ab/ab male. What phenotypes and percentages will the offspring have? **Solution:** 20 % crossover gametes (Ab and aB — 10 % each) and 80 % non-crossover gametes (AB and ab — 40 % each). The male gives only ab gametes. Offspring: AB/ab — 40 %, ab/ab — 40 %, Ab/ab — 10 %, aB/ab — 10 %. In the trans arrangement (Ab/aB) it is the reverse: Ab and aB — 40 % each, AB and ab — 10 % each.
Example 2. Haemophilia (X-linked recessive)

**Problem:** a healthy woman whose father had haemophilia married a healthy man. What is the probability of an affected child? **Solution:** the woman received X^h^ from her father, so she is a carrier — X^H^X^h^. The man is X^H^Y. Children: X^H^X^H^ (healthy daughter), X^H^X^h^ (carrier daughter), X^H^Y (healthy son), X^h^Y (affected son) — 25 % each. The probability of an affected child is 25 % of all children and 50 % of sons; all daughters are phenotypically healthy.
Example 3. Autosomal and X-linked genes together

**Problem:** a blue-eyed (aa) woman with normal colour vision whose father was colour-blind married a brown-eyed (Aa) colour-blind man. Find the probability of a blue-eyed colour-blind daughter. **Solution:** the woman is aaX^D^X^d^ and the man AaX^d^Y. Eye colour: aa × Aa → blue eyes 1/2. Vision: X^D^X^d^ × X^d^Y → colour-blind daughter (X^d^X^d^) 1/4. Product rule: 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8 = 12,5 %.

parts.text: In sex-linked problems the genotype is always written together with the sex chromosome: X^A^X^a^, X^a^Y. The Y chromosome carries no alleles of X genes, so a man has only one allele of each X gene.

skills.title: Skill: building a genetic map from the distances between three genes

items: Write the percentage of crossing over between each pair of genes (for example, A–B = 12 %, B–C = 5 %, A–C = 7 %).
Find the largest distance — these are the two outer genes (A and B).
The third gene (C) lies between them: check that 7 % + 5 % = 12 %.
Draw the map: A — 7 cM — C — 5 cM — B.
If the sum of the smaller distances is slightly larger than the large distance, explain it by double crossing over.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In humans the gene for color vision (D, dominant) and the gene for color blindness (d, recessive) are on the X chromosome. A color-blind daughter was born to a color-blind man and a woman with normal vision.
cases.ask: Determine the genotypes of the parents.
cases.answer: The color-blind daughter is X^d^X^d^ — she received one X^d^ from the father and the other from the mother. The father is color-blind — X^d^Y. The mother has normal vision but passed on X^d^, so she is a carrier — X^D^X^d^. In this family 50 % of both daughters and sons may be color-blind.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Hypertrichosis (hair growth on the ear pinna) is Y-linked, and one form of ichthyosis is an X-linked recessive trait. A child with ichthyosis was born in the family of a woman healthy for both traits and a man with hypertrichosis.
cases.ask: Can this child have hypertrichosis? What is the child’s sex?
cases.answer: Ichthyosis is X-linked recessive; from healthy parents an affected child can only be a son (X^i^Y) who received X^i^ from a carrier mother (the father is X^I^Y, so his daughters cannot be affected). Since the child is a boy, he received the Y chromosome carrying the hypertrichosis gene from his father — he will have both ichthyosis and (at puberty) hypertrichosis.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In humans cataract (A) and polydactyly (B) are determined by dominant genes completely linked on one autosome (no crossing over). The woman and the man are both diheterozygous; in each case the father had cataract and the mother had polydactyly.
cases.ask: What will be the genotypes and phenotypes of the children?
cases.answer: Each parent received the Ab chromosome from the father and aB from the mother, i.e., is a diheterozygote in the trans position Ab/aB. Without crossing over each forms only Ab and aB gametes. F~1~: Ab/Ab (cataract only) — 25 %, Ab/aB (cataract + polydactyly) — 50 %, aB/aB (polydactyly only) — 25 %. A healthy child (ab/ab) will not be born.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A man with haemophilia A married a healthy (non-carrier) woman. They are worried about their grandchildren.
cases.ask: Can the disease appear in the children and grandchildren of this family?
cases.answer: The father is X^h^Y and the mother X^H^X^H^. All **sons** are healthy (they receive Y from the father) and do not transmit the disease. All **daughters** are obligate carriers (X^H^X^h^) because they receive X^h^ from the father. If the daughters marry healthy men, 50 % of their sons will have haemophilia and 50 % of their daughters will be carriers. So the disease can appear in the grandchildren — **in grandsons through the daughters** (“skipping a generation”). Prenatal diagnosis is recommended for the daughters in pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: In Drosophila grey body (B) is dominant over black (b) and normal wings (V) over short wings (v). A BbVv female crossed with a bbvv male gave 1000 offspring: grey normal-winged — 415, black short-winged — 415, grey short-winged — 85, black normal-winged — 85.
cases.ask: Are the genes linked? Find the distance between them and the genotype of the female.
cases.answer: With independent assortment a ratio of 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (250 each) would be expected; two classes are large (415 each) and two small (85 each) — the genes are **linked**, with incomplete linkage. The large classes (BV and bv) are parental (non-crossover), the small classes (Bv and bV) are crossovers. rf = (85 + 85) / 1000 × 100 = 17 %, so the distance between the genes is **17 cM**. The female's genotype is **BV/bv** (cis), because the non-crossover classes are BV and bv.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: Examination of an 18-year-old patient with a female phenotype, well-developed breasts but no menstruation showed no uterus and testes in the abdominal cavity. The karyotype is 46,XY. No sex chromatin (Barr body) was found.
cases.ask: What condition is this? Which level of sex formation is disturbed?
cases.answer: This is **testicular feminisation syndrome** (complete androgen insensitivity) — a mutation of the X-linked androgen receptor gene. Chromosomal sex (46,XY) and gonadal sex (testis — the SRY gene worked) are male, and the testes produce testosterone, but because the tissues lack the receptor it has no effect — the **somatic (phenotypic) sex** develops as female. The uterus did not develop because anti-Müllerian hormone worked. Testosterone is converted to oestrogen and develops the breasts. The absence of a Barr body confirms that there is one X chromosome.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The greater the distance between genes, the more crossing over; **1 % = 1 morganid**, maximum crossing over — **50 %**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: X-recessive: **“Mother gives, son suffers”**; Y-linked: **“From father to every son”**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: In a family where a boy with hemophilia or Duchenne dystrophy is born, the mother is considered a carrier; the risk for later sons is 50 %, which is taken into account in genetic counseling.

topics.title: Molecular basis of life. Nucleic acids and their role in passing hereditary traits from generation to generation. The role of DNA in protein biosynthesis. Genetic engineering. Variability and its forms

goals.text: To teach the student the evidence that DNA is the hereditary material, the structure and replication of nucleic acids, the properties of the genetic code, the stages of transcription and translation, the regulation of gene activity, the basics of gene and cell engineering, and the forms of variability and the classification of mutations.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the essence of the experiments on transformation, transduction and conjugation;
the structure of DNA and RNA, Chargaff’s rules and the semiconservative mode of replication;
the properties of the genetic code and the stages of protein biosynthesis;
the operon theory (induction and repression);
the types of variability, the classification of mutations, DNA repair and antimutagens.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the complementary strand, mRNA and amino acid sequence from a DNA strand;
calculate the percentage of nucleotides using Chargaff’s rule;
identify the type of mutation from a description or a diagram.

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: F. Griffith's experiment (1928): mice survive when given live unencapsulated R-strain or heat-killed S-strain alone, but die when given live S-strain or the mixture of the two — the virulence trait passed from dead S-bacteria to live R-bacteria (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In Griffith's experiment the nature of the “transforming principle” remained unknown. In 1944 **O. Avery, C. MacLeod and M. McCarty** separated protein, polysaccharide and DNA from the S-strain and showed that only **DNA** turned the R-strain into the S-strain, and that this ability was lost after treatment with DNase. This was the first direct proof that DNA is the hereditary material.

**Plasmids** are small circular DNA molecules in bacteria outside the chromosome; they replicate independently. The F plasmid ensures conjugation, and R plasmids provide **antibiotic resistance** and spread rapidly between bacteria. Plasmids are used as **vectors** in genetic engineering.

sections.title: 2. Structure of nucleic acids and DNA replication

blocks.text: Nucleic acids are biopolymers built of **nucleotides**. Each nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a pentose (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) and a phosphate residue. Nitrogenous bases: **purines** — adenine (A) and guanine (G); **pyrimidines** — cytosine (C), thymine (T, only in DNA) and uracil (U, only in RNA).

In 1953 **J. Watson and F. Crick** proposed the double helix model of DNA (based on the X-ray diffraction data of R. Franklin and M. Wilkins). DNA consists of two **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′) polynucleotide strands; the strands are joined by hydrogen bonds between nitrogenous bases according to the principle of **complementarity**: A=T (2 hydrogen bonds), G≡C (3 hydrogen bonds). The helix diameter is 2 nm, one turn contains 10 nucleotide pairs, the pitch is 3.4 nm and the distance between neighboring nucleotides is 0.34 nm (Figure 6.2).

blocks.title: Table 6.2. Main parameters of the DNA double helix
head: Parameter
Value
rows: Hydrogen bonds in an A–T pair
Hydrogen bonds in a G–C pair
Length of DNA in one diploid cell

blocks.label: Figure 6.2
blocks.caption: The twisted double-stranded DNA molecule: complementary base pairs and dimensions of the helix (diameter 2 nm, one turn 3.4 nm, distance between bases 0.34 nm) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: **Chargaff’s rules:** A = T, G = C; the sum of purines equals the sum of pyrimidines (A + G = T + C). So if you know the percentage of one base in DNA, you can calculate the others: for example, if G = 20 %, then C = 20 % and A = T = 30 %.

blocks.title: Table 6.3. Differences between DNA and RNA
head: Feature
DNA
RNA
rows: mRNA (carries information), tRNA (carries amino acids), rRNA (part of ribosomes)

blocks.text: **Replication** is the self-duplication of DNA; it takes place in the S period of interphase. M. Meselson and F. Stahl (1958) proved that replication is **semiconservative**: each new DNA molecule has one old (template) strand and one new strand. In the process **helicase** unwinds the double helix, **topoisomerase** relieves the twisting, **primase** synthesizes an RNA primer and **DNA polymerase** builds the new strand only in the 5′→3′ direction; therefore one strand is made continuously (leading) and the other as Okazaki fragments (lagging), which are joined by **ligase**.

blocks.label: Figure 6.3
blocks.caption: Scheme of the Meselson–Stahl experiment: parental molecules and first- and second-generation DNA molecules — the semi-conservative, conservative and dispersive models of replication (1, 2, 3) compared (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Meselson and Stahl grew *E. coli* on heavy nitrogen (^15^N) medium and then moved it to ordinary nitrogen (^14^N) medium. In the first generation all DNA had **intermediate density** (^15^N/^14^N); in the second generation half was intermediate and half light. This result fits only the semi-conservative model.

blocks.label: Figure 6.4
blocks.caption: The replication fork: helicase separates the strands, topoisomerase relieves tension, primase makes an RNA primer, DNA polymerase synthesises the leading strand continuously and the lagging strand as Okazaki fragments, and DNA ligase joins them (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 6.4. Enzymes and proteins taking part in replication
head: Enzyme (protein)
Function
rows: Breaks hydrogen bonds and “unzips” the double helix
Removes the twisting tension created as the helix unwinds
Keep the separated single strands from re-joining
Synthesises a short RNA primer to which the polymerase adds nucleotides
Builds the new strand only in the 5′→3′ direction and proofreads errors
Joins Okazaki fragments with a phosphodiester bond

blocks.text: Because DNA polymerase works only in the 5′→3′ direction, the two strands are built differently: the **leading strand** is made continuously in the direction of fork movement, and the **lagging strand** in the opposite direction as short pieces — **Okazaki fragments** (100–200 nucleotides in eukaryotes). In a eukaryotic chromosome replication starts at thousands of points (**replicons**) at once, so the huge DNA is doubled in a few hours.

sections.title: 3. The genetic code and protein biosynthesis

blocks.text: The **genetic code** is the system of recording the amino acid sequence of a protein by the nucleotide sequence of mRNA. Its properties:

items: **Triplet** — each amino acid is coded by three nucleotides (a codon); there are 4^3^ = 64 codons, 61 of which code amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are **stop codons**.
**Degeneracy (redundancy)** — most amino acids are coded by several codons (only methionine and tryptophan by one each).
**Unambiguity (specificity)** — each codon specifies only one amino acid.
**Continuity and non-overlapping** — there are no “commas” between codons, and one nucleotide does not belong to two codons.
**Universality** — the code is almost the same in all organisms.
**Start codon** — AUG (methionine).

blocks.title: Table 6.5. mRNA codons of some amino acids
head: Amino acid
Codons
Amino acid
Codons
rows: UCU, UCC, UCA, UCG, AGU, AGC
UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG

blocks.text: **Transcription** is the synthesis of mRNA on one (template) strand of DNA by RNA polymerase (Figure 6.5). It starts at the promoter and ends at the terminator. In eukaryotes pre-mRNA is formed first; during **processing** a “cap” is added to the 5′ end and a poly-A “tail” to the 3′ end, and in **splicing** introns are cut out and exons are joined.

blocks.label: Figure 6.5
blocks.caption: Diagram of transcription: RNA polymerase opens the DNA double helix and synthesizes an RNA strand complementary to the template strand (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 6.6. Types of RNA
head: Type
Share in the cell
Function
rows: Part of the ribosome; catalyses peptide-bond formation
Brings the amino acid to the ribosome; “recognises” the codon with its anticodon
Carries gene information from the nucleus to the ribosome
Regulate gene activity by degrading mRNA or blocking translation

blocks.text: **Structure of a eukaryotic gene.** At the start of the gene is the **promoter** (TATA box) where RNA polymerase binds, then alternating **exons** (protein-coding parts) and **introns** (non-coding parts), and at the end the **terminator**. More distant **enhancers** boost transcription. In splicing the introns are cut out and the exons joined; joining the exons of one gene in different ways (**alternative splicing**) allows several different proteins to be made from one gene. Only ≈ 1,5 % of the human genome codes for protein.

**Translation** is the synthesis of a polypeptide chain on the ribosome according to the information in mRNA (Figure 6.7). Amino acids are activated by special enzymes (aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases) and attached to tRNA. The **anticodon** of tRNA binds to the mRNA codon by complementarity.

blocks.label: Figure 6.6
blocks.caption: Secondary structure of alanine tRNA (“cloverleaf”): the amino acid attaches to the 3′ end, and the anticodon in the lower loop pairs complementarily with the mRNA codon (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

items: **Initiation** — the small ribosomal subunit binds to mRNA, the tRNA carrying methionine takes its place at the start codon AUG, and then the large subunit joins.
**Elongation** — the next aminoacyl-tRNA arrives at the A site, a peptide bond forms between the amino acids, and the ribosome moves one codon (translocation).
**Termination** — when the ribosome reaches a stop codon, the polypeptide is released and the ribosome dissociates into subunits.

blocks.label: Figure 6.7
blocks.caption: Stages of protein biosynthesis (translation): initiation, elongation and termination; small and large ribosomal subunits, tRNA and mRNA (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Many antibiotics stop bacterial translation: tetracyclines (binding of tRNA), streptomycin (the small subunit), chloramphenicol and macrolides (the large subunit). They act selectively on the 70S ribosomes of bacteria.

sections.title: 4. Regulation of gene activity and cytoplasmic heredity

blocks.text: F. Jacob and J. Monod (1961) created the **operon** theory in Escherichia coli. An operon is a group of structural genes transcribed together under one promoter and operator. A regulator gene synthesizes a **repressor** protein, which binds to the operator and blocks the movement of RNA polymerase.

items: **Induction** (lactose operon): without lactose in the medium the repressor is bound to the operator and the genes are off; lactose (the inducer) binds and inactivates the repressor — enzymes that break down lactose are synthesized.
**Repression** (tryptophan operon): when the end product (tryptophan) accumulates, it activates the repressor as a corepressor and synthesis stops.

blocks.text: In eukaryotes gene activity is regulated at many levels: chromatin condensation (DNA methylation, histone modification), transcription factors and enhancers, splicing, mRNA stability and translation.

**Epigenetic regulation** is a heritable change in gene activity without a change in the DNA nucleotide sequence. Its main mechanisms are cytosine **methylation** (a methylated promoter is “switched off”), acetylation and methylation of histones, and non-coding RNAs. **Genomic imprinting** means that for some genes only the copy from the father or only the copy from the mother works. For example, if the same region of chromosome 15 is lost on the paternal copy, **Prader–Willi syndrome** (obesity, intellectual disability) develops; if it is lost on the maternal copy, **Angelman syndrome** (seizures, unprovoked laughter) develops.

**Cytoplasmic (extranuclear) heredity** is the inheritance of traits through the DNA of mitochondria and plastids. In humans mitochondria pass to the zygote only through the egg, so mitochondrial diseases (Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, MELAS) are passed **only from the mother** to all her children.
**Genetic engineering** is the set of methods for isolating desired genes, transferring them into the cells of another organism with a vector and using them. Its main stages:

items: Obtaining the desired gene — cutting DNA with **restriction enzymes** (for example, EcoRI) or synthesizing complementary DNA from mRNA with reverse transcriptase.
Joining the gene into a **vector** (plasmid, bacteriophage, virus) with **ligase** — forming recombinant DNA.
Introducing the recombinant DNA into a recipient cell (bacterium, yeast).
Selecting and multiplying (cloning) the cells that received the gene and isolating the product.

blocks.label: Figure 6.8
blocks.caption: Action of the restriction enzyme EcoRI: the enzyme recognises the sequence GAATTC and cuts both strands in a staggered way, forming “sticky ends”; these ends pair complementarily with other DNA cut by the same enzyme (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Genetic engineering is used to produce **human insulin**, growth hormone, interferons, hepatitis B vaccine and blood clotting factors; **gene therapy**, transgenic plants and animals, PCR (polymerase chain reaction) diagnosis and genome editing with CRISPR-Cas9 are developing.
The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

PCR (K. Mullis, 1983) is a method of multiplying a desired piece of DNA millions of times in a test tube. Template DNA, two **primers** (short strands complementary to the ends of the region to be copied), the four nucleotides and heat-stable **Taq polymerase** are added to the reaction mixture. Each cycle has three steps and doubles the amount of DNA: 30 cycles give 2^30^ ≈ 1 billion copies.

items: **Denaturation** (94–95 °C) — the DNA strands separate.
**Primer annealing** (50–65 °C) — the primers bind complementarily to the template.
**Elongation** (72 °C) — Taq polymerase builds the new strand starting from the primer.

parts.text: PCR is widely used in medicine: detection of infections (SARS-CoV-2, HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, tuberculosis), DNA diagnosis of hereditary diseases and carrier status, prenatal diagnosis, forensic identification and paternity testing (DNA “fingerprints”) and molecular diagnosis of tumours.

blocks.text: **Cell engineering** is growing cells, hybridizing them (somatic hybridization) and cloning by nuclear transfer. **Hybridomas** obtained by fusing a lymphocyte with a tumor cell produce monoclonal antibodies. The sheep “Dolly” was cloned by nuclear transfer in 1996.

blocks.text: By the site of origin, **somatic** mutations (in body cells — not inherited, cause tumors and mosaicism) and **generative** mutations (in sex cells — passed to offspring) are distinguished. By cause, there are **spontaneous** (natural, cause unknown) and **induced** (under the action of mutagens) mutations. Mutagens: **physical** (ionizing and ultraviolet radiation, high temperature), **chemical** (alkylating agents, nitrous acid, benzopyrene, some drugs), **biological** (viruses, mobile genetic elements).

**DNA repair** is the system that restores damaged DNA: **photoreactivation** (splitting thymine dimers in light), **excision repair** (cutting out the damaged segment and rebuilding it with DNA polymerase and ligase) and **postreplicative repair**. If repair fails, mutations accumulate: for example, in **xeroderma pigmentosum** ultraviolet light causes skin cancer. **Antimutagens** are substances that reduce the frequency of mutations: vitamins (A, E, C), selenium, some amino acids, antioxidants.

parts.text: **Sickle cell anemia** is a classic point mutation: the substitution GAG → GTG in codon 6 of the β-globin gene puts valine in place of glutamic acid (HbS). At low oxygen HbS polymerizes, the erythrocyte takes a sickle shape and blocks the capillaries.

blocks.text: **Antimutagens** are substances that reduce the frequency of mutations: antioxidants (vitamins C and E, β-carotene), some amino acids (cysteine), selenium and plant flavonoids. They bind free radicals and enhance repair.

**N.I. Vavilov's law of homologous series in hereditary variability (1920):** genetically close species and genera show similar series of hereditary variation. Therefore a mutation found in one species allows a similar mutation to be predicted in related species. In medicine this law underlies the creation of animal **models** of human hereditary diseases (haemophilia, albinism, muscular dystrophy).
Modification variability and the norm of reaction

The genotype determines not the trait itself but the range within which it can vary with the environment — the **norm of reaction**. Traits with a wide norm of reaction (body weight, muscle mass, skin tanning) change a lot with the environment, while traits with a narrow norm (eye colour, blood group) hardly change. Modifications are **group**, **adaptive** and **reversible**, and they are not inherited. They are studied statistically by building a **variation series**: from the variants (v) and their frequencies (p) the mean is found by the formula M = Σ(v · p) / n; its graph is the **variation curve** (normal distribution).

parts.text: **Xeroderma pigmentosum** is a hereditary deficiency (autosomal recessive) of the **excision repair** enzymes that cut out thymine dimers formed by UV light. Patients develop spots and ulcers on the skin after sunlight and skin cancer at a young age; they must be fully protected from sunlight.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The nucleotides of an mRNA are: guanine — 34 %, uracil — 18 %, cytosine — 28 %, adenine — 20 %.
cases.ask: Determine the percentage of nitrogenous bases in the double-stranded DNA segment from which this mRNA was copied.
cases.answer: The template DNA strand is complementary to the mRNA: C — 34 %, A — 18 %, G — 28 %, T — 20 %. The second (coding) strand is similar to the mRNA (T instead of U): G — 34 %, T — 18 %, C — 28 %, A — 20 %. In double-stranded DNA: G = C = (34 + 28) / 2 = 31 %; A = T = (18 + 20) / 2 = 19 %. Check: 31 + 31 + 19 + 19 = 100 %.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: The template strand of DNA is: ACC-ATA-GTC-CAA-GGA-CCA-AAC-AGA-AAA-TTT.
cases.ask: Which amino acids make up the polypeptide synthesized from this segment?
cases.answer: mRNA: UGG-UAU-CAG-GUU-CCU-GGU-UUG-UCU-UUU-AAA. Polypeptide: tryptophan — tyrosine — glutamine — valine — proline — glycine — leucine — serine — phenylalanine — lysine.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a patient’s β-globin gene, the sequence GAG in triplet 6 was found to be replaced by GTG.
cases.ask: What kind of mutation is this, and what disease does it cause?
cases.answer: This is a gene (point) mutation — a base substitution (transversion A → T). In mRNA the codon GAG (glutamic acid) becomes GUG (valine); at position 6 of the β-globin chain valine stands instead of glutamic acid — hemoglobin S is formed. As a result sickle cell anemia develops (autosomal recessive); heterozygotes are relatively resistant to malaria.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: In a laboratory, a single viral DNA molecule from a patient's blood was amplified by PCR. The reaction ran for 25 cycles.
cases.ask: How many DNA copies are formed in theory? What happens in each cycle?
cases.answer: Each cycle doubles the amount of DNA: 2^25^ = 33 554 432, that is ≈ 33,5 million copies. In each cycle: (1) **denaturation** at 94–95 °C — the strands separate; (2) **primer annealing** at 50–65 °C; (3) **elongation** at 72 °C — heat-stable Taq polymerase builds the new strands. This is why PCR can detect even a very small amount of a pathogen.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: The beginning of an mRNA is: AUG-UUU-GGC-AAA-CUG-UAA. A mutation deleted the first U of the second codon.
cases.ask: What peptide is made before and after the mutation? What kind of mutation is this?
cases.answer: Before the mutation: AUG (Met) – UUU (Phe) – GGC (Gly) – AAA (Lys) – CUG (Leu) – UAA (stop) → Met–Phe–Gly–Lys–Leu. After the deletion the mRNA is AUG-UUG-GCA-AAC-UGU-AA… → Met–Leu–Ala–Asn–Cys and so on — every amino acid after the first codon has changed and the stop codon is lost. This is a **frameshift** — a deletion of one nucleotide; the protein is usually completely non-functional.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A 5-year-old child develops severe redness, pigment spots and ulcers on the skin even after a short time in the sun. The parents are healthy and are blood relatives.
cases.ask: What disease should be considered? What are its molecular mechanism and mode of inheritance?
cases.answer: This is **xeroderma pigmentosum**. UV light forms **thymine dimers** between neighbouring thymines in DNA; in a normal cell these are cut out by **excision repair** enzymes and the strand is rebuilt. In the patient these enzymes are hereditarily lacking, damage accumulates and mutations and skin cancer develop. The disease is **autosomal recessive**: the healthy parents are heterozygous carriers, and a consanguineous marriage increases the chance that the same recessive gene meets. Management is complete protection from the sun and early detection of tumours.

topics.title: Methods of studying human genetics: the genealogical, twin and population-statistical methods

goals.text: To teach the student the specific features of studying humans as a genetic object, the rules of drawing a pedigree and the criteria for determining the type of inheritance by the genealogical method, the assessment of the role of heredity and environment by the twin method, and the population-statistical method and the Hardy-Weinberg law.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the difficulties of studying human genetics and the system of methods;
the terms and symbols used in drawing a pedigree;
the criteria of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and sex-linked inheritance;
monozygotic and dizygotic twins, concordance and Holzinger’s formula;
the concepts of population, deme and isolate and the Hardy-Weinberg law.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: draw and analyze a pedigree of one’s own family and from the conditions of a problem;
determine the type of inheritance and assess the risk for the next children;
calculate allele and genotype frequencies by the Hardy-Weinberg formula.

blocks.text: Human genetics obeys the laws of heredity common to all living organisms, but the classical hybridization method cannot be used to study humans. The reasons are:

items: experimental (purposeful) crossing is impossible in humans;
generations change slowly (25–30 years) and the number of children is small;
the karyotype is complex (46 chromosomes) and there are many linkage groups;
humans cannot be kept and observed under identical environmental conditions;
there are medical and ethical restrictions.

blocks.text: Therefore special methods are used in human genetics: the **genealogical, twin, population-statistical, cytogenetic, dermatoglyphic, biochemical, molecular genetic and immunogenetic** methods, somatic cell genetics and modeling. Human genetics also has advantages: the human phenotype and diseases are studied more deeply than in other organisms, populations are large, and written records exist for many generations.

The relative share of heredity and environment in forming a trait

blocks.text: The **genealogical method** (F. Galton, 1865) determines whether a trait is hereditary, its type of inheritance and the genotypes of family members by drawing and analyzing a pedigree. The method has two stages: collecting information and drawing the pedigree; genetic analysis of the pedigree.

blocks.title: Table 7.2. Basic terms of the genealogical method
head: Term
Meaning
rows: The person from whom the pedigree is started (usually the patient who consulted the doctor); shown with an arrow in the pedigree
Children of the same parents (brothers and sisters)
One row of the pedigree; numbered with Roman numerals, and the persons in each generation are numbered with Arabic numerals from left to right
A dot inside a circle or square, or a half-shaded symbol

blocks.label: Figure 7.1
blocks.caption: Main symbols used in drawing pedigrees: male (square), female (circle), affected (shaded), marriage, consanguineous marriage, sibs, twins, carriers, stillborn child and others (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Rule of drawing a pedigree: each generation is written in one horizontal row; the parents are joined by a marriage line, and the children are placed on a “sibship” line hanging from it in order of birth from left to right; a key (legend) to the symbols is given under the pedigree.

sections.title: 3. Criteria of the types of inheritance

blocks.title: Table 7.3. Criteria for determining the type of inheritance from a pedigree
head: Type
Main features
Examples
rows: The trait occurs in every generation (“vertical” transmission); at least one parent of an affected child is affected; males and females are affected equally; 50 % of children of an affected heterozygote and a healthy partner are affected
Polydactyly, achondroplasia, Marfan syndrome, Huntington disease, brachydactyly

The trait skips generations (“horizontal” transmission — among sibs); affected children are often born to healthy parents; the risk in a marriage of two carriers is 25 %; frequent in consanguineous marriages
Phenylketonuria, albinism, cystic fibrosis, Wilson disease, galactosemia

Women are affected 2 times more often; all daughters of an affected father are affected, his sons are healthy
Only in males, from father to all sons

blocks.label: Figure 7.2
blocks.caption: Inheritance of an autosomal dominant trait (pedigree): affected individuals (black symbols) appear in every generation, all of them heterozygous (Aa); healthy individuals are aa (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 7.3
blocks.caption: Inheritance of a recessive trait (phenylketonuria): affected children are born to phenotypically healthy heterozygous (Aa) parents; the affected persons in generation IV come from a consanguineous marriage (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The classic example of a hemophilia pedigree is the family of **Queen Victoria** of Great Britain (Figure 7.4). Victoria was a carrier of the hemophilia gene; her son Leopold was affected and her daughters Alice and Beatrice were carriers, and the gene spread to the royal families of Germany, Russia and Spain (the Russian heir to the throne Alexei also had hemophilia).

blocks.label: Figure 7.4
blocks.caption: Transmission of hemophilia — the descendants of Queen Victoria of Great Britain (shaded square — affected male, circle with a dot — carrier female) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Criteria of **mitochondrial (cytoplasmic) inheritance**: the trait passes only from the **mother** to all her children (sons and daughters); it is not transmitted by an affected father; severity varies within a family because the cell contains a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondria (**heteroplasmy**). Examples: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, MELAS and MERRF syndromes.
Algorithm for determining the mode of inheritance from a pedigree

items: Is the trait present in every generation? Yes — suspect a dominant type; if it skips generations — recessive.
Was an affected child born to healthy parents? If yes — recessive type.
Are men and women affected equally? If equally — autosomal; if mainly men — X-recessive; if only men and from father to son — Y-linked.
Are all daughters of an affected father affected and all sons healthy? If yes — X-dominant.
If the trait passes only through the mother to all children — mitochondrial.
Finally write the genotype of each individual and calculate the risk for the next child.

blocks.text: **Consanguineous marriage** (first cousins and others) increases the risk of recessive diseases, because relatives may have received the same recessive allele from a common ancestor. First cousins share 1/8 of their genes; the probability that both alleles in their child come from the common ancestor (the **inbreeding coefficient**, F) is 1/16. That is why parents of children with rare recessive diseases (for example, many enzymopathies) are often blood relatives.

The **twin method** (F. Galton, 1876) compares traits in monozygotic and dizygotic twins to determine the relative role of heredity and environment in their formation. Twins are born in about 1 % of human births.

blocks.title: Table 7.4. Types of twins
head: Feature
Monozygotic (identical, MZ)
Dizygotic (fraternal, DZ)
rows: One zygote splits into two at the early stages of cleavage
Two eggs are fertilized by two sperm
On average 50 % genes in common (like ordinary sibs)

blocks.text: The structure of monozygotic twins depends on when the zygote divided: if it divides in the first **3 days** after fertilisation, each twin has its own placenta and membranes (dichorionic-diamniotic); on **days 4–8** — a shared placenta and separate amnions (monochorionic-diamniotic, the most common); on **days 8–13** — a shared amnion; if incomplete division occurs **after day 13**, **conjoined (Siamese) twins** arise. Zygosity is determined by similarity in many traits (hair and eye colour, ear shape), blood groups, dermatoglyphics and, most precisely, DNA analysis.

The presence of a trait in both twins is called **concordance**, and its presence in only one is called **discordance**. The percentage of concordance is compared in MZ and DZ pairs: if concordance in MZ is much higher than in DZ, heredity plays an important role in the development of the trait. The **coefficient of heritability** is calculated by Holzinger’s formula:
Here C is the percentage of concordance, H the share of heredity and E the share of environment. If H > 0.7, the trait is determined mainly by heredity; if H < 0.4, mainly by the environment.

blocks.title: Table 7.5. Concordance of twins for some traits and diseases (%)
head: Trait / disease
MZ
DZ

parts.text: In measles concordance is almost equally high in MZ and DZ — susceptibility to this disease depends mainly on the environment (contact with the virus). In schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes MZ concordance is much higher — these are **diseases with a hereditary predisposition (multifactorial)**.

blocks.text: **Limitations** of the twin method: monozygotic twins grow in the same conditions both in the uterus and in the family, so the share of the “shared environment” may add to the heritability and overstate it; twins are often born premature and with low birth weight. For this reason some studies compare monozygotic twins raised apart in different families — this shows the role of heredity most precisely.

A **population** is a group of individuals of one species living for a long time in a certain area and freely marrying each other. In humans small groups are distinguished within large populations: a **deme** (1500–4000 people, marriages within the group 80–90 %) and an **isolate** (up to 1500 people, marriages within the group more than 90 %). In isolates consanguineous marriages are common, so the frequency of recessive diseases rises (geographic, religious, ethnic isolates).

In a population of self-fertilizing organisms the proportion of heterozygotes halves in each generation and the population splits into homozygous lines. In cross-fertilizing (panmictic) populations the ratio of genotypes obeys the **Hardy-Weinberg law**:

Here p is the frequency of the dominant allele (A), q the frequency of the recessive allele (a), and p^2^, 2pq and q^2^ the frequencies of the genotypes AA, Aa and aa. The law holds for an **ideal population**: the population is large, mating is random (panmixia), and there are no mutations, natural selection or migration.

parts.text: Calculation always starts from the **recessive homozygotes**, because only their phenotype matches their genotype: for example, if phenylketonuria occurs at 1 : 10000, then q^2^ = 0.0001, q = 0.01 and p = 0.99; heterozygous carriers 2pq ≈ 0.02, i.e., one in every 50 people.

blocks.text: **Stages of the population-statistical method:** choosing the population, collecting data (frequency of the disease or trait), statistical analysis. The method is used to determine allele and genotype frequencies, the spread of hereditary diseases and carriers and their geographic and ethnic differences, the frequency of mutations, and to plan medical genetic services.

blocks.title: Table 7.6. Factors disturbing the genetic equilibrium of a population (elementary factors of evolution)
head: Factor
Effect
Human example
rows: Create new alleles; frequency 10^−5^–10^−6^ per gene per gamete
Reduces harmful alleles or preserves them by heterozygote advantage
Random change of allele frequencies in small populations
Increase of rare diseases in isolates
When a small group settles a new area, the founders' alleles become common
Tay–Sachs in Ashkenazi Jews, specific diseases in Finland

blocks.text: For X-linked traits the Hardy–Weinberg calculation starts with men: because men are hemizygous, the frequency of affected men equals q directly. For example, if colour blindness occurs in 8 % of men, q = 0,08; in women colour blindness is q^2^ = 0,0064 (≈ 0,6 %), and carrier women are 2pq = 2 × 0,92 × 0,08 ≈ 0,147 (≈ 15 %). This is why X-recessive diseases are many times more common in men than in women.

parts.text: Population-statistical data are the basis for planning **newborn screening** programmes in public health: for example, all newborns are tested for phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism and cystic fibrosis. In regions with many carriers (thalassaemia in the Mediterranean) carrier testing before marriage is carried out.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The proband is a boy with hemophilia; his parents are healthy. The proband’s maternal grandfather has hemophilia and his grandmother is healthy. Hemophilia has not been observed on the father’s side.
cases.ask: Draw the pedigree and determine the type of inheritance and the genotypes of the family members.
cases.answer: The disease occurs only in males and passes through the maternal line (grandfather → mother → grandson), with no father-to-son transmission — X-linked recessive type. Grandfather — X^h^Y, grandmother — X^H^X^H^; their daughter (the proband’s mother) is an obligate carrier — X^H^X^h^; the proband’s father — X^H^Y; the proband — X^h^Y. In this family the risk for later sons to have hemophilia is 50 %, and for daughters to be carriers 50 %.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a city 51 % of the population is brown-eyed and 49 % blue-eyed. Brown eyes (A) are completely dominant over blue eyes (a).
cases.ask: What are the frequencies of homozygous and heterozygous genotypes in the population?

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Two populations of the same origin but living under different conditions differ sharply in the frequency of a certain recessive disease: 1 : 5000 in one and 1 : 50000 in the other.
cases.ask: Explain the reason.
cases.answer: The population with the higher frequency is probably an isolate or a deme: consanguineous marriages (inbreeding), gene drift and the “founder effect” (an allele that by chance was common in the small group from which the population descended) act in it. In such a population recessive alleles often become homozygous. In a large panmictic population there are few consanguineous marriages and the allele is expressed less often.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: The frequency of haemophilia A among men is 1 : 5000.
cases.ask: Calculate the frequency of carrier women and affected women in the population.
cases.answer: Men are hemizygous, so q = 1/5000 = 0,0002; p ≈ 0,9998. Carrier women: 2pq ≈ 2 × 0,0002 = 0,0004, i.e. one in every 2500 women. Affected women: q^2^ = 0,00000004, i.e. one in 25 million — practically very rare. This is why haemophilia occurs almost only in men.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: In a family where the parents are first cousins, one of two children was born with phenylketonuria. The parents and their parents are healthy.
cases.ask: How is the disease inherited? What is the role of the consanguineous marriage? What is the probability that the healthy child is a carrier?
cases.answer: An affected child of healthy parents means **autosomal recessive** inheritance; both parents are heterozygous (Aa × Aa). Because they are cousins, they are likely to have received the same recessive allele from a common grandparent — consanguineous marriage raises the risk of a rare recessive disease. The healthy child cannot be aa; of the remaining AA : 2 Aa, the probability that he or she is a carrier is **2/3**. For each further child the risk of disease is 25 %.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: Monozygotic twins were born with one shared placenta but separate amniotic membranes.
cases.ask: When did the zygote probably divide? What will these twins be like in sex and blood group?
cases.answer: A shared placenta with separate amnions (monochorionic-diamniotic twins) arises when the inner cell mass splits in two at the blastocyst stage, **4–8 days** after fertilisation. Since they come from one zygote, they have the same genotype: their **sex, blood groups**, HLA antigens and dermatoglyphics match, and a skin graft from one to the other is not rejected.
