summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Dominant type — **“vertical”** (every generation), recessive type — **“horizontal”** (among sibs, skipping generations).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Hardy-Weinberg is a squared binomial: **(p + q)^2^ = p^2^ + 2pq + q^2^** — AA, Aa, aa.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Pedigree analysis is the basis of genetic counseling: it reveals the type of inheritance and the risk for the next child, while the twin method assesses the share of heredity in multifactorial diseases.

topics.title: Methods of studying human genetics: cytogenetic, dermatoglyphic and biochemical methods. Prenatal diagnosis

goals.text: To teach the student the methods of analyzing the human karyotype, the classification of chromosomes (Denver and Paris nomenclatures), the detection of sex chromatin and its medical importance, the basics of dermatoglyphic analysis, biochemical, molecular genetic and immunogenetic methods, and the methods of prenatal diagnosis.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the stages of karyotype preparation and the methods of staining chromosomes;
the Denver groups of chromosomes (A–G);
sex X chromatin (the Barr body) and “drumsticks”, and the Lyon hypothesis;
the types of finger and palm patterns, the atd angle and dermatoglyphic changes in diseases;
screening and biochemical tests, PCR, FISH and the methods of prenatal diagnosis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: read a karyogram and write the karyotype formula;
determine the number of X chromosomes from the number of sex chromatin bodies;
determine the pattern type from a fingerprint and the atd angle on the palm.

sections.title: 1. The cytogenetic method and karyotype analysis

blocks.text: The **cytogenetic method** is the microscopic study of the number and structure of chromosomes. The number of human chromosomes was established precisely in 1956 by J. Tjio and A. Levan (2n = 46). **Peripheral blood lymphocytes** are most often used for the test, as well as bone marrow, skin fibroblasts, amniocytes and chorionic cells.

items: Lymphocytes are cultured in a nutrient medium for 72 hours under the action of **phytohemagglutinin** (a mitogen).
Division is arrested in metaphase with **colchicine**.
The cells are treated with a **hypotonic solution** (0.075 M KCl) — they swell and the chromosomes spread out.
Fixation (methanol + acetic acid), dropping onto a slide and staining.
Metaphase plates are studied under the microscope and photographed, and a **karyogram** (chromosomes arranged in pairs) is made.

blocks.text: **Staining methods:** routine staining allows chromosomes to be grouped only by size and shape; **differential staining** (G-, Q-, R- and C-banding) produces a specific pattern of transverse bands on each chromosome and makes it possible to identify each pair and small aberrations (Figure 8.1). Modern methods are **FISH** (fluorescence in situ hybridization) and chromosomal microarray analysis.

blocks.label: Figure 8.1
blocks.caption: Diagram of differentially stained human chromosomes (idiogram): 22 pairs of autosomes and the sex chromosomes (X, Y); the outlined pairs — 13, 18, 21 — are those most often involved in chromosomal diseases (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 8.1. Denver classification of human chromosomes (1960)
head: Group
Pairs
Description

blocks.label: Figure 8.2
blocks.caption: Normal male karyotype: left — a metaphase spread, right — the karyogram (chromosomes arranged in Denver groups A–G, with X and Y shown separately) (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Karyotype notation (ISCN):** first the total number of chromosomes, then the sex chromosomes, then the anomaly: 46,XX — normal female; 46,XY — normal male; 47,XY,+21 — male with Down syndrome; 46,XX,5p^−^ — deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5; 46,XY/47,XY,+21 — mosaicism. Chromosome arms: p — short, q — long.

**Band nomenclature.** In differential staining each arm (p — short, q — long) is divided, starting from the centromere, into **regions** and **bands**. For example, 5p15.2 is sub-band 2 of band 5 in region 1 of the short arm of chromosome 5; 7q31 is band 1 of region 3 of the long arm of chromosome 7 (the location of the cystic fibrosis gene). Abbreviations: del — deletion, dup — duplication, inv — inversion, t — translocation, r — ring chromosome, i — isochromosome; “mos” — mosaicism.

blocks.text: Indications for karyotyping

items: Multiple congenital defects, delay in mental and physical development.
Disorders of sexual development, ambiguous genitalia, primary amenorrhoea.
Infertility, recurrent miscarriage, stillbirths.
A chromosomal disease in the family or a balanced translocation in one parent.
Leukaemias and other tumours (karyotype of tumour cells — for diagnosis and prognosis).

parts.text: An **idiogram** is a schematic drawing of chromosomes with their differentially stained bands. A **karyogram** is a picture of the chromosomes of a metaphase plate of a particular person arranged in pairs.

blocks.text: **Sex X chromatin (the Barr body)** is a small (≈ 1 µm), densely staining triangular or crescent-shaped body lying under the nuclear envelope in the interphase nucleus. It was discovered in 1949 by M. Barr and E. Bertram in cat neurons. The Barr body is an **inactivated X chromosome**.

**The Lyon hypothesis** (M. Lyon, 1961): in the somatic cells of a woman, at an early stage of embryonic development (about day 16), one of the X chromosomes is randomly inactivated and becomes heterochromatin. Because of this the female body is a **mosaic** of cells with an active paternal or maternal X chromosome; this equalizes the dosage of genes in males and females (**dosage compensation**).

parts.text: **Number of Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes − 1.** 46,XY and 45,X — 0; 46,XX and 47,XXY — 1; 47,XXX and 48,XXXY — 2.

blocks.text: Sex chromatin is detected in the epithelium of the oral mucosa (buccal smear) and vaginal epithelium: the smear is stained with aceto-orcein or hematoxylin and 100 nuclei are counted. In a normal woman X chromatin is found in 20–40 % of nuclei, in a man in 0–2 %. In neutrophil leukocytes X chromatin appears as a **“drumstick”** projecting from the segmented nucleus (in 1–5 % of neutrophils in women) (Figure 8.3). **Y chromatin** is detected in male cells stained with quinacrine as a bright dot under the fluorescence microscope.

**Y chromatin (F body)** — when male cells are stained with acriquine (quinacrine), the distal part of the long arm of the Y chromosome glows as a bright dot under ultraviolet light. In a normal man more than 50 % of nuclei contain one F body, and in the 47,XYY karyotype — two. Y chromatin can also be detected in sperm and amniocytes.

blocks.label: Figure 8.3
blocks.caption: Sex X chromatin in leukocytes and an epithelial cell: left — “drumsticks” on neutrophil nuclei, right — a Barr body in the nucleus of a buccal epithelial cell (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Dermatoglyphics** is the study of the papillary ridges (patterns) on the skin of the fingers, palms and soles. The patterns form in months 3–6 of fetal life and do not change throughout life; they are inherited **polygenically**. **Dactyloscopy** studies finger patterns, **palmoscopy** palm patterns and **plantoscopy** sole patterns.

rows: Ridges pass from one side to the other forming an arch

blocks.label: Figure 8.4
blocks.caption: Ridge patterns on the skin of the fingers: top — photographs of arch, loop and whorl patterns; bottom — 1 — arch; 2 — loop; 3 — transition from loop to whorl; 4 — double loop (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: On the palm there are **triradii** (a, b, c, d) at the bases of four fingers and the **axial triradius t** near the wrist. The **atd angle** formed by joining points a, t and d is normally about 48°; when triradius t is displaced distally, the angle increases. The **flexion creases** of the palm are also analyzed.

blocks.label: Figure 8.5
blocks.caption: Dermatoglyphic analysis of the palm: the a, b, c, d triradii at the bases of the fingers, the axial triradius t and measurement of the atd angle; palm areas and patterns are marked with numbers (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Ridge count** (TRC) is the number of papillary ridges counted between the centre of a pattern and the triradius; the total ridge count over ten fingers averages ≈ 145 in men and ≈ 127 in women. It depends on the number of sex chromosomes: it decreases as X chromosomes increase (low in Klinefelter syndrome) and increases in the 45,X karyotype.

blocks.label: Figure 8.6
blocks.caption: The main flexion creases of the palm (1–5): finger-base creases, distal and proximal palmar creases, thenar crease and wrist crease; in Down syndrome creases 2 and 3 merge into a single transverse (“simian”) crease (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Dermatoglyphics is a quick, cheap and painless **auxiliary** method used when chromosomal diseases are suspected, to determine the zygosity of twins and in forensic medicine (personal identification); the final diagnosis is made only by karyotyping.

sections.title: 4. Biochemical, molecular genetic and immunogenetic methods

blocks.text: The **biochemical method** detects hereditary disorders of metabolism (enzymopathies). It is carried out in two stages: (1) **screening (rapid)** — testing many people with simple qualitative reactions (for example, a green color when FeCl~3~ is added to urine in phenylketonuria; measuring phenylalanine and TSH in a drop of heel blood in newborns); (2) **confirmatory** — quantitative measurement of metabolites and enzyme activity in blood, urine and tissues (chromatography, electrophoresis, tandem mass spectrometry).

blocks.title: Table 8.6. Biochemical screening and confirmatory tests
head: Test
Essence
For which disease
rows: 10 % iron (III) chloride is dropped into urine — a blue-green colour appears if phenylpyruvic acid is present
Excess phenylalanine in a dried blood spot on filter paper is detected by bacterial growth
Dozens of amino acids and acylcarnitines are measured in one blood spot
Detection of reducing sugars in urine
Enzyme activity is measured in leucocytes or fibroblasts

blocks.text: **Molecular genetic methods** analyze at the DNA level: isolating DNA and RNA from biological material (blood, buccal epithelium, chorion, amniocytes), **PCR** (polymerase chain reaction — copying a desired DNA segment millions of times), cutting with restriction enzymes and gel electrophoresis, **sequencing** (reading the nucleotide sequence), hybridization with DNA probes and FISH. They are used to detect gene mutations and carriers, for prenatal diagnosis and to establish paternity.

The **immunogenetic method** studies the polymorphism of blood groups, erythrocyte and leukocyte antigens (the HLA system) and serum proteins by antigen-antibody reactions. It is used to select donors in transplantation, to prevent Rh incompatibility, to establish paternity and to assess predisposition to diseases. **Monoclonal antibodies** are identical antibodies obtained from a single cell clone (a hybridoma) and directed against one antigenic determinant; **polyclonal** antibodies come from different clones and are directed against several determinants of the antigen.

**Prenatal diagnosis** is the detection of hereditary diseases and developmental defects in the fetus before birth. Its tasks are to prevent the birth of a child with a severe hereditary pathology, to plan pregnancy and delivery correctly and to start early treatment of some diseases.

Amniotic fluid is taken: karyotype of amniocytes, sex chromatin, biochemical and DNA analysis (Figure 8.7)

blocks.text: In first-trimester combined screening (weeks 11–14) the mother's age, the **nuchal translucency** on ultrasound (risk is high if it exceeds 3 mm) and blood hCG and PAPP-A are combined to calculate the risk of a chromosomal disease. If the risk is high (for example, greater than 1 : 100), the woman is offered an invasive test (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis) and determination of the fetal karyotype. Screening does not make a diagnosis; it only selects a risk group.

**Preimplantation genetic diagnosis** — in in vitro fertilisation (IVF), 1–5 cells are taken from a 3–5-day embryo and tested for a chromosomal or gene disease, and only a healthy embryo is transferred to the uterus. In families with a high risk of severe hereditary disease it avoids the need to terminate a pregnancy.

blocks.label: Figure 8.7
blocks.caption: Examination of cells obtained from amniotic fluid (amniocentesis): the fluid around the fetus is taken; the cells are cultured for karyotyping, sex chromatin and biochemical tests (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Invasive methods (chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis, cordocentesis) carry a risk of miscarriage (≈ 0.5–1 %), so they are performed only when there is an **indication**: maternal age over 35, a chromosomal or gene disease in the family, a translocation carrier in a parent, or a screening result showing high risk.

skills.title: Skill: detecting sex chromatin in a buccal smear

items: After rinsing the mouth with water, scrape the surface epithelial layer from the inner surface of the cheek with a sterile spatula (discard the first scraping).
Spread the material thinly on a slide and fix it in 96 % alcohol.
Stain with aceto-orcein for 3–5 minutes, remove the excess stain and cover with a coverslip.
Under the immersion objective look for dense triangular bodies beneath the nuclear envelope.
Count 100 well-stained nuclei and calculate the percentage of nuclei with X chromatin.
Evaluate the result: 20–40 % — female (XX), 0–2 % — male (XY); nuclei with two bodies indicate X polysomy.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: When the cells of a newborn with a female phenotype were examined cytogenetically, the karyogram showed 44 autosomes and the X and Y chromosomes.
cases.ask: What is the doctor’s conclusion?
cases.answer: The karyotype is 46,XY — genetically male, while the phenotype is female. This is a disorder of sexual differentiation: most often a mutation of the androgen receptor gene (testicular feminization syndrome — the testes lie in the abdomen or the inguinal canal) or loss/mutation of the SRY gene (Swyer syndrome). No X chromatin is found in a buccal smear. Hormonal and molecular tests and consultation with an endocrinologist and a geneticist are needed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: The karyogram of a child referred for genetic counseling showed trisomy for one of the chromosomes of group D (pairs 13–15).
cases.ask: What is the doctor’s conclusion, and how can the exact pair be determined?
cases.answer: Group D trisomy most often concerns pair 13 (Patau syndrome, 47,XX(XY),+13): microcephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, heart defects, microphthalmia. With routine staining chromosomes 13, 14 and 15 cannot be told apart, so the exact pair must be determined by differential (G-) banding or FISH.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Buccal smears were examined in patients with the karyotypes 47,XXY; 48,XXYY; 48,XXXY.
cases.ask: How many Barr bodies will there be in each case? Prove your answer.
cases.answer: The number of Barr bodies is one less than the number of X chromosomes (the Lyon rule: all X chromosomes except one are inactivated). 47,XXY — 1; 48,XXYY — 1; 48,XXXY — 2. The number of Y chromosomes does not affect the number of Barr bodies. All are variants of Klinefelter syndrome; intellectual disability becomes more severe as the number of X chromosomes increases.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: In a 38-year-old pregnant woman at week 12, ultrasound shows a nuchal translucency of 3,5 mm, the blood hCG β-subunit is raised and PAPP-A is lowered.
cases.ask: What risk should be considered and what is the next test?
cases.answer: The mother's age (over 35), increased nuchal translucency (over 3 mm), raised hCG and lowered PAPP-A together indicate a high risk of **Down syndrome (trisomy 21)**. Screening is not a diagnosis, so the woman is offered genetic counselling and **invasive prenatal diagnosis** — chorionic villus sampling at weeks 10–13 or amniocentesis at weeks 15–20 to **determine the fetal karyotype** (the miscarriage risk of ≈ 0,5–1 % is explained). An alternative is a cell-free fetal DNA test in maternal blood (NIPT); if it is positive, it is still confirmed by an invasive method.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: In the maternity hospital, a blood spot taken on day 4 (Guthrie test) showed a high level of phenylalanine in a newborn. The baby looks healthy.
cases.ask: How is this result interpreted and what should be done?
cases.answer: This is suspected **phenylketonuria** (a newborn-screening result). To confirm the diagnosis, the blood phenylalanine level is measured again quantitatively and, if needed, DNA analysis of the phenylalanine hydroxylase gene is done. If confirmed, the baby is put at once on a **low-phenylalanine diet** — early diet prevents intellectual disability. It is natural that the baby looks healthy: signs appear after a few months, once phenylalanine has accumulated and damaged the brain. The parents receive genetic counselling (autosomal recessive, 25 % risk for the next child).

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A child with delayed mental development whose cry resembles a cat's mewing has the karyotype 46,XY,del(5)(p15).
cases.ask: Explain the karyotype notation. What syndrome is this?
cases.answer: 46 — the total chromosome number is normal; XY — male sex; del(5)(p15) — **a deletion in band 15 of the short (p) arm of chromosome 5** (a segment is lost). This is **cri-du-chat syndrome** (5p^−^, Lejeune syndrome): a typical cry due to an underdeveloped larynx, microcephaly, a moon face, widely spaced eyes and intellectual disability. Because the chromosome number is unchanged, such defects are detected only by differential staining or FISH.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The karyotype is the **“gold standard”** for diagnosing chromosomal diseases; dermatoglyphics and sex chromatin are auxiliary rapid methods.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Number of pairs in the Denver groups: **“3-2-7-3-3-2-2”** — autosome pairs in groups A, B, C, D, E, F, G (22 in total).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Prenatal diagnosis (ultrasound, biochemical screening, NIPT, invasive methods) prevents the birth of children with severe hereditary pathology; invasive methods are used only when indicated.

topics.title: Hereditary diseases: chromosomal diseases, gene diseases and diseases with hereditary predisposition. Types of marriage. Medical genetic counseling

goals.text: To teach the student the classification of hereditary diseases, the causes, signs and diagnosis of syndromes caused by changes in the number and structure of autosomes and sex chromosomes, hereditary metabolic diseases, multifactorial diseases, the medical genetic consequences of consanguineous marriage and the principles of medical genetic counseling (MGC).
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the classification of hereditary diseases (chromosomal, gene, multifactorial, mitochondrial);
the karyotype and main signs of Down, Edwards, Patau, Klinefelter and Shereshevsky-Turner syndromes;
hereditary disorders of the metabolism of amino acids, carbohydrates, lipids and purines;
the concepts of genocopy and phenocopy, inbreeding and outbreeding;
the aim and stages of MGC and the levels of genetic risk.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify a syndrome from its karyotype formula;
calculate the proportion of shared genes from the degree of kinship;
assess the recurrence genetic risk for a family.

blocks.text: **Hereditary diseases** are diseases caused by changes in the hereditary apparatus (gene, chromosome, genome) that can be passed on to the next generations. They may be congenital or may appear later (for example, Huntington disease at the age of 35–45). A **congenital disease** is not always hereditary: congenital defects also arise from intrauterine infection or teratogens.

Microcephaly, cleft lip and palate, microphthalmia, polydactyly, scalp defects, heart and kidney defects; most die before 1 year

parts.text: The main risk factor for Down syndrome is **maternal age**: at 25 years the risk is ≈ 1 : 1250, at 35 years ≈ 1 : 350, at 40 years ≈ 1 : 100, at 45 years ≈ 1 : 30. In the **translocation** form (for example, a Robertsonian translocation of chromosome 21 onto chromosome 14) one parent is a balanced translocation carrier and the recurrence risk is high, so the parents’ karyotype is examined.

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: Palm dermatoglyphics: a — normal palm print; b, c — the single transverse (“simian”) crease and altered papillary patterns in Down syndrome (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In Down syndrome, besides intellectual disability, there are **congenital heart defects** (in 40–50 % of patients, most often atrioventricular canal), duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, reduced immunity, a 10–20-fold increased risk of **acute leukaemia** and early **Alzheimer's disease** after age 40 (an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21). With early rehabilitation and surgical correction of heart defects the average life expectancy has increased to 60 years.

parts.text: A carrier of a **balanced translocation** (45 chromosomes but complete genetic material) is healthy, but some of his or her gametes are unbalanced. So in recurrent miscarriage, stillbirth or the birth of children with Down syndrome, **the karyotypes of both parents** are examined.

blocks.text: **Syndromes caused by changes in chromosome structure:** **cri-du-chat** syndrome (46,5p^−^ — deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5): the infant’s cry resembles a cat’s mewing (underdeveloped larynx), microcephaly, moon face, hypertelorism, severe intellectual disability. **18q^−^ syndrome** (deletion of the long arm of chromosome 18): intellectual disability, microcephaly, facial and ear anomalies. **Wolf-Hirschhorn** (4p^−^), **Williams** (7q11.23 microdeletion) and **DiGeorge** (22q11.2 microdeletion) syndromes also belong to this group.

blocks.text: Chromosomal abnormalities cause ≈ 50 % of early miscarriages: the most common among them are autosomal trisomies (especially trisomy 16), 45,X and **triploidy** (69,XXX or 69,XXY). In live-born babies the frequency of chromosomal diseases is ≈ 0,5–0,6 %.

parts.text: Common signs of chromosomal diseases: **multiple congenital defects**, delay of intellectual and physical development, a dysmorphic face (minor anomalies) and altered dermatoglyphics. The diagnosis is confirmed only by **karyotyping**. Most of them arise anew (de novo) and are not passed on, because patients are often infertile.

sections.title: 4. Gene (monogenic) diseases — hereditary disorders of metabolism

blocks.text: Most gene diseases are **enzymopathies**: as a result of a mutation an enzyme is not synthesized or its activity decreases, the preceding metabolites accumulate and have a toxic effect, while the next product is deficient. They are mostly inherited as autosomal recessive.

parts.text: Phenylketonuria, galactosemia and congenital hypothyroidism are detected by **newborn screening**: a drop of blood from the baby’s heel is tested. A special diet or hormone therapy started early (in the first weeks of life) prevents intellectual disability.

sections.title: 5. Diseases with hereditary predisposition. Genocopy and phenocopy

blocks.text: **Diseases with hereditary predisposition (multifactorial)** are produced by the sum of the small effects of several genes (a polygenic system) together with environmental factors. They are the most common (hypertension, atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes, bronchial asthma, peptic ulcer, schizophrenia, psoriasis, many congenital defects). Typical features: clustering of the disease in families, but not in Mendelian ratios; the risk rises with closer kinship and with more affected persons in the family; prevention is possible by changing environmental factors (diet, smoking, stress).

Multifactorial diseases are explained by the **threshold model**: each person has a sum of predisposing genes and environmental factors — the **liability**; when it exceeds a certain threshold the disease appears. Therefore: (1) the risk for relatives of an affected person is higher than in the general population but does not fit Mendelian ratios; (2) the more affected relatives and the more severe the disease in the family, the higher the risk; (3) the risk is higher for relatives of a patient of the less often affected sex (for example, relatives of a girl with pyloric stenosis).

sections.title: 6. Principles of treatment and prevention of hereditary diseases

blocks.text: Although a hereditary disease is linked to the genotype, many of its forms can be treated or made less severe. Methods of treatment:

blocks.title: Table 9.10. Methods of treating hereditary diseases
head: Method
Essence
Examples

Giving the hormone, enzyme or protein
Thyroxine in congenital hypothyroidism, factor VIII in haemophilia, enzyme in Gaucher disease
Correcting a defect or transplanting an organ
Surgery for cleft lip and heart defects; bone-marrow transplantation in thalassaemia
Introducing a normal gene copy into cells with a viral vector or editing the gene
Spinal muscular atrophy, some immunodeficiencies, haemophilia

blocks.text: Prevention of hereditary pathology

items: **Primary (before marriage and pregnancy)** — genetic counselling, carrier testing, pregnancy planning, folic acid, avoiding mutagens and teratogens, having children before the mother is 35.
**Secondary (prenatal)** — screening and prenatal diagnosis in pregnancy; if severe pathology is found, the family makes a decision.
**Tertiary (postnatal)** — newborn screening, early detection of disease and starting treatment before signs appear.

blocks.text: **Outbreeding** is marriage between unrelated persons; it reduces the probability that recessive alleles become homozygous and increases heterozygosity in the population. **Inbreeding** is marriage between relatives. Relatives may have received the same recessive alleles from a common ancestor, so such marriages increase the frequency of autosomal recessive diseases, congenital defects, stillbirths and miscarriages.

parts.text: In a marriage of first cousins the risk of a child with severe hereditary pathology is about 2 times higher (≈ 5–6 %) than the risk in the general population (≈ 3 %); if there is a recessive disease in the family, the risk is even higher. Such couples should definitely undergo genetic counseling.

blocks.text: **Medical genetic counseling** is specialized medical care aimed at preventing the birth of children with hereditary pathology. Its aim is to determine and explain the level of genetic risk to the family and to help it make a decision about having children. Counseling is **prospective** (before marriage or pregnancy, before an affected child is born) or **retrospective** (after an affected child has been born in the family).
Indications for referral to MGC

items: a child with a hereditary disease or congenital defect in the family;
consanguineous marriage;
maternal age over 35;
recurrent miscarriage, stillbirth, infertility;
exposure to teratogenic factors (drugs, radiation, infections) during pregnancy;
high risk in prenatal screening.

blocks.text: Stages of MGC

items: **Clarifying the diagnosis** — clinical, cytogenetic, biochemical and molecular tests.
**Drawing a pedigree** and determining the type of inheritance.
**Calculating the genetic risk** (by Mendel’s laws or empirical tables).

**Conclusion and explanation** — the risk, the severity of the disease and the possibilities of treatment and prenatal diagnosis are explained to the family in plain words; the decision is made by the family.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the recurrence genetic risk in a family

items: Establish the diagnosis of the proband’s disease and its type of inheritance (pedigree, karyotype, biochemical analysis).
For a monogenic disease write the parents’ genotypes: in AR both Aa, in AD one Aa, in X-recessive the mother X^A^X^a^.
Calculate the risk by Mendel’s laws: AR — 25 %, AD — 50 %, X-recessive — 50 % for sons.
For a chromosomal disease examine the parents’ karyotypes: in simple trisomy the recurrence risk is low (≈ 1 % + age-related risk), in balanced translocation carriage it is high.
For multifactorial diseases use empirical risk tables.
Assign the risk level (low, moderate, high) and explain the possibility of prenatal diagnosis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: When the patient’s karyotype was examined, some cells were found to be 45,X and others 46,XX.
cases.ask: How can this be explained?
cases.answer: This is mosaicism — 45,X/46,XX (the mosaic form of Shereshevsky-Turner syndrome). The zygote was normal (46,XX), but in one of the early cleavage divisions an X chromosome was lost (anaphase lag) or failed to separate, giving rise to two cell lines. The signs are usually milder than in the complete form of the syndrome, and some patients may be fertile.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A marriage of first cousins produced 2 children: one had developmental defects, the other severe intellectual disability.
cases.ask: Explain the cause genetically.
cases.answer: First cousins share 1/8 of their genes, and the inbreeding coefficient of their children is 1/16: there is a high probability that both parents carry the same recessive allele from the common grandparents. As a result the children become homozygous (aa) for that allele and autosomal recessive diseases appear (for example, enzymopathies with intellectual disability such as phenylketonuria, or syndromes of congenital defects). Genetic counseling, clarification of the diagnosis and prenatal diagnosis are recommended before the next pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A child with a hereditary disease was born in a family that had undergone genetic counseling and in which an affected child was not expected.
cases.ask: How can this be explained?
cases.answer: Possible reasons: (1) a new (de novo) mutation or chromosomal error arose in a sex cell of one parent — such cases cannot be predicted in advance; (2) low risk does not mean zero risk — the probability was realized; (3) the disease was hidden in the family because of incomplete penetrance or genocopy; (4) germline mosaicism; (5) uncertain paternity or an incorrect diagnosis. The diagnosis of the new child must be clarified and the risk recalculated.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: The second child of a 25-year-old woman was born with Down syndrome; before that she had two miscarriages. The mother's karyotype is 45,XX,t(14;21). The father's karyotype is normal.
cases.ask: Which form of Down syndrome does the child have? Why did this happen even though the mother is young? What is the risk for the next child?
cases.answer: The mother is a carrier of a **balanced Robertsonian translocation**: her chromosome 21 is fused with chromosome 14, giving 45 chromosomes in total but complete genetic material, so she is healthy. Some of her gametes carry the fused 14/21 chromosome together with a free chromosome 21 — at fertilisation the child has three doses of chromosome 21 material (**translocation Down syndrome**, 46 chromosomes). Some gametes are unbalanced and monosomic embryos die — this explains the miscarriages. The risk does not depend on the mother's age; the risk of Down syndrome for the next child is ≈ 10–15 %, so prenatal diagnosis is recommended in every pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: A woman whose first child was born with spina bifida is planning another pregnancy.
cases.ask: What preventive measures are recommended?
cases.answer: Neural tube defects are a **multifactorial** disease; after one affected child the recurrence risk is much higher than in the general population (≈ 2–5 %). Recommendations: (1) take **high-dose folic acid** at least 1–3 months before planned conception and throughout the 1st trimester (reduces the risk by ≈ 70 %); (2) control diabetes well if present, reduce obesity and avoid some anticonvulsants (valproate); (3) in pregnancy, measure maternal blood **α-fetoprotein** and do ultrasound (weeks 16–20) — early detection of the defect.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A 40-year-old man has developed involuntary jerky movements and disturbances of memory and behaviour. His father had the same illness at this age. The patient has an 18-year-old son.
cases.ask: What disease should be considered? What is the son's risk and what ethical issues arise?
cases.answer: This is **Huntington's chorea** — an autosomal dominant disease caused by expansion of CAG trinucleotide repeats in a gene on chromosome 4. It usually begins at 35–45 years, often after the person has had children. The patient is heterozygous, so his son's risk of inheriting the gene is **50 %**. The number of repeats may increase when passed from the father, leading to earlier onset (**anticipation**). DNA analysis can diagnose the disease before signs appear, but it cannot yet be cured; therefore presymptomatic testing is done only at the free wish of an adult and after psychological counselling.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Chromosomal diseases are confirmed by **karyotyping**, enzymopathies by **biochemical** and **molecular** tests.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Trisomy numbers: **“13 — Patau, 18 — Edwards, 21 — Down”** — the smaller the number, the larger the chromosome and the more severe the syndrome.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Newborn screening (PKU, hypothyroidism, galactosemia) and genetic counseling are the most effective prevention of hereditary diseases.

topics.title: General laws of proembryonic (progenesis), embryonic (embryogenesis) and postembryonic development. Teratogenic factors. Gerontology. Regeneration. Homeostasis. Transplantation

goals.text: To teach the student the periods of ontogenesis, the stages of gametogenesis (spermatogenesis and oogenesis), the types of eggs, the laws of fertilization, cleavage, gastrulation and organogenesis, the mechanisms of ontogenesis, critical periods and teratogenic factors, postnatal development and aging, and the basics of regeneration, transplantation and homeostasis.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the kinds, types and periods of ontogenesis;
the stages of spermatogenesis and oogenesis and the chromosome set and DNA content in them;
the types of eggs by the amount and distribution of yolk and the types of cleavage;
the methods of gastrulation and the derivatives of the germ layers;
embryonic induction, critical periods and teratogens;
the theories of aging, types of regeneration, types of transplantation and the mechanisms of homeostasis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write the genetic formula of the cell at each stage of gametogenesis;
identify the organs that develop from each germ layer;
assess the consequence of a teratogenic effect according to the stage of pregnancy.

blocks.text: **Ontogenesis** (E. Haeckel, 1866) is the individual development of an organism: the set of changes from the formation of the zygote (in asexual reproduction — from separation from the parent) until death. It is **direct** (without a larva — reptiles, birds, mammals) or **indirect** (with metamorphosis — amphibians, insects). Direct development is in turn divided into the **egg-laying** and **intrauterine** types; the intrauterine type is characteristic of humans.

head: Period

rows: Fertilization, cleavage, gastrulation, histo- and organogenesis; the embryonic period (up to 8 weeks) and the fetal period (from week 9 until birth)

blocks.text: **Gametogenesis** is the formation of gametes in the gonads. **Spermatogenesis** proceeds in four stages in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, and **oogenesis** in three stages in the ovary (Figure 10.1).

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: Gametogenesis — spermatogenesis and oogenesis: periods of multiplication, growth, maturation and formation; chromosome set and DNA content of the cells at each stage (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 10.2. Stages of spermatogenesis and oogenesis
head: Stage
Spermatogenesis

Genetic formula
rows: Spermatogonia divide by mitosis (from puberty throughout life)
Oogonia divide by mitosis (only in fetal life)
Primary oocytes (yolk accumulates); arrested in prophase of meiosis I until birth
Meiosis I → secondary spermatocytes (n2c) → meiosis II → spermatids

blocks.text: The **spermatozoon** is a motile cell consisting of a head (the nucleus and, in front of it, the enzyme-rich **acrosome**), a neck (centrioles), a middle piece (spirally arranged mitochondria — energy for movement) and a tail (axoneme, 9 + 2). A human spermatozoon is ≈ 60 µm long. The **egg** is immotile and large (≈ 130–150 µm in humans), with nutrients (yolk) in its cytoplasm; it is surrounded by a transparent coat (zona pellucida) and the **corona radiata** made of follicular cells.

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Cross-section of a seminiferous tubule: from the wall towards the centre lie spermatogonia, primary and secondary spermatocytes, spermatids and spermatozoa, with Sertoli cells between them (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In humans spermatogenesis continues from puberty throughout life; the formation of a mature spermatozoon from one spermatogonium takes ≈ 64–74 days. It is regulated by **follicle-stimulating hormone** (FSH — acts on Sertoli cells) and **luteinising hormone** (LH — stimulates testosterone synthesis in Leydig cells). Spermatogenesis requires the testis to be 2–3 °C below body temperature, so failure of the testis to descend into the scrotum (**cryptorchidism**) leads to infertility. A normal ejaculate contains at least 15 million spermatozoa per 1 ml.

blocks.label: Figure 10.3
blocks.caption: A mature (Graafian) ovarian follicle: 1 — follicle wall (granulosa layer); 2 — oocyte; 3 — zona pellucida; 4 — cumulus oophorus; 5 — corona radiata; 6 — follicular cavity (fluid); 7, 8 — theca layers (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: At birth a girl's ovaries contain ≈ 1–2 million primary oocytes, and at puberty ≈ 400 thousand, but only ≈ 400–500 of them reach ovulation in a lifetime; the rest undergo atresia. In each menstrual cycle a group of follicles grows under FSH; one becomes a **Graafian follicle** and, at the LH surge (≈ day 14 of the cycle), ruptures and releases a secondary oocyte into the abdominal cavity (**ovulation**). In place of the follicle a progesterone-producing **corpus luteum** forms. The egg can be fertilised for 12–24 hours after ovulation, and spermatozoa keep this ability for 2–5 days in the female genital tract.

parts.text: In oogenesis, **dictyotene** is the arrest of primary oocytes in diplotene of meiosis I from birth until ovulation (12–50 years). Meiosis I is completed before ovulation, and meiosis II is completed only when a spermatozoon enters the egg.

blocks.text: **Fertilization** is the fusion of a spermatozoon and an egg forming a diploid **zygote**; in humans it takes place in the ampulla of the uterine tube. Stages: approach of spermatozoa to the egg and the **acrosome reaction** (enzymes dissolve the corona radiata and zona pellucida), entry of one spermatozoon, the **cortical reaction** (blocking entry of other spermatozoa — prevention of polyspermy), and fusion of the male and female pronuclei (syngamy).

blocks.label: Figure 10.4
blocks.caption: Stages of fertilisation: top — secondary oocyte (in metaphase of meiosis II) with zona pellucida and corona radiata; middle — release of the second polar body after sperm entry, male and female pronuclei; bottom — the pronuclei approach each other and the zygote forms (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

items: **Capacitation** — maturation of spermatozoa in the female genital tract (5–7 hours) by which they gain the ability to fertilise.
**Acrosome reaction** — acrosomal enzymes (hyaluronidase, acrosin) are released and dissolve the corona radiata and zona pellucida.
**Cortical reaction** — after one spermatozoon enters, the cortical granules of the oocyte undergo exocytosis and change the zona pellucida — other spermatozoa cannot enter (**block to polyspermy**).
The oocyte completes meiosis II and the second polar body is released; the male and female **pronuclei** approach and the chromosomes unite — **syngamy**.

blocks.text: **Cleavage** is a series of mitotic divisions of the zygote; the cells formed (**blastomeres**) do not grow and become smaller with each division. The type of cleavage depends on the amount of yolk: **complete (holoblastic)** — equal (lancelet) or unequal (amphibians; asynchronous in humans); **incomplete (meroblastic)** — discoidal (birds, reptiles) or superficial (insects) (Figure 10.5). Cleavage gives a **morula** and then a hollow **blastula**; in mammals it is called a **blastocyst** (trophoblast + embryoblast) and is **implanted** in the uterine wall on day 7.

blocks.label: Figure 10.5
blocks.caption: Types of cleavage: 1 — radial (lancelet, mammals); 2 — spiral (flatworms and annelids, mollusks); 3 — bilateral (ascarids); 4 — anarchic; on the right — holoblastic, discoidal and superficial cleavage (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Gastrulation** is the formation of a two- and then three-layered embryo — the **gastrula** — from the single-layered blastula; the **germ layers** — **ectoderm**, **endoderm** and **mesoderm** — are formed (Figure 10.6). Methods: **invagination** (infolding — lancelet), **immigration** (migration of cells inward), **delamination** (splitting into layers) and **epiboly** (overgrowth — amphibians). Then **neurulation** (formation of the neural tube and notochord) and **histo-organogenesis** begin.

blocks.label: Figure 10.6
blocks.caption: Stages of embryonic development — cleavage, gastrulation and histo-organogenesis: 1 — blastocoel; 2 — blastopore; 3 — ectoderm; 4 — endoderm; 5 — mesoderm; 6 — neural tube; 7 — notochord; 8 — primitive gut (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

head: Layer

rows: Epidermis and its derivatives (hair, nails, sweat and mammary glands), nervous system, receptors of the sense organs, lens of the eye, tooth enamel, epithelium of the oral and anal cavities, anterior pituitary, adrenal medulla
Epithelium of the digestive tube (middle part) and airways, liver, pancreas, epithelium of the thyroid, parathyroid glands and thymus, epithelium of the urinary bladder
Skeleton, striated and smooth muscles, connective tissue, heart and blood vessels, blood, kidneys, gonads, adrenal cortex, serous membranes

blocks.text: The human embryo cleaves to become a **morula** on day 4 and a **blastocyst** on day 5: the outer cells are the **trophoblast** (forming the fetal part of the placenta), and the inner cell cluster is the **embryoblast** (the embryo itself). On days 6–7 the blastocyst sinks into the uterine lining (**implantation**). Gastrulation occurs in week 3, followed by **neurulation**: the neural plate and then the neural tube form from the ectoderm; failure of its closure causes neural tube defects. In weeks 4–8 the rudiments of all main organs form (**organogenesis**).

blocks.title: Table 10.6. Extra-embryonic (provisional) organs
head: Organ
Origin
Function (in humans)
rows: Aquatic environment with amniotic fluid, mechanical protection
Primordial germ cells and the first blood cells form
Forms the basis for the umbilical vessels
Its villi form the fetal part of the placenta; produces hCG
Nutrition, respiration, excretion, hormones, transfer of IgG, barrier function

sections.title: 4. Mechanisms of ontogenesis, critical periods and teratogenic factors

blocks.text: In ontogenesis cells **divide, migrate, differentiate** and **die** (apoptosis). Early blastomeres are **totipotent** — each can give rise to a whole organism (identical twins arise on this basis). **Differentiation** is the structural and functional specialization of cells with the same genotype as a result of activation of different genes. **Embryonic induction** (H. Spemann, 1924) is the determination of the developmental fate of one part of the embryo by another part (the inducer, for example chordamesoderm) (formation of the neural tube from ectoderm).

**Embryonic induction** is the determination by one part of the embryo of the developmental fate of another. It was proved by H. Spemann and H. Mangold (1924) in the frog embryo: when the dorsal lip of the blastopore was transplanted into another embryo, a second neural tube and a second body axis formed (the **organiser**). The position of organs along the body axis is controlled by **homeobox (HOX) genes**; their mutations cause organs to develop in the wrong place.

**Critical periods** are the periods when the embryo is most sensitive to harmful factors (P.G. Svetlov): the period of **implantation** (weeks 1–2 — harmful effects follow the “all or nothing” principle: the embryo dies or recovers completely) and the period of **organogenesis** (weeks 3–8 — severe congenital defects), as well as the period of **placentation**. In the fetal period harmful effects mainly cause functional disorders and growth retardation.

blocks.title: Table 10.7. Teratogenic factors
head: Group
Examples
Consequences
rows: Thalidomide, retinoids, warfarin, valproate, alcohol, nicotine, heavy metals (mercury, lead)
Phocomelia (thalidomide), fetal alcohol syndrome, neural tube defects
Deafness, cataract, heart defects (rubella), hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis (toxoplasmosis)
Heart and skeletal defects, intellectual disability, cretinism

parts.text: When planning a pregnancy, taking **folic acid** (3 months before pregnancy and in the first trimester) markedly reduces the risk of neural tube defects; alcohol, smoking and taking drugs without a doctor’s advice are forbidden in pregnancy, and vaccination against rubella is given before pregnancy.

blocks.text: **The thalidomide tragedy** (1957–1961): because pregnant women took thalidomide as a sedative, more than 10 thousand children worldwide were born with **phocomelia** (short limbs resembling “seal flippers”). Since then all new drugs must be tested for teratogenicity. **Fetal alcohol syndrome** results from drinking alcohol in pregnancy: microcephaly, a thin upper lip and smooth philtrum, growth delay and intellectual disability; there is no safe dose of alcohol in pregnancy.

In postnatal development the organism grows, organs mature and puberty occurs. Growth and development are controlled by the **genotype**, **hormones** (growth hormone, thyroxine, sex hormones, insulin) and **environmental** factors (nutrition, physical activity, social conditions). The biological age of the organism is assessed by the skeleton, teeth, sexual maturation and other indicators and may differ from the chronological age (acceleration and retardation).

**Aging** is a natural process in which the adaptive capacity of the organism gradually decreases and the probability of disease and death increases. Aging and old age are studied by **gerontology**, and the diseases of the elderly and their treatment by **geriatrics**.

blocks.title: Table 10.8. Main theories of aging
head: Theory
Essence
rows: Human fibroblasts divide only ≈ 50 times in culture; telomeres shorten with each division
Reactive oxygen species damage DNA, proteins and membranes; the damage accumulates
Mutations accumulate in somatic cells and impair cell function
Age-related changes in the hypothalamus and endocrine regulation
Weakening of immunity and strengthening of autoimmune reactions

blocks.text: **Progeria** is a hereditary disease with premature aging: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria in children (mutation of the lamin A gene) and Werner syndrome in adults (a DNA helicase gene). **Death** is the cessation of the vital activity of the organism: **clinical death** (breathing and heart activity have stopped, but recovery by resuscitation is possible within 5–6 minutes) and **biological death** (irreversible changes, first of all in the cerebral cortex).

**Biological age** is the age of the organism by its morphofunctional state; it may differ from the **calendar (passport) age**. Biological age is assessed by the degree of ossification (“bone age”), tooth eruption and sexual maturation, and in the elderly by cardiovascular and respiratory indices and telomere length. Lifestyle (physical activity, proper nutrition, not smoking) slows biological ageing.

blocks.title: Table 10.9. Stages of dying
head: Stage
Signs
Possibility of reversal
rows: Disturbed consciousness, sharp fall in blood pressure, disturbed breathing and heart rhythm
Breathing and heartbeat have stopped, no reflexes, but cells are still alive
Possible with resuscitation for 5–6 minutes at normal temperature
Cells of the cerebral cortex have died; later livor mortis, rigor mortis and cooling

blocks.text: **Regeneration** is the restoration of lost or damaged parts of the organism. **Physiological regeneration** is the renewal of worn-out cells in the normal course of life (epidermis, intestinal epithelium, blood cells). **Reparative regeneration** is restoration after injury: **complete** (restitution — the original tissue is restored) and **incomplete** (substitution — a scar forms). Methods: epimorphosis (growth from the wound surface), morphallaxis (rebuilding of the remaining part), regenerative hypertrophy (in the liver and kidney — the volume of the organ is restored, but not its shape). The capacity for regeneration decreases in the course of evolution and with age.

blocks.title: Table 10.10. Forms of reparative regeneration
head: Form
Essence
Example
rows: A regeneration bud (blastema) forms on the wound and the lost part grows out
Tissues of the remaining part are rebuilt into a smaller whole organism
The remaining part of an organ restores the former mass by cell division, but not the shape
Recovery of the liver after removal of 2/3 of it
When one of a paired organ is removed, the other enlarges and takes over the function
The second kidney after removal of one kidney

blocks.text: In humans the ability to regenerate depends on the tissue: epithelium, blood, bone and liver regenerate well; skeletal muscle partly (by satellite cells); the myocardium and neurons of the central nervous system hardly regenerate — a connective-tissue **scar** forms in their place (for example, after myocardial infarction).

blocks.title: Table 10.11. Types of transplantation
head: Type
Donor and recipient
Result
rows: The same organism (from oneself to oneself — skin, bone)
Genetically different individuals of the same species
Rejected if HLA does not match; immunosuppression needed
Different species (for example, from a pig to a human)

blocks.label: Figure 10.7
blocks.caption: Types of transplantation: auto-, iso-, allo- and xenotransplantation (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Graft rejection is the response of the recipient’s immune system to the donor’s foreign **HLA antigens** (histocompatibility antigens, on chromosome 6). To prevent rejection, the donor is selected by HLA and immunosuppressants are used. Avascular tissues such as the cornea and cartilage are rarely rejected.

**Homeostasis** (W. Cannon, 1929) is the ability of the organism to keep its internal environment (temperature, pH, osmotic pressure, glucose and ion levels) relatively constant. It is maintained at the **genetic** (stability of genotype and karyotype — DNA repair), **structural** (preservation of the composition of cells and tissues — regeneration) and **physiological** levels by the nervous, endocrine and immune systems on the principle of **feedback**.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In humans 4 spermatozoa are formed from one spermatogonium during spermatogenesis.
cases.ask: How many stages does spermatogenesis have? At which stage are spermatozoa formed? What are their chromosome set and DNA content?
cases.answer: Spermatogenesis has 4 stages: multiplication (spermatogonia, 2n2c), growth (primary spermatocyte, 2n4c), maturation (meiosis I — secondary spermatocytes n2c, meiosis II — spermatids 1n1c) and formation (spermiogenesis — spermatozoa from spermatids). Spermatozoa are formed at the formation stage; they are haploid — 1n1c (in humans 23 chromosomes: 22 autosomes + X or Y).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In human oogenesis one egg is formed from one oogonium at the maturation stage.
cases.ask: What stages does oogenesis have? What other cells are formed at the maturation stage, and what process is this stage related to?
cases.answer: Oogenesis has 3 stages: multiplication (completed in fetal life), growth and maturation. In maturation, meiosis I gives a secondary oocyte and the first polar body, and meiosis II gives the egg and the second polar body; in total 1 egg and 3 polar bodies (the cytoplasm is divided unequally and nutrients accumulate in the egg). Maturation is related to monthly ovulation after puberty: meiosis I is completed before ovulation, and meiosis II at fertilization.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In week 5 of pregnancy a woman took a drug for a long time without medical supervision, and later heart and limb defects were found in the fetus. Another woman took the same drug in week 30 of pregnancy, but no defects were found.
cases.ask: Explain the difference in the results.
cases.answer: Week 5 falls in the critical period of organogenesis (weeks 3–8): in this period the organ primordia are formed, and a teratogenic effect leads to severe anatomical defects. By week 30 the organs are already formed (fetal period), so a teratogenic effect may cause mainly functional disorders and growth retardation rather than major defects. The consequence of a teratogenic effect depends on the type of substance, its dose and the stage of pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A 28-year-old man in whom unilateral cryptorchidism (undescended testis) was found in childhood but not treated has infertility and a low sperm count on semen analysis.
cases.ask: How does cryptorchidism affect spermatogenesis?
cases.answer: Spermatogenesis requires the testis to be 2–3 °C below body temperature. In a testis left in the abdomen or inguinal canal the temperature is higher, so the spermatogenic epithelium is damaged and spermatozoa are not formed; Leydig cells continue to produce testosterone, so male sexual characters are preserved. Such a testis also has a higher risk of tumour. Therefore cryptorchidism is corrected surgically before the age of 1–2 years.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: In weeks 3–4 of pregnancy, before she knew she was pregnant, a woman had a high fever and took valproate. Ultrasound showed spina bifida in the fetus.
cases.ask: Why did the defect arise exactly at this time?
cases.answer: Weeks 3–4 are the period of **neurulation**: the neural tube forms from the neural plate and closes completely by the end of week 4. This is a **critical period** for the nervous system: teratogens (high temperature, valproate, folic acid deficiency) disturb closure of the neural tube, and spina bifida or anencephaly develops. During organogenesis (weeks 3–8) each organ is damaged at its own critical time; later in pregnancy teratogens mainly affect growth and function.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A patient had 60 % of the liver removed because of a tumour. 3 months later the liver mass was found to be almost back to normal, but its shape had changed.
cases.ask: What kind of regeneration is this? What is its mechanism?
cases.answer: This is **regenerative hypertrophy** — a form of reparative regeneration. Liver cells (hepatocytes) are normally in G~0~; when organ mass falls, under growth factors (hepatocyte growth factor and others) they return to the mitotic cycle and divide. As a result the organ's mass and function are restored, but the removed lobe does not grow back — so the shape is not restored. This property of the liver makes transplantation of a liver lobe from a living donor possible.

topics.title: Flagellates — human parasites: trypanosomes, leishmania, trichomonads and giardia. Sporozoa — human parasites: malaria parasites, toxoplasma. Intestinal parasites: dysentery amoeba, intestinal balantidium

goals.text: To teach the student the basic concepts of parasitology and the origin of parasitism, the general features of the phylum Protozoa, and the structure, life cycle, routes of transmission, pathogenic effect, laboratory diagnosis and prevention of the flagellates, sporozoa, sarcodines and ciliates that parasitize humans.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of parasite, host (definitive, intermediate, reservoir), vector, vector-borne and natural focal disease;
the features of trypanosomes, leishmania, trichomonads and giardia;
the life cycle of malaria plasmodia and the differences between their species;
the life cycle and diagnosis of toxoplasma, the dysentery amoeba and balantidium.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe a parasite in the following order: name (Latin), disease, distribution, morphology, localization, life cycle, route of transmission, pathogenic effect, diagnosis, prevention;
identify the species of plasmodium in a blood smear;
distinguish the forms of amoeba and giardia in a stool smear.

blocks.text: **Parasitism** is a form of relationship in which one organism (the parasite) uses another (the host) as its habitat and source of food and harms it. **Medical parasitology** studies protozoa (**protozoology**), helminths (**helminthology**) and arthropods (**arachnoentomology**) that parasitize humans.

blocks.title: Table 11.1. Basic terms of parasitology
head: Term
Definition
rows: A parasite that can only live as a parasite, and one that can also live freely
A parasite living on the surface of the host’s body (louse, tick) and inside it (helminths, protozoa)
The host in which the parasite reproduces sexually or lives as an adult
The host in which the larval stage or asexual reproduction of the parasite takes place
An animal that maintains the parasite in nature and is a source for humans
An arthropod inside which the parasite develops or multiplies (the malaria mosquito)
Carries the agent unchanged on its body surface or in its gut (the house fly)
A disease transmitted by blood-sucking arthropods
A disease whose agent circulates in nature among animals independently of humans (E.N. Pavlovsky’s doctrine)

blocks.text: Parasites enter humans by the **oral** (alimentary), **airborne**, **contact** (skin, sexual), **vector-borne** (arthropod bites) and **transplacental** routes. They harm the host by **mechanical** action (tissue damage, blocking ducts), **toxic-allergic** action, **taking nutrients** and **opening the way to secondary infection**.
Mutual adaptations of parasite and host

blocks.title: Table 11.2. Adaptations of parasites to a parasitic way of life
head: Adaptation
Examples
rows: Suckers, hooks (tapeworms), sucking disc (Giardia), toothed buccal capsule (hookworm)
Cuticle and tegument resistant to digestive enzymes, cyst walls and egg shells
Absence of a digestive system in tapeworms, simplified sense organs
Ascaris lays up to 200 thousand eggs a day; hermaphroditism, parthenogenesis, multiplication of larvae
Changing antigens (trypanosomes), living inside cells (Leishmania, Plasmodium), “masking” with host antigens (schistosomes)

blocks.text: **The doctrine of natural focality** (E.N. Pavlovsky, 1939): the agents of some diseases circulate in nature independently of humans — between wild animals (reservoirs) and vectors. A person becomes infected on entering such a focus (for example, a desert inhabited by gerbils). A natural focus has three links: the **agent**, the **reservoir host** and the **vector** (and the landscape where they live). Cutaneous leishmaniasis, tick-borne encephalitis, tularaemia and plague are examples of natural-focal diseases.

blocks.title: Table 11.3. Methods of diagnosing parasitic diseases
head: Method
Material examined and examples
rows: Faeces — cysts, eggs; blood — plasmodia, trypanosomes; scraping of a skin ulcer — leishmaniae; discharges — trichomonads
Antibodies (IgM — recent, IgG — past infection) and antigens in blood; toxoplasmosis, echinococcosis, amoebiasis
Detection of parasite DNA — very sensitive
Ultrasound, CT, X-ray — liver abscess, echinococcal cysts, calcifications
Material is injected into a laboratory animal (toxoplasmosis, trypanosomiases)

sections.title: 2. The phylum Protozoa. Flagellates — human parasites

blocks.text: **Protozoa** are eukaryotes consisting of a single cell that performs all vital functions as an independent organism. Organelles of movement: pseudopodia (sarcodines), flagella (flagellates), cilia (ciliates); sporozoa have no special organelles of movement. Under unfavorable conditions most of them form a **cyst** — this is important for their spread.

Members of the **class Flagellata** have one or more flagella, often an **undulating membrane** and a **kinetoplast** (a mass of mitochondrial DNA at the base of the flagellum); they reproduce by longitudinal binary fission.

blocks.label: Figure 11.1
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the African trypanosome: metacyclic trypanosomes develop in the gut and salivary glands of the tsetse fly (vector) and pass by its bite to the vertebrate host (human, antelope) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 11.2
blocks.caption: Circulation of the agent of American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease): the triatomine bug (1) passes trypanosomes in its faeces while sucking blood, and they enter through a wound in the skin of a human (2); reservoirs are the armadillo and other wild animals (3) (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The life cycle of Leishmania has two forms: the **amastigote** (leishmanial, without a flagellum) — inside macrophages of humans and animals, oval, 2–5 µm, with a nucleus and kinetoplast; and the **promastigote** (leptomonad, flagellated) — in the sandfly gut and in culture, elongated, 10–20 µm, with one flagellum at the front end. When a sandfly sucks the blood of an infected person or animal it swallows amastigotes, which turn into promastigotes in its gut, multiply and pass to a human at the next bite.

blocks.label: Figure 11.3
blocks.caption: Life cycle of visceral leishmaniasis: reservoir hosts — the dog and jackal, vector — the sandfly; humans are infected by the sandfly bite (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar)** runs with prolonged undulating fever, marked enlargement of the liver and especially the spleen, anaemia, leucopenia and wasting; untreated it is fatal. Diagnosis is by finding amastigotes inside macrophages in a sternal or splenic aspirate. In Central Asia the main reservoirs are dogs and jackals, and children are affected more often.

The trophozoite of **Giardia** is pear-shaped, 10–18 µm long and bilaterally symmetrical: it has two nuclei, four pairs of flagella and a ventral **sucking disc**; with the disc it attaches to the intestinal epithelium and impairs absorption (Figure 11.4). Its cysts are oval, with 4 nuclei, and resistant in the environment.

blocks.label: Figure 11.4
blocks.caption: *Lamblia intestinalis* — the trophozoite (left — diagram, two nuclei and flagella) and giardia on the surface of the intestinal epithelium as seen in the scanning electron microscope (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 11.5
blocks.caption: Life cycle of Giardia: cysts are swallowed with contaminated food and water, turn into the vegetative form and multiply in the small intestine, then form cysts again in the large intestine and are passed in the faeces (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 11.6
blocks.caption: *Trichomonas vaginalis* — a pear-shaped parasite with four anterior flagella, an undulating membrane and an axostyle (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Trichomoniasis** is the most widespread sexually transmitted parasitic disease. *T. vaginalis* causes vaginitis in women (frothy, foul-smelling discharge, itching) and urethritis and prostatitis in men; it often runs without symptoms. Because it forms no cysts, it dies quickly in the environment. Both sexual partners are treated at the same time (metronidazole), otherwise re-infection occurs.

parts.text: In Uzbekistan **cutaneous leishmaniasis** (oriental sore) forms natural foci in desert and semi-desert areas near gerbil burrows. A papule appears at the bite site and turns into a long-lasting ulcer that heals with a scar. Prevention: protection from sandflies (nets, repellents), control of rodents, vaccination.

blocks.text: All members of the **class Sporozoa** are obligate parasites; they have no organelles of movement, and at the anterior end there is an **apical complex** for entering the host cell. Their life cycle alternates asexual reproduction (**schizogony**), sexual reproduction (**gametogony**) and **sporogony**.
**Malaria plasmodia** belong to the genus *Plasmodium*; the definitive host and specific vector is the female **Anopheles** mosquito, and the intermediate host is the human (Figure 11.7).

items: When the mosquito bites, **sporozoites** enter the blood with its saliva and within 30 minutes enter liver cells.

**Tissue (pre-erythrocytic) schizogony** — multiplication in the liver cell produces thousands of **merozoites** (incubation period). In *P. vivax* and *P. ovale* some sporozoites become dormant **hypnozoites** — the cause of late relapses of the disease.

**Erythrocytic schizogony** — merozoites enter erythrocytes: ring trophozoite → amoeboid trophozoite → schizont → morula (8–24 merozoites). When the erythrocytes burst and merozoites enter the blood, a **malaria paroxysm** (chills, fever, sweating) occurs.
Some merozoites give rise to male and female **gametocytes**; they pass with blood into the mosquito.

In the mosquito’s stomach **gametogony** (fertilization → motile zygote — ookinete → oocyst) and **sporogony** (thousands of sporozoites in the oocyst) take place; sporozoites gather in the salivary glands.

blocks.label: Figure 11.7
blocks.caption: Life cycle of *Plasmodium falciparum*: the process in the Anopheles mosquito (gametogony and sporogony) and in the human body (tissue schizogony in the liver, erythrocytic schizogony in the blood, formation of gametocytes) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

head: Feature
*P. vivax*
*P. ovale*
*P. malariae*
*P. falciparum*
rows: Oval, with fimbriated edges, James’s dots
Unchanged; several rings in one erythrocyte

blocks.label: Figure 11.8
blocks.caption: Differential diagnosis of plasmodia (blood smear): I — *P. vivax*; II — *P. malariae*; III — *P. ovale*; IV — *P. falciparum*. 1 — uninfected erythrocyte; 2–3 — ring-form schizonts; 4–6 — various stages of the parasite; 7 — schizont; 8 — morula; 9 — female gametocyte; 10 — male gametocyte (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Diagnosis — a **thick drop** and a **thin smear** taken during a paroxysm are stained by the Romanowsky-Giemsa method and examined; rapid antigen tests are also used. **Tropical malaria** is the most dangerous: infected erythrocytes stick to capillaries, causing cerebral malaria and death. Every person with fever returning from a malaria area must be tested immediately. Uzbekistan was certified malaria-free by the WHO in 2018.

blocks.title: Table 11.6. Clinical and parasitological features of the forms of malaria
head: Form
Agent
Periodicity of attacks
Features
rows: May persist for years, kidney damage possible
Cerebral malaria, may lead to coma; high risk of death

blocks.text: **Control and prevention of malaria:** early detection and treatment of patients (artemisinin drugs, chloroquine; primaquine against hypnozoites in *P. vivax* and *P. ovale*), draining or treating water bodies against mosquito larvae, spraying houses with insecticide, insecticide-treated nets, and **chemoprophylaxis** for people travelling to endemic areas. Uzbekistan was certified malaria-free by the World Health Organization in 2018, but the risk of imported cases remains.

**Toxoplasma** (*Toxoplasma gondii*) is an intracellular parasite shaped like a crescent or an orange segment, 4–7 µm long and 2–4 µm wide. **The definitive host is the cat** (sexual reproduction in its intestine, oocysts in feces); the **intermediate hosts** are humans and many mammals and birds (cysts in tissues). It enters humans through hands, vegetables and water contaminated with oocysts, through undercooked meat containing cysts and by the **transplacental** route. Primary infection in pregnancy causes fetal death, hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and calcifications in the brain; in immunodeficiency (AIDS) it causes severe encephalitis. Diagnosis — serology (IgM, IgG), PCR.

blocks.label: Figure 11.9
blocks.caption: Circulation of Toxoplasma: definitive host — the cat (sexual reproduction in its gut, oocysts passed in the faeces); intermediate hosts — birds, mammals and humans; humans are infected through vegetables contaminated with oocysts and undercooked meat, and the fetus from the mother through the placenta (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Congenital toxoplasmosis** develops if the mother is infected **for the first time** during pregnancy: early in pregnancy the risk of transmission is low but the consequences are severe (miscarriage, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis — the **classic triad**), while late in pregnancy transmission is frequent but mild. The fetus of a woman who had antibodies (IgG) to Toxoplasma before pregnancy is not at risk. Prevention: cooking meat well, washing vegetables, wearing gloves when handling cat faeces and soil, and serological testing of pregnant women.
**Coccidia** (*Isospora*, *Cryptosporidium*) parasitize the intestinal epithelium and cause diarrhea; cryptosporidiosis is severe in patients with AIDS.

sections.title: 4. Intestinal parasites: the dysentery amoeba and balantidium

blocks.text: The **dysentery amoeba** (*Entamoeba histolytica*, class Sarcodina) is the agent of **amoebiasis**; it is widespread in tropical and subtropical countries, including Central Asia. It lives in the large intestine and occurs in several forms (Figure 11.10):

items: **small vegetative (luminal) form** — 15–20 µm, feeds on bacteria and does not cause disease (carrier state);
**large vegetative, tissue and erythrophagous form** — 30–40 µm, invades the intestinal wall, forms ulcers and **ingests erythrocytes** (the main diagnostic sign);
**cyst** — 10–15 µm, with 4 nuclei, the invasive form; survives for a long time in the environment.

blocks.label: Figure 11.10
blocks.caption: Various forms of the dysentery amoeba: tissue form, small vegetative form, cyst and the hematophagous (erythrophagous) form with ingested erythrocytes (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Humans swallow cysts with contaminated water, unwashed fruit and vegetables, hands and flies. Amoebiasis causes **diarrhea with blood and mucus** (“raspberry jelly”), abdominal pain and ulcers in the large intestine; complications are intestinal perforation and **liver abscess**. Diagnosis — tissue forms with ingested erythrocytes in a wet smear of fresh stool (within 15–20 minutes), cysts in remission; endoscopy, serology.

Extra-intestinal complications of amoebiasis: the tissue form passes with the blood through the portal vein to the **liver** and forms an **amoebic abscess** (usually in the right lobe; fever, pain under the right ribs); lung and brain abscesses are less common. In diagnosis, finding **tissue forms that have engulfed red cells** in the faeces is important; cysts or small vegetative forms alone indicate carrier status. Among free-living amoebae, *Naegleria fowleri* enters through the nose when swimming in warm fresh water and causes acute **amoebic meningoencephalitis**.

**Intestinal balantidium** (*Balantidium coli*, class Ciliata) is the only ciliate that parasitizes humans and the largest protozoan (50–80 µm). Its body is covered with cilia; it has a large (macronucleus) and a small (micronucleus) nucleus, a mouth opening (cytostome) and contractile vacuoles. **The main reservoir is the pig**; pig farm workers are affected more often. It forms ulcers in the wall of the large intestine and causes **balantidiasis** with bloody-purulent diarrhea. Diagnosis — motile trophozoites and cysts in stool.

blocks.label: Figure 11.11
blocks.caption: *Balantidium coli*: the vegetative form (cilia, cytostome, macro- and micronucleus, contractile vacuoles) and the cyst (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Prevention of intestinal protozoan infections is common to all: drinking boiled water, washing fruit and vegetables, washing hands before meals and after the toilet, fly control, examining food workers and treating carriers.

items: Examine the stained blood smear under the immersion objective.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Workers who spent 2 months surveying gas fields in the Kyzylkum desert developed slowly healing ulcers on the exposed parts of their bodies.
cases.ask: What can you say about the nature and origin of this disease?
cases.answer: This is the rural (zoonotic) type of cutaneous leishmaniasis — the agent is *Leishmania major*. In the natural focus the reservoir is gerbils and the vector is sandflies; they breed near burrows and bite exposed parts of the body at night. A papule appears at the bite site, then a wet ulcer that heals with a scar in a few months. Diagnosis: amastigotes in a smear from the edge of the ulcer. Prevention: nets, repellents, rodent control, vaccination.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A person who had worked in equatorial Africa developed drowsiness, weakness and headache that are getting worse.
cases.ask: What disease could this be? Is it contagious to others?
cases.answer: African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense* or *T. b. rhodesiense*. The parasite multiplies first in the blood and lymph and then in the central nervous system, causing drowsiness, weakness and encephalitis. Diagnosis: smears of blood, lymph node aspirate and cerebrospinal fluid. It is not transmitted directly from person to person — only by the tsetse fly (vector-borne); since there are no tsetse flies in Uzbekistan, it will not spread to others.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A pregnant woman had a spontaneous abortion. Parasites 4–7 µm long and 2–4 µm wide, shaped like a crescent or an orange segment, were found in the abortion material.
cases.ask: What caused the death of the fetus?
cases.answer: This is *Toxoplasma gondii* — congenital toxoplasmosis. The woman was infected for the first time during pregnancy (through oocysts in cat feces or cysts in undercooked meat); the parasite crossed the placenta into the fetus, damaged its tissues and caused its death. Prevention: serological testing before pregnancy, thorough cooking of meat, not handling cat litter without gloves, washing fruit and vegetables.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A soldier returning from Afghanistan has repeated attacks every third day (every 48 hours) with chills, high fever and heavy sweating. 8 months after treatment the attacks recurred.
cases.ask: Which agent should be suspected? What is the cause of the late relapse and how should it be treated?
cases.answer: A 48-hour periodicity is typical of **tertian malaria** (*P. vivax*) or ovale malaria. Attacks occur when red cells burst and merozoites and toxins enter the blood. Late relapses are due to activation of **hypnozoites** dormant in the liver. Diagnosis is by examining a thick drop and a thin smear during an attack. Treatment combines a drug against erythrocytic forms (chloroquine or artemisinin drugs) with **primaquine**, which kills hypnozoites (G6PD deficiency is checked first, because primaquine causes haemolysis in it).

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: A woman at week 10 of pregnancy keeps a cat at home and was not tested for Toxoplasma before pregnancy. She is worried about the risk of toxoplasmosis.
cases.ask: What tests and advice should be given?
cases.answer: **IgG and IgM antibodies** to Toxoplasma are measured in the blood. If IgG is positive and IgM negative, the woman was infected earlier and is immune; the fetus is not at risk. If both are negative, she has no immunity: prevention must be strict and tests repeated during pregnancy. If IgM is positive, a new infection is possible; additional tests and, if needed, PCR of amniotic fluid are done. Advice: let someone else clean the cat's litter tray (or wear gloves and clean it daily), do not feed the cat raw meat, cook meat well, wash vegetables and wear gloves when gardening.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A 5-year-old child attending kindergarten has poor appetite, intermittent abdominal pain, frothy fatty diarrhoea and weight loss.
cases.ask: What parasitic disease should be considered? What are the diagnosis and prevention?
cases.answer: **Giardiasis** (*Lamblia intestinalis*) should be considered. Giardia attach with the sucking disc to the epithelium of the duodenum and small intestine and impair absorption (especially of fats) — hence the fatty diarrhoea and weight loss. Diagnosis: vegetative forms in fresh faeces, **cysts** in formed faeces (repeated tests several times) or Giardia antigen in faeces. The disease spreads by the faecal-oral route, especially quickly in children's groups; prevention is hand hygiene, boiled water, cleaning toys and testing family contacts.
