summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The malaria mosquito is the **definitive host** and the human the **intermediate host**; in toxoplasma the definitive host is the **cat**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Malaria periodicity: **“Vivax and Ovale — every 3rd day, Malariae — every 4th day, Falciparum — fatal (tropical)”**.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The blood of every feverish patient returning from the tropics is tested for malaria at once; serological testing for toxoplasmosis in pregnant women prevents congenital defects.

topics.title: Flukes — human parasites: the liver fluke, lancet fluke, cat liver fluke, lung fluke and blood flukes. Tapeworms — human parasites: the pork and beef tapeworms, dwarf tapeworm, broad fish tapeworm, Echinococcus and Alveococcus

goals.text: To teach the student the general features of the phylum Platyhelminthes, the structure and development of the classes Trematoda and Cestoda, and the life cycle, routes of transmission, pathogenic effects, diagnosis and prevention of the trematodes and cestodes that parasitize humans.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the general features of flatworms and their larval stages (miracidium, sporocyst, redia, cercaria, metacercaria, adolescaria; oncosphere, types of metacestodes);
the causative agents of fascioliasis, dicrocoeliasis, opisthorchiasis, paragonimiasis and schistosomiasis;
taeniasis, taeniarhynchosis, cysticercosis, hymenolepiasis, diphyllobothriasis, echinococcosis and alveococcosis;
the differences between the pork and beef tapeworms.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify flukes and tapeworms in preparations;
identify the tapeworm species from a gravid segment (proglottid);
state the hosts, infective stage and route of transmission for each helminthiasis.

blocks.text: **Flatworms (Plathelminthes)** are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic animals with a dorsoventrally flattened body. They have no body cavity — the spaces between organs are filled with **parenchyma**. The body is covered by a **dermo-muscular sac**. The digestive system is blind (no anus; in tapeworms it is absent altogether), the excretory system consists of **protonephridia**, and the nervous system of paired cerebral ganglia and nerve cords. Most are **hermaphrodites**. The classes of medical importance are the flukes (**Trematoda**) and the tapeworms (**Cestoda**).

**Class Trematoda** — leaf-shaped parasites with an **oral** and a **ventral sucker**; the gut is blind and has two branches. Development involves a change of hosts: the definitive host is a vertebrate or a human, and the first intermediate host is always a **mollusc**. Larval stages: egg → **miracidium** (ciliated, swims in water) → **sporocyst** → **redia** → **cercaria** (tailed, leaves the mollusc) → **metacercaria** or **adolescaria** (the infective stage).

blocks.label: Figure 12.1
blocks.caption: Larval stages of flukes: miracidium, sporocyst, redia, cercaria and adolescaria (metacercaria) (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 12.1. Description of the larval stages of flukes
head: Stage
Structure
Where it develops
rows: A ciliated larva that swims in water
Hatches from the egg in water and actively enters a mollusc
In the mollusc's body; multiplies parthenogenetically
Has a mouth and a rudimentary gut
In the mollusc's liver; produces new rediae and cercariae
Leaves the mollusc into the water
An invasive larva that has shed its tail and is enclosed in a cyst
In the second intermediate host (fish, crab, ant) or on a plant (in Fasciola)

parts.text: Order of the larvae: **“Mi-Spo-Re-Cer-Meta”** — Miracidium, Sporocyst, Redia, Cercaria, Metacercaria. Thanks to parthenogenesis in the mollusc, thousands of cercariae arise from one egg.

Location

blocks.label: Figure 12.2
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the liver fluke *Fasciola hepatica*: the definitive host (herbivorous mammals and humans), the miracidium in water, development in the intermediate host — the small pond snail, the cercaria and the adolescaria attached to plants (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Opisthorchiasis** is widespread in the Ob–Irtysh basin (Western Siberia) and along the Volga and Dnieper. Humans become infected by eating cyprinid fish (carp bream, ide, roach) containing metacercariae that are undercooked or lightly salted (Figure 12.3). The parasite damages the bile and pancreatic ducts, causing cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis and liver cirrhosis, and raises the risk of **cholangiocarcinoma**. Diagnosis — small (≈ 30 µm) operculated eggs in the faeces and duodenal fluid.

blocks.label: Figure 12.3
blocks.caption: The cat liver fluke *Opisthorchis felineus*: A — morphology (intestinal branches, vitellaria, uterus, ovary, seminal receptacle, testes); B — life cycle: the definitive host, the first intermediate host — the Bithynia snail, the second intermediate host — carp fish (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In chronic opisthorchiasis the bile and pancreatic ducts are inflamed for a long time (cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis) and the risk of **bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma)** rises; for this reason Opisthorchis and the related Chinese liver fluke (*Clonorchis sinensis*) are classed as carcinogens by the World Health Organization. Prevention: cooking or frying fish well, prolonged freezing (7 hours at −40 °C or 32 hours at −28 °C) and proper salting.

parts.text: **Transit eggs:** a person who has eaten the liver of an animal infected with Fasciola (for example, liver kebab) may pass liver fluke eggs in the faeces for 1–2 days — this is **false fascioliasis**. To distinguish it from true infection, the patient is re-examined after 3–5 days on a liver-free diet.

blocks.label: Figure 12.4
blocks.caption: The lung fluke *Paragonimus westermani*: structure (A) and life cycle (B): eggs coughed up in the sputum of a patient give miracidia in water, cercariae in a mollusc and metacercariae in the muscles of freshwater crabs; humans are infected by eating undercooked crab (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Schistosomiases** (bilharziasis) affect more than 200 million people in tropical countries. Schistosomes are **dioecious**: the male carries the female in a groove of its body. When a person bathes or works in fresh water, **cercariae actively penetrate the skin** (an itchy “cercarial dermatitis” at the site of entry). Adults live in veins, and their eggs break through tissues into the bladder (*S. haematobium* — blood in urine, risk of bladder cancer) or the intestine (*S. mansoni*, *S. japonicum* — diarrhoea, liver fibrosis). Diagnosis is by finding spined eggs in urine or faeces.

**Tapeworms (Cestoda)** have a ribbon-like body consisting of a **scolex** (head with suckers, sometimes hooks, or sucking grooves — bothria), a **neck** (growth zone) and a **strobila** (a chain of segments — proglottids). There is no digestive system — nutrients are absorbed through the whole body surface. Each segment is hermaphroditic: in immature segments the reproductive organs develop, in **hermaphroditic** segments fertilization takes place, and in **gravid** segments only the uterus filled with eggs remains.

The egg contains a six-hooked embryo — the **oncosphere**. In the intermediate host the oncosphere develops into a larva — the **metacestode** (finna). Types of metacestode: the **cysticercus** (a vesicle with a single scolex — in Taenia), the **cysticercoid** (tailed, in the dwarf tapeworm), the **hydatid cyst** (with many scolices and daughter cysts), the **alveococcus** (a mass of many small vesicles that grows like a tumour), and the **procercoid** and **plerocercoid** (in the broad fish tapeworm).

blocks.title: Table 12.3. Types of tapeworm larvae (metacestodes)

Structure

rows: A fluid-filled vesicle with one invaginated scolex
A small larva without a cavity, with a tail and one scolex
A large cyst with daughter cysts and thousands of scolices
A cluster of tiny vesicles that grows into tissue
Elongated larvae: the first in a copepod, the second in a fish

blocks.label: Figure 12.5
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the pork tapeworm *Taenia solium*: the adult worm in the human intestine, gravid segments and eggs passed in the faeces, the intermediate host — cysticerci (metacestodes) in the muscles of the pig (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

head: Feature
*Taenia solium*

rows: 4 suckers and a crown of hooks (“armed”)

blocks.label: Figure 12.6
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the beef tapeworm *Taeniarhynchus saginatus*: definitive host — humans, intermediate host — cattle; cattle eat grass contaminated with eggs, larvae develop in their muscles, and humans are infected by undercooked meat containing larvae (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: **Cysticercosis** develops when a person with taeniasis swallows the eggs themselves (dirty hands, gravid segments entering the stomach during vomiting — autoinfection) or infects others. Cysticerci in the brain cause seizures and hydrocephalus. Therefore a patient with taeniasis must be treated urgently and the people around them examined.

blocks.text: **Echinococcus** (*Echinococcus granulosus*) is a small tapeworm 3–6 mm long with 3–4 segments; its scolex has 4 suckers and hooks. The adult lives in the intestine of the **dog**, wolf and jackal. The eggs are passed in the faeces and contaminate the dog's fur, grass, water and vegetables. The intermediate hosts are sheep, cattle, camels, pigs and **humans**: in the intestine the oncospheres hatch and travel in the blood to the **liver** (≈ 70 %), **lungs** (≈ 20 %) and other organs, where a slowly growing **hydatid cyst** forms (Figure 12.7).

blocks.label: Figure 12.7
blocks.caption: Life cycle of *Echinococcus granulosus*: the definitive host — the dog (adult worm in the intestine), eggs in the environment, hydatid cysts in the liver and lungs of the intermediate hosts (sheep, pig, cattle, human); dogs become infected by eating infected internal organs (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The hydatid cyst consists of an outer chitin-like (laminated) layer and an inner **germinal** layer; it is filled with fluid, **daughter cysts** and numerous scolices (“hydatid sand”). The cyst compresses the surrounding tissue and impairs organ function; rupture can cause anaphylactic shock and the formation of many new cysts. Treatment is mainly surgical.

Echinococcosis is diagnosed by **ultrasound and CT** (a cyst with clear fluid containing daughter cysts) and **serological** tests (antibodies). **Puncture of a suspected cyst is forbidden**: if the fluid leaks, thousands of scolices spread around and secondary echinococcosis or **anaphylactic shock** develops. Treatment is surgery (removal of the cyst) and albendazole; in some cases the PAIR method (puncture, aspiration, injection of a scolicide, re-aspiration) is used with special precautions.

**Alveococcus** (*Alveococcus multilocularis*) — its definitive hosts are the fox, arctic fox and dog; its metacestode is a mass of small vesicles that **grows infiltratively like a tumour** in the liver and metastasizes; it runs a more severe course than echinococcosis. Humans become infected when handling fox pelts or eating unwashed wild berries.

blocks.label: Figure 12.8
blocks.caption: Life cycle of Alveococcus: the adult form lives in the intestine of foxes, dogs and wolves; the larval stage in the liver of intermediate hosts (mouse-like rodents and humans) (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 12.6. Prevention of echinococcosis and alveococcosis
head: Measures
Content
rows: Regular (every 1–3 months) treatment of pet, shepherd and guard dogs with praziquantel
Not giving infected organs (liver, lungs) to dogs; destroying them
Washing hands after contact with dogs, keeping children from kissing dogs
Washing wild berries and greens thoroughly; hunters handling fox skins with gloves
Ultrasound and serological screening of shepherds, butchers and dog handlers

parts.text: In echinococcosis **the human is a biological dead end**: the parasite does not pass from human cysts to another host. Humans are infected **only by swallowing eggs**; eating undercooked meat or liver does not transmit echinococcosis. Prevention: regular deworming of dogs, not feeding the infected internal organs of slaughtered animals to dogs, and washing hands after contact with dogs.

sections.title: 4. The dwarf tapeworm and the broad fish tapeworm

blocks.text: **The dwarf tapeworm** (*Hymenolepis nana*) is 1–5 cm long; the human is both the definitive and the intermediate host. After the eggs are swallowed, a **cysticercoid** develops in the villi of the small intestine, then emerges into the intestinal lumen and matures. Hundreds or thousands of parasites can accumulate in one person (**autoreinfection**). It spreads mainly in children's institutions by the contact-household route.

blocks.label: Figure 12.9
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the dwarf tapeworm: oncospheres hatched from eggs enter the intestinal villi, where a cysticercoid develops; it then emerges into the gut lumen, attaches with its scolex and becomes an adult worm — all stages take place in one person (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **The broad fish tapeworm** (*Diphyllobothrium latum*) is the longest human helminth (10 m or more); its scolex bears two sucking grooves (**bothria**); its segments are wider than they are long, and the uterus is rosette-shaped. Development takes place in water: a **coracidium** hatches from the egg → **procercoid** in the 1st intermediate host (Cyclops) → **plerocercoid** in the muscles and roe of the 2nd intermediate host (a predatory fish) → humans are infected by eating undercooked fish or salted roe. In the intestine the parasite takes up vitamin B~12~, causing **B~12~-deficiency (megaloblastic) anaemia**.

blocks.label: Figure 12.10
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the broad fish tapeworm: a coracidium hatches from the egg in water; 1st intermediate host — a copepod (procercoid), 2nd intermediate host — pike and other fish (plerocercoid); definitive hosts — humans, dogs and cats (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In diphyllobothriasis the worm takes up **vitamin B~12~** in the intestine, so some patients develop B~12~-deficiency (megaloblastic) **anaemia**. The source of infection is undercooked, lightly salted fish and roe. Prevention: cooking fish well, freezing it and not polluting water bodies with sewage.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the tapeworm species from a gravid segment

items: Wash the segment separated from the faeces with water and press it between two glass slides.
Hold it up to the light or look under a magnifier at the central stem and lateral branches of the uterus (if necessary, inject ink or carmine).
Count the number of lateral branches on one side.
If there are 7–12 — conclude *Taenia solium*; if there are 17–35 — *Taeniarhynchus saginatus*.
Follow safety precautions: pork tapeworm eggs are dangerous to humans (cysticercosis) — work in gloves and disinfect the material.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A man returning from a business trip to Siberia has signs of disease of the liver and bile ducts. Ovohelminthoscopic examination finds small operculated helminth eggs in his faeces.
cases.ask: What disease could this be?
cases.answer: The most likely diagnosis is opisthorchiasis (agent *Opisthorchis felineus*). Western Siberia (the Ob–Irtysh basin) is the world's largest focus of opisthorchiasis; humans are infected by eating cyprinid fish containing metacercariae that are undercooked, dried or lightly salted. The parasite lives in the bile ducts, gallbladder and pancreatic ducts. Confirmation — eggs in the duodenal fluid, serology; treatment — praziquantel.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Tapeworm segments were found in a patient's faeces. When the lateral uterine branches were counted, there were 30 on one side.
cases.ask: What diagnosis can be made?
cases.answer: 17–35 pairs of lateral uterine branches are typical of the beef tapeworm (*Taeniarhynchus saginatus*) — taeniarhynchosis. The patient ate undercooked beef containing cysticerci. Unlike the pork tapeworm, this species does not cause cysticercosis in humans. Confirmation is the active emergence of segments and eggs in a perianal scraping; treatment — praziquantel or niclosamide.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Can Echinococcus be transmitted to humans by eating undercooked kebab and liver kebab?
cases.ask: Justify your answer.
cases.answer: No. The hydatid cysts (metacestodes) in the meat or liver of sheep and cattle are infective only for the definitive host — dogs and other canids: when they eat infected internal organs, the adult worm develops in their intestine. Humans are intermediate hosts and become infected only by swallowing eggs passed in dog faeces (from fur, dirty hands, unwashed vegetables). However, other helminthiases (taeniarhynchosis, taeniasis) can be transmitted through undercooked meat.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A 35-year-old man from a fishing family complains of weakness, dizziness and a red, burning tongue. The blood test shows anaemia with large red cells (megaloblastic). He likes lightly salted pike roe.
cases.ask: Which helminthiasis should be considered? What is the cause of the anaemia?
cases.answer: **Diphyllobothriasis** (*Diphyllobothrium latum*). Humans are infected by **plerocercoids** in lightly salted roe or undercooked fish. The long worm living in the intestine takes up **vitamin B~12~** and disturbs its absorption — this leads to B~12~-deficiency megaloblastic anaemia (Hunter's glossitis — a red, burning tongue). Diagnosis is by finding operculated eggs in the faeces. Treatment: praziquantel, then vitamin B~12~. Prevention: cooking or freezing fish and roe well.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: 4 children in a kindergarten have abdominal pain, loss of appetite and irritability. Eggs with a transparent shell containing an oncosphere with six hooks were found in the faeces. One child was re-infected after treatment.
cases.ask: What helminthiasis is this? Why is re-infection common?
cases.answer: This is **hymenolepiasis** (*Hymenolepis nana*, the dwarf tapeworm). Humans are both the definitive and the intermediate host: after eggs are swallowed, a cysticercoid develops in the intestinal villi and then an adult worm forms. Because the eggs are immediately infective, self-re-infection through dirty hands (**autoreinvasion**) and rapid contact spread in children's groups are typical. Therefore treatment is given in repeated courses, together with testing of all contact children and strict hygiene (hand washing, short nails, cleaning toys).

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A 42-year-old shepherd feels heaviness under the right ribs. Ultrasound shows an 8 cm cyst in the liver containing small daughter cysts. The doctor wanted to puncture the cyst with a needle to take fluid for diagnosis.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Is the doctor's action correct?
cases.answer: The occupation (constant contact with dogs) and a cyst with daughter cysts on ultrasound are typical of **echinococcosis** (the larva of *Echinococcus granulosus* — a hydatid cyst). Puncturing the cyst for diagnosis is **wrong and dangerous**: if the fluid leaks into the abdominal cavity, scolices spread and cause secondary echinococcosis, and antigens in the fluid can cause **anaphylactic shock**. The diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasound/CT and serological tests; treatment is surgery and albendazole. Family members are examined and the dogs are dewormed.

topics.title: Roundworms: Ascaris, pinworm, filariae, Trichinella, hookworm, guinea worm, whipworm. Methods of ovohelminthoscopy. Dehelminthization and devastation

goals.text: To teach the student the general features of the phylum Nemathelminthes and the class Nematoda, the concepts of geohelminths and biohelminths, the structure, life cycle, routes of transmission, pathogenic effects, diagnosis and prevention of the main nematodes that parasitize humans, and the methods of detecting helminth eggs.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the general features of nematodes and the concepts of geohelminth and biohelminth;
the types of infection: autoinfection, reinfection, autoreinfection, active and passive infection;
ascariasis, enterobiasis, trichuriasis, hookworm disease, strongyloidiasis, trichinellosis, dracunculiasis and the filariases;
the methods of ovohelminthoscopy and the concepts of dehelminthization and devastation.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify nematodes and their eggs in preparations;
prepare a direct smear and take a perianal scraping;
state the route of transmission and preventive measures for each nematode infection.

blocks.text: **Roundworms (Nemathelminthes)** are animals with a spindle-shaped or thread-like body that is round in cross-section and not divided into segments. The body is covered by a dense **cuticle**, beneath which lie the hypodermis and longitudinal muscles. They have a **primary body cavity (pseudocoel)** filled with fluid that acts as a hydroskeleton. The digestive system ends with an **anus** (fore-, mid- and hindgut). There are no circulatory or respiratory systems. Nematodes have **separate sexes** and marked sexual dimorphism: the male is smaller and its tail end is curved.

blocks.text: By type of development, helminths fall into two groups. **Geohelminths** develop without an intermediate host — their eggs or larvae mature **in the soil** (Ascaris, whipworm, hookworm). **Biohelminths** develop with the participation of an intermediate host (Trichinella, guinea worm, filariae, and all flukes and tapeworms). **Contact helminths** (pinworm, dwarf tapeworm) hardly mature in the environment at all and are transmitted via dirty hands and objects.

Develop with the participation of an intermediate host

Eggs are infective at once or within hours; directly from person to person

items: **Autoinfection** — the parasite reinfects the same organism without leaving it (dwarf tapeworm, strongyloidiasis).
**Reinfection** — repeated infection from outside.
**Autoreinfection** — swallowing one's own eggs again via the hands (pinworm).
**Active infection** — the larva enters through the skin by itself (hookworm, schistosomes); **passive infection** — via food, water or a vector.

sections.title: 2. The human roundworm and the pinworm

blocks.text: **The human roundworm** (*Ascaris lumbricoides*) is the agent of **ascariasis**, a geohelminth found everywhere. The female is 20–40 cm long, the male 15–25 cm; the mouth is surrounded by three lips. It lives in the small intestine; the female lays up to 200 thousand eggs a day. Eggs passed in the faeces are **not immediately infective** for humans — they mature in the soil over 2–3 weeks given oxygen, moisture and warmth (≈ 24 °C), and an infective larva develops inside.

blocks.label: Figure 13.1
blocks.caption: Adult male and female worms of the human roundworm *Ascaris lumbricoides* (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 13.2
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the human roundworm *Ascaris lumbricoides*: maturation of the eggs in soil, swallowing of the infective egg, larval migration (intestine → vein → liver → heart → lungs → alveoli → bronchi → trachea → pharynx → intestine) and maturation in the small intestine (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Humans swallow mature eggs with unwashed vegetables and fruit, dirty hands and water. Larvae hatching in the intestine pass through the gut wall into the blood and **migrate** (Figure 13.2), causing eosinophilic infiltrates in the lungs, cough and allergic reactions (**migratory phase**). The swallowed larvae mature in the small intestine within 2–3 months (**intestinal phase**): abdominal pain, weight loss, intestinal obstruction, blockage of the bile ducts. Diagnosis — eggs in the faeces; in the migratory phase, larvae in the sputum and eosinophilia.

In the **migratory (early) stage** of ascariasis the larvae break out of lung capillaries into the alveoli: cough, fever, blood **eosinophilia** and rapidly disappearing “flying” eosinophilic infiltrates on X-ray (**Löffler syndrome**) are seen. In the **intestinal stage** there is abdominal pain, nausea, weight loss and allergic reactions. Complications: **intestinal obstruction** by a mass of worms, entry into the bile and pancreatic ducts causing **obstructive jaundice** and **pancreatitis**, appendicitis. Diagnosis: in the migratory stage — larvae in the sputum and serology (no eggs yet!); in the intestinal stage — eggs in the faeces.

**Toxocariasis** is infection with the larvae of the dog roundworm (*Toxocara canis*). People (most often children) swallow eggs from soil contaminated with dog faeces. In humans the larvae do not mature but **wander** through the organs for a long time (“visceral larva migrans”): an enlarged liver, cough and high eosinophilia; if a larva reaches the eye, vision falls (ocular toxocariasis). No eggs are found in the faeces — diagnosis is serological.

**The pinworm** (*Enterobius vermicularis*) is the agent of **enterobiasis**, a contact helminth found mainly in children. The female is 9–12 mm long, the male 2–5 mm; they are white (Figure 13.3). It lives in the initial part of the large intestine. At night the females crawl out of the anus and lay eggs in the perianal folds, causing intense **itching**. The eggs become infective within 4–6 hours; when the child scratches, they get under the fingernails and are swallowed again (**autoreinfection**). Diagnosis — a **perianal scraping** or adhesive tape test in the morning; stool examination is ineffective.

blocks.label: Figure 13.3
blocks.caption: The pinworm *Enterobius vermicularis*: female (left) and male (right); the mouth, vesicle, oesophageal bulb, midgut, reproductive system, vulva and anus are shown (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: At night the female pinworm crawls out of the anus and lays up to 10–15 thousand eggs in the perianal folds, causing itching; the eggs become infective in 4–6 hours. When the child scratches, eggs get under the nails and into the mouth (**autoreinvasion**) and spread to others through bedding and toys. That is why in enterobiasis **all family members are treated at the same time**, treatment is repeated after 2 weeks, underwear and bedding are washed and ironed daily, and nails are kept short.

sections.title: 3. The whipworm, the hookworm and the threadworm

blocks.text: **The whipworm** (*Trichocephalus trichiurus*) is the agent of **trichuriasis**, a geohelminth 3–5 cm long. The front part of its body is hair-thin, and with it the worm “stitches” itself into the mucosa of the caecum and colon and feeds on blood (Figure 13.4). Its eggs are **lemon-shaped** with plugs at both poles; they mature in the soil in 3–4 weeks. Heavy infection causes anaemia, colitis and, in children, rectal prolapse.

blocks.label: Figure 13.4
blocks.caption: The whipworm *Trichocephalus trichiurus*: male, female and egg (left); the worm with its thin anterior end embedded in the intestinal mucosa (right) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **The Old World hookworm** (*Ancylostoma duodenale*) and **Necator** (*Necator americanus*) cause **hookworm disease**, which is common in hot, humid areas (mines, rice fields). They are 8–13 mm long, with cutting teeth or plates in the buccal capsule. In the soil a rhabditiform and then a **filariform** larva develops from the egg; it **actively** penetrates human skin (Figure 13.5), travels in the blood to the lungs, ascends to the pharynx, is swallowed and matures in the duodenum. The parasite sucks blood and injures the intestinal wall — severe **iron-deficiency anaemia** develops.

blocks.label: Figure 13.5
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the hookworm *Ancylostoma duodenale*: eggs passed in the faeces, rhabditiform and filariform larvae in the soil, entry through the skin, migration through the lungs and maturation in the small intestine (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Hookworms attach to the intestinal mucosa with the teeth of their buccal capsule, suck blood and secrete an anticoagulant; one *A. duodenale* causes a loss of ≈ 0,15–0,25 ml of blood a day. Therefore patients with many worms develop severe **iron-deficiency anaemia** (in children growth and mental development slow down). Where larvae enter the skin an itchy rash — “ground itch” — appears. Prevention: wearing shoes and disposing of faeces safely.

**The threadworm** (*Strongyloides stercoralis*) is the agent of **strongyloidiasis**; it is ≈ 2 mm long. Transmission resembles that of hookworm (filariform larvae through the skin). Its special feature is **autoinfection** in the intestine, so the disease lasts for decades; when immunity is weakened (glucocorticoids, HIV), a severe disseminated form develops. Diagnosis — larvae in the faeces.

parts.text: In strongyloidiasis, autoinvasion makes the disease persist for decades. In immunosuppressed patients (glucocorticoid treatment, HIV, tumours, transplantation) the larvae multiply explosively and spread throughout the body — **hyperinfection syndrome** (often fatal). Therefore testing for strongyloidiasis is recommended before prescribing glucocorticoids to a patient from an endemic area.

blocks.text: **Trichinella** (*Trichinella spiralis*) is the agent of **trichinellosis**; it is 1.5–4 mm long. One animal serves first as the definitive and then as the intermediate host. Humans are infected by eating undercooked **pork**, wild boar or bear meat containing larvae. In the small intestine the larvae mature and the females give birth to live larvae; these travel in the blood to the **striated muscles** (diaphragm, masticatory, intercostal and eye muscles), become encapsulated and remain alive for years. Signs: fever, **swelling of the face and eyelids**, severe muscle pain and marked **eosinophilia**. Diagnosis — serological tests, muscle biopsy, **trichinoscopy** of the remaining meat.

blocks.label: Figure 13.6
blocks.caption: Trichinella larvae coiled and encapsulated between striated muscle fibres (trichinelloscopy) (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Signs of trichinellosis appear 1–4 weeks after infection: high fever, **swelling of the face and eyelids**, severe muscle pain (especially in the masticatory, eye, diaphragm and calf muscles) and high blood **eosinophilia**; in severe cases myocarditis and pneumonia. Diagnosis: epidemiological history (a group of people who ate the same meat falling ill), serological tests, muscle biopsy; **trichinelloscopy** of the remaining meat. Prevention: veterinary inspection of pork and game meat and thorough cooking (salting and smoking do not kill the larvae).

**The guinea worm** (*Dracunculus medinensis*) is the agent of **dracunculiasis**; the female is up to 120 cm long. Its intermediate host is the **Cyclops**. Humans are infected by drinking pond water containing Cyclops with larvae; the female worm settles in the subcutaneous tissue (usually of the legs), forms a blister on the skin and releases its larvae into the water when the leg touches water. **In Uzbekistan** the guinea worm was completely eradicated in 1932 as a result of measures led by L.M. Isaev — a classic example of **devastation**.

blocks.label: Figure 13.7
blocks.caption: A female guinea worm (*Dracunculus medinensis*) emerging from a skin ulcer on the leg (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The guinea worm was once widespread in Central Asia, especially in **Bukhara**; under the leadership of L.M. Isaev it was completely **eliminated** there by 1932 by draining ponds and improving the water supply — a classic example of devastation. Today, thanks to the global eradication programme, only a few dozen cases a year are recorded in the world.

parts.text: In diagnosing the filariases, microfilariae are found in the blood; the microfilariae of *Wuchereria bancrofti* appear in the peripheral blood mainly **at night**, so the blood smear is taken at night.

blocks.label: Figure 13.8
blocks.caption: The filaria *Loa loa* moving under the conjunctiva of the eye (shown by the arrow) (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Dirofilariasis** is a filariasis that also occurs in Uzbekistan: its definitive hosts are dogs and cats, and its vectors are mosquitoes (*Culex*, *Aedes*, *Anopheles*). In humans the larva does not mature and forms a moving nodule under the skin, often around the eye; diagnosis and treatment consist of surgical removal of the nodule. **Onchocerciasis** (“river blindness”, *Onchocerca volvulus*) is transmitted in Africa by blackflies and is one of the main infectious causes of blindness.

**Ovohelminthoscopy** is the set of methods for finding helminth eggs and larvae. In the **macroscopic** method, adult worms and segments in the faeces are examined with the naked eye or a magnifier. **Microscopic** methods: the **direct smear** (a drop of faeces with glycerol or saline), the **Kato thick smear**, **sedimentation** methods (formalin-ether — for heavy eggs such as fluke eggs) and **flotation** methods (Fülleborn — light eggs float to the surface in saturated NaCl solution). Pinworm and beef tapeworm eggs are detected with a **perianal scraping** or adhesive tape (Figure 13.9).

blocks.text: **Dehelminthization** comprises the measures that rid the human body (treatment) and the environment (disinfection of faeces, protection of soil and water) of helminths and their eggs. **Devastation** — a term introduced by academician **K.I. Skryabin** — is the **complete extermination** of a helminth species in a given area at all of its stages (adult, larva, egg) by a combination of biological, chemical and organizational measures. Its aim is not to reduce disease but to eliminate the causative agent from the area.

skills.title: Skill: preparing a direct smear and taking a perianal scraping

items: Place a drop of 50 % glycerol or saline on a glass slide.
With a wooden stick take a match-head-sized sample from different parts of the faeces, spread it evenly in the drop and cover with a coverslip.
Examine the whole preparation first under the low-power and then the high-power objective; identify the eggs by shape, size, shell and operculum.
A perianal scraping is taken in the morning, before washing and defecation: material is collected from the perianal folds with a stick moistened in glycerol or with adhesive tape.
Stick the tape onto a slide and examine it under the microscope; pinworm eggs are asymmetrical, flattened on one side.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: It was found that toys in a kindergarten might be contaminated with Ascaris eggs.
cases.ask: Can such eggs cause ascariasis in the children?
cases.answer: Ascaris is a geohelminth: eggs freshly passed in the faeces are not infective; they become infective only after maturing in the soil over 2–3 weeks given oxygen, moisture and warmth. Therefore fresh eggs that reach a toy directly from a patient's faeces do not cause ascariasis. However, if the toys are contaminated with soil (a sandpit), it may contain mature infective eggs — in that case there is a risk of infection. Prevention: replacing the sand in sandpits, washing toys and teaching children to wash their hands.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Small, motile, white worms were seen in a child's faeces. The mother complains that the child sleeps restlessly at night and scratches around the anus.
cases.ask: What parasitic disease can be suspected? What should be done to confirm it?
cases.answer: Enterobiasis is suspected (agent — the pinworm, *Enterobius vermicularis*): at night the female pinworms crawl out to the perianal area, lay eggs and cause itching. To confirm, material is taken in the morning, before washing, by perianal scraping or the adhesive tape method, and asymmetrical eggs are found under the microscope; the test is repeated 3 times. To stop autoreinfection, the child and family members are treated at the same time, the nails are cut short, and underwear is changed and ironed daily.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A hunter shared wild boar meat with his fellow villagers. A few days later, most of those who ate the meat came to the clinic with facial swelling, fever and severe muscle pain.
cases.ask: What disease might the doctor suspect? How can the suspicion be confirmed?
cases.answer: Trichinellosis (agent — *Trichinella spiralis*). The encapsulated larvae in the wild boar meat mature in the intestine, and new larvae spread in the blood to the striated muscles — this causes fever, swelling of the face and eyelids, and myalgia. Group illness from a single source is typical. Confirmation: marked eosinophilia in the blood, serological tests (ELISA), muscle biopsy; trichinoscopy of the remaining meat. Prevention — veterinary inspection and thorough cooking of meat.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A 7-year-old child has had a dry cough and low-grade fever for 2 weeks. Blood eosinophils are 25 %. X-rays show lung infiltrates that change position within a few days. No helminth eggs were found in the faeces. The child lives in a village and eats unwashed vegetables.
cases.ask: Which helminthiasis can be suspected? Why were no eggs found in the faeces?
cases.answer: This is the **migratory stage of ascariasis** (Löffler syndrome): larvae hatched from eggs pass from the intestinal wall into the blood and migrate through the liver and lungs, causing “flying” eosinophilic infiltrates in the lungs and cough. At this stage there are no adult female worms in the intestine yet, so there are **no eggs** in the faeces (they appear after ≈ 2–2,5 months). Diagnosis: finding larvae in the sputum and serological tests; the stool test is repeated after 2–3 months. Prevention: washing vegetables and fruit well and hand hygiene.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: A 30-year-old farmer who works barefoot in rice fields has weakness, shortness of breath and pale skin. Blood tests show haemoglobin 70 g/l, signs of iron-deficiency anaemia and eosinophilia. A few months ago he had an itchy rash on his feet.
cases.ask: What helminthiasis could this be? Explain the mechanism of the anaemia.
cases.answer: **Hookworm disease** (*Ancylostoma duodenale* or *Necator americanus*). Filariform larvae in warm moist soil actively penetrated the skin (the itchy rash on the feet — “ground itch”), then travelled with the blood to the lungs and on to the duodenum, where they matured. The worms attach to the mucosa with the teeth of the buccal capsule, suck blood and secrete an anticoagulant — continuous blood loss leads to **iron-deficiency anaemia**. Diagnosis: eggs with a thin shell containing 4–8 blastomeres in the faeces. Treatment: an anthelmintic and iron preparations; prevention — working in shoes.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A 45-year-old woman who keeps a dog developed an itchy nodule under the skin of her lower eyelid that changed position over a few days. She says she was bitten by many mosquitoes in the summer.
cases.ask: What parasitic disease should be considered? What are the diagnosis and treatment?
cases.answer: **Dirofilariasis** (*Dirofilaria repens*). The definitive hosts are dogs and cats; a mosquito sucks microfilariae from an infected dog and transmits an infective larva when it bites a person. Humans are an **accidental (dead-end) host**: the larva does not mature and forms a moving nodule in the subcutaneous tissue, often around the eye. Diagnosis and treatment: **surgical removal** of the nodule and identification of the worm under the microscope. Prevention: examining and treating dogs and protection from mosquitoes.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Ascaris eggs are **not infective until they mature in the soil**; pinworm eggs, by contrast, become infective within a few hours — which is why enterobiasis spreads quickly within a family.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Skin penetrators: **“Hookworm, Strongyloides, Schistosoma — they find whoever walks barefoot”**.

summary.label: Clinical relevance
summary.text: Facial swelling + myalgia + eosinophilia + a group that ate the same meat = **trichinellosis**; perianal itching in a child = **enterobiasis**.

topics.title: Arachnids of medical importance: the village tick, the scabies mite, the dog and taiga ticks. Insects of medical importance: lice, fleas, mosquitoes, flies, sandflies. Venomous animals

goals.text: To teach the student the general features and classification of the phylum Arthropoda, the medically important members of the classes Arachnida and Insecta — their structure, development, the diseases they spread and the measures used to control them — and the venomous animals found in Uzbekistan and first aid for their bites and stings.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the general features and classification of arthropods;
the structure and medical importance of argasid and ixodid ticks and the scabies mite;
the medical importance of lice, fleas, bedbugs, cockroaches, mosquitoes, sandflies, flies and horseflies;
the concepts of specific and mechanical vectors, transovarial transmission and natural focality;
the classification of venomous animals and first aid for their bites and stings.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: distinguish argasid and ixodid ticks, lice and fleas in preparations;
tell the malaria mosquito from the common mosquito at every stage of development;
explain the procedure for first aid after a bite or sting by a venomous animal.

blocks.text: **Arthropods (Arthropoda)** are the largest phylum of the animal kingdom. General features: the body and legs are **jointed**, the external skeleton is a **chitinous** cuticle, growth takes place by **moulting**, the body cavity is mixed (**mixocoel**), and the circulatory system is open. Three subphyla matter for medicine: the **gill-breathers** (crustaceans — Cyclops and crabs are intermediate hosts of helminths), the **chelicerates** (arachnids) and the **tracheates** (insects).

blocks.text: **Arachnids (Arachnida)** have a body divided into a **cephalothorax** and an **abdomen**, 4 pairs of walking legs, chelicerae and pedipalps around the mouth, and no antennae. Of medical importance are scorpions, spiders and especially the order of **ticks and mites (Acari)**. Ticks and mites are divided into the **acariform** group (the scabies mite and the follicle mite — *Demodex*) and the **parasitiform** group (argasid and ixodid ticks). Tick development: egg → **larva** (3 pairs of legs) → **nymph** → **imago** (4 pairs of legs).

blocks.text: **Transovarial and transstadial transmission in ticks:** the pathogen multiplies in the tick and passes through the egg to the next generation (**transovarial**) and from larva to nymph and from nymph to imago (**transstadial**). Ticks are therefore not only vectors but also **natural reservoirs** of the pathogen. Academician **Ye.N. Pavlovsky** developed the doctrine of the **natural focality** of vector-borne diseases: the pathogen circulates among wild animals and vectors independently of humans.

parts.text: **When a tick has attached:** do not crush it; grasp it close to the skin with tweezers or a thread loop and pull it out with a twisting movement; wipe the site with alcohol or iodine; send the tick to a laboratory in a test tube. Crushing it with the fingers or applying oil or petrol is forbidden — the tick regurgitates and injects more of the pathogen. In endemic areas emergency prophylaxis (immunoglobulin, antibiotic) is given after a tick bite; prevention is vaccination, closed clothing, repellents and checking oneself and pets.

blocks.text: **The scabies mite** (*Sarcoptes scabiei*) is the agent of **scabies**; it measures 0.3–0.4 mm. The female burrows tunnels in the stratum corneum of the skin and lays her eggs there. Favourite sites are the spaces between the fingers, the wrists, abdomen and inner thighs. The main sign is **itching that worsens at night**. Transmission — direct skin contact, shared bedding and clothing. Diagnosis — finding the mite in a scraping taken from a burrow.

Scabies spreads from person to person mainly by **direct prolonged skin contact** (sleeping in one bed, sexual contact), less often through clothing and bedding; the mite survives 2–3 days off the body. Treatment: all family members and contacts are treated at the same time with acaricidal ointments (benzyl benzoate, permethrin), and underwear and bedding are boiled and ironed. **Demodex** — *Demodex folliculorum* lives in hair follicles and sebaceous glands and, when immunity is lowered, causes a facial rash and eyelid inflammation. **House dust mites** (*Dermatophagoides*) are not parasites, but their secretions are an important cause of bronchial asthma and allergic rhinitis.

sections.title: 2. Class Insecta. Lice, fleas, bedbugs, cockroaches

blocks.text: **Insects (Insecta)** have a body consisting of a **head**, **thorax** and **abdomen**; the thorax bears 3 pairs of legs and usually 2 pairs of wings, and the head 1 pair of antennae; they breathe through tracheae. Development is of two kinds: with **incomplete metamorphosis** (egg → larva → imago: lice, bedbugs, cockroaches) and with **complete metamorphosis** (egg → larva → **pupa** → imago: fleas, Diptera).

blocks.title: Table 14.4. Types of insect development
head: Type
Stages
Examples
rows: Egg → larva (nymph) → adult; the larva resembles the adult
Egg → larva → pupa → adult; the larva differs sharply from the adult

blocks.text: **Lice (Anoplura)** are wingless permanent ectoparasites that feed only on human blood throughout their life (Figure 14.4). Three species parasitize humans: the **head louse** (*Pediculus humanus capitis*), the **body louse** (*P. h. corporis*) and the **pubic louse** (*Phthirus pubis*). A louse feeds 2–3 times a day for 3–10 minutes each time; the female lays 6–14 eggs (nits) a day, gluing them to hair or clothing fibres; development from egg to imago takes 16–20 days. Louse infestation is called **pediculosis**.

blocks.label: Figure 14.4
blocks.caption: Lice: a — male head louse; b — female head louse; c — pubic louse clinging to a hair; d — louse engorged with blood (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: **The body louse** is the vector of epidemic **typhus** (*Rickettsia prowazekii*) and epidemic **relapsing fever** (*Borrelia recurrentis*). The pathogens are not transmitted with saliva when the louse bites: in typhus the rickettsiae are passed in the louse's **faeces** and rubbed into scratched skin; in relapsing fever the borreliae are in the louse's haemolymph and enter skin wounds **when the louse is crushed**. In wars, famine and breakdowns of hygiene these diseases become epidemic.

blocks.text: **Pediculosis** (lice infestation) — infestation with lice; head lice often spread in children's groups. The female louse lays 5–10 eggs (**nits**) a day and glues them to the hair with a special cement. Treatment: pediculicidal shampoos or solutions (permethrin), a repeat treatment after 7–10 days (against larvae hatched from nits) and combing out the nits with a fine comb; for body lice, boiling and ironing clothes and bedding or treating them in a disinfestation chamber. All contacts are examined.

**Fleas (Siphonaptera)** are wingless insects, flattened from side to side, with jumping legs; they develop with complete metamorphosis, and their larvae live in floor cracks and rubbish. **The rat flea** (*Xenopsylla cheopis*) is the vector of **plague** (*Yersinia pestis*): the bacteria form a “block” in the flea's proventriculus and are regurgitated into the wound when it feeds. **The human flea** (*Pulex irritans*) can also carry plague.

blocks.label: Figure 14.5
blocks.caption: Flea: a — adult flea (laterally compressed body, jumping hind legs); b — life cycle with complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Mechanism of plague transmission by fleas:** in a rat flea (*Xenopsylla cheopis*) that has sucked rodent blood, plague bacilli multiply in the proventriculus and form a “plug” (**block**). Such a “blocked” flea stays hungry, tries again and again to feed, and each time regurgitates the sucked blood together with bacteria into the wound. When rodents die off, the fleas pass to humans — this is how a plague epidemic begins.

**The bedbug** (*Cimex lectularius*) feeds at night, and its bites cause itching and allergy. **Cockroaches** (*Blattella germanica, Periplaneta americana*) are **mechanical carriers** of intestinal infections, helminth eggs and protozoan cysts; their chitin remains and secretions are strong **allergens** that cause bronchial asthma and allergic reactions in children.

**Diptera** are insects with one pair of membranous wings, the second pair having become vibrating halteres; they develop with complete metamorphosis. They are divided into two suborders: the **long-horned** (mosquitoes, sandflies, black flies — *Simulium*) and the **short-horned** (flies, horseflies).

blocks.text: ***Aedes*** mosquitoes carry the dengue, yellow fever and Zika viruses. **Sandflies** (*Phlebotomus*) are small and hairy and breed in rodent burrows in hot regions; they are the vectors of the **leishmaniases** (cutaneous and visceral) and of sandfly (pappataci) fever. **Black flies** (*Simulium*) carry onchocerciasis.

blocks.label: Figure 14.7
blocks.caption: a — developmental stages of the sandfly (egg, larvae, pupa and adult sandfly); b — the house fly, its eggs, larva and pupa (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Besides leishmaniases, sandflies also carry the **pappataci (sandfly) fever** virus. *Culex* mosquitoes transmit West Nile fever and Japanese encephalitis viruses, as well as filariae and dog dirofilariae. The **tsetse fly** (*Glossina*) carries sleeping sickness in Africa, and **blackflies** (*Simulium*) carry onchocerciasis.

**The housefly** (*Musca domestica*) is a **mechanical carrier** of intestinal infections (dysentery, typhoid fever, cholera), helminth eggs and protozoan cysts: microbes are carried on the sticky hairs of its feet, on its proboscis and in its gut, and reach food in vomit and faeces. **Wohlfahrt's fly** (*Wohlfahrtia magnifica*) deposits live larvae in wounds, ears, nose and eyes — causing **obligate myiasis**. **The stable fly** (*Stomoxys calcitrans*) and **horseflies** (*Tabanidae*) suck blood but are only **mechanical** carriers of anthrax and tularaemia. **The tsetse fly** (*Glossina*) carries sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis) in Africa.

items: **Specific (biological) vector** — the pathogen multiplies in it or completes part of its life cycle there (Anopheles — malaria, sandfly — Leishmania, louse — rickettsia, tick — encephalitis virus).
**Mechanical carrier** — the pathogen stays unchanged in the carrier and is merely transferred on its body surface or proboscis (housefly, cockroach, horsefly, stable fly).

blocks.text: **Myiases** are infestations of human tissues by fly larvae. **Wohlfahrt's fly** (*Wohlfahrtia magnifica*) deposits live larvae in wounds or on the mucosa of the ear, nose or eye; the larvae destroy tissue, causing severe wounds and even bone damage (in Central Asia especially in summer, in shepherds and bedridden patients). Larvae of **botflies** (*Gasterophilus*, *Oestrus*) mainly infest animals, sometimes causing cutaneous or ocular myiasis in humans. Prevention: keeping wounds covered, personal hygiene and fly control.

blocks.text: **Venomous animals** produce or accumulate substances that are toxic to humans and animals. **Primarily venomous** animals produce venom in special glands themselves; they are either **actively armed** (with a venom gland and a stinging or biting apparatus: snakes, scorpions, spiders, wasps) or **passive** (with venom glands but no delivery apparatus: frogs, some fish). **Secondarily venomous** animals accumulate toxins from their food (some fish and molluscs). By their action, venoms are **neurotoxic** (acting on the nervous system) or **haemotoxic** (acting on the blood and vessels).

blocks.label: Figure 14.8
blocks.caption: Venomous arachnids found in Uzbekistan: a — scorpion; b — karakurt (*Latrodectus tredecimguttatus*) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 14.9
blocks.caption: Venomous snakes: a — tiger snake (*Notechis scutatus*, Australia); b — cobra — snakes with neurotoxic venom (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The main treatment for snake envenoming is **antivenom** (monovalent or polyvalent), given only in a medical facility when indicated. After a snake bite **applying a tourniquet, cutting, cauterising, sucking out the venom by mouth and giving alcohol are forbidden**: a tourniquet increases tissue necrosis with haemotoxic venom, and cutting causes infection and bleeding.

blocks.label: Figure 14.10
blocks.caption: Venomous and poisonous fish: a — the greater weever (*Trachinus draco*) — actively venomous, its fin spines and gill-cover spine are linked to venom glands; b — the marinka (*Schizothorax intermedius*) — passively poisonous, its roe, male gonads and black peritoneum are toxic (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Secondarily (passively) poisonous animals** do not inject venom with a special apparatus — poisoning occurs when they are eaten. The flesh of the **marinka** and **osman** fish living in Central Asian rivers is tasty, but their roe, milt and black peritoneum are highly toxic: if they are not cleaned well, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, respiratory paralysis develop. Marine **puffer fish** (fugu) contain tetrodotoxin. The secretion of the skin glands of some toads has a cardiotoxic effect.

parts.text: **First aid for snakebite:** calm the patient and lay them down; immobilize the bitten limb with a splint; remove rings and bracelets; give plenty of fluids; take the patient to hospital urgently — there **snake antivenom** is given. **Do not:** apply a tourniquet, cut or cauterize the wound, or give alcohol. For a karakurt bite, **anti-karakurt serum** is used.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing argasid and ixodid ticks in a preparation

items: Examine the tick from the dorsal side with a magnifier or the low-power objective of a microscope.
Determine whether there is a chitinous scutum on the back.
Check whether the mouthparts (capitulum) are visible from above or hidden under the body.
No scutum and mouthparts not visible from above — conclude an argasid tick; scutum present and mouthparts visible at the front end — an ixodid tick.
Count the legs to identify the stage: 3 pairs — larva, 4 pairs — nymph or imago (the nymph has no genital opening).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Scabies was found in most of the students sent to pick cotton.
cases.ask: Explain the reasons. What measures can eliminate the disease?
cases.answer: The scabies mite, *Sarcoptes scabiei*, is transmitted by direct skin contact, shared beds, bedding and clothing. Crowded living in dormitories, sleeping on shared bedding and limited opportunities to wash and change clothes caused the disease to spread quickly. Measures: treating all patients and their contacts at the same time (permethrin, benzyl benzoate), boiling or hot-ironing underwear and bedding, isolating patients, examining contacts and improving sanitary and hygienic conditions.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A tick taken from an animal was examined under the microscope: no chitinous scutum was found on its back, and its mouthparts are not visible from above. Among other ticks, there are also specimens in which the pathogen was found even though they had not fed on blood.
cases.ask: Which family does this tick belong to? How can the presence of the pathogen in ticks that have not fed be explained?
cases.answer: The absence of a scutum and the position of the mouthparts on the underside of the body are typical of argasid ticks (*Argasidae*), for example the village tick — the vector of tick-borne relapsing fever. The pathogen in unfed ticks is explained by transovarial transmission: the pathogen multiplies in the mother tick and passes through the egg to the next generation, and it is also retained from larva to nymph and imago by the transstadial route. Ticks are therefore natural reservoirs of the pathogen.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A person bitten by a snake has bleeding from the bite site, severe pain, rapidly spreading swelling and a sharp fall in blood pressure. Another patient, after a snakebite, developed difficulty breathing and swallowing, numbness of the body and difficulty moving.
cases.ask: In each case, what kind of snake might be suspected?
cases.answer: The first case shows the effect of a haemotoxic venom — impaired blood clotting, damage to the vessel walls and local tissue necrosis; this is seen after bites by vipers such as the Levant viper (gyurza), the saw-scaled viper or the Halys pit viper. The second case shows the effect of a neurotoxic venom — blockade of neuromuscular transmission, paralysis and respiratory failure; this is seen after a bite by the Central Asian cobra. In both cases the limb is immobilized, no tourniquet is applied, and the patient is taken urgently to hospital and given snake antivenom; in neurotoxic poisoning one must be ready for artificial ventilation.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A 35-year-old man who rested in a mountainous area in May presented 7 days later with high fever, headache, muscle pain, bleeding gums and pinpoint haemorrhages on the skin. He says he had contact with sheep and crushed a tick that had attached to his body with his fingers.
cases.ask: What disease should be considered? Which action of the patient was dangerous?
cases.answer: The spring–summer season, contact with livestock, a tick bite and haemorrhagic syndrome are typical of **Crimean–Congo haemorrhagic fever**; its vector is *Hyalomma* ticks, which also have natural foci in Uzbekistan. **Crushing the tick with the fingers** was dangerous: the virus can pass with the tick's haemolymph through micro-wounds in the skin. The patient is admitted at once to an infectious-diseases hospital; strict protective measures are taken because the disease can spread to medical staff through blood and secretions. Prevention: protection from ticks, correct tick removal and treating livestock with acaricides.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: At a medical check in grade 3 of a school, small whitish “grains” — nits — and head lice were found in the hair of 6 pupils.
cases.ask: What measures should be taken?
cases.answer: This is **head pediculosis**. Measures: (1) the affected children are treated with pediculicides (permethrin shampoo or solution) and the nits are combed out with a fine comb; (2) the treatment is repeated after 7–10 days, because the drugs do not act well on nits and new larvae hatch from them; (3) all classmates and family members are examined; (4) hats, combs and pillowcases are washed or treated; (5) the children are kept away from the group until treated and are re-examined. Head lice do not carry disease, but itching and scratching lead to secondary infection.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: In July a 25-year-old woman working in a cotton field was bitten by a black widow spider. 30 minutes later she developed severe muscle pain all over the body, board-like rigidity of the abdominal muscles, heavy sweating, fear and shortness of breath.
cases.ask: How does the venom act and what help is given?
cases.answer: Black widow (*Latrodectus*) venom is **neurotoxic**: it causes massive release of mediators (acetylcholine, noradrenaline) from nerve endings — hence severe muscle pain and rigidity, sweating, fear, tachycardia and raised blood pressure. Rigidity of the abdominal muscles resembles an “acute abdomen”, but it is not a surgical disease. Help: calm the patient, cool the bite site and transport quickly to hospital, where **black widow antivenom**, calcium preparations, analgesics and muscle relaxants are given. The bite site must not be cut or cauterised.

topics.title: Onto-phylogenesis of organ systems: skin, skeleton, nervous system, circulation, endocrine system, excretory system. Ecology. The human as an ecological factor. The biosphere and its problems

goals.text: To teach the student the main lines of evolution of the organ systems of vertebrates, the phylogenetic causes of congenital defects found in humans (atavisms, rudiments), as well as the basics of ecology, the role of humans as an ecological factor and the problems of the biosphere.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of homologous and analogous organs, rudiments and atavisms;
the evolution of the integumentary, skeletal, circulatory, nervous, excretory, digestive, respiratory and endocrine systems;
the phylogenetically determined congenital defects found in humans;
the ecological factors, the doctrine of the biosphere and noosphere, and the genetic consequences of environmental pollution.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: compare the heart, arterial arches and brain of vertebrates of different classes;
explain whether a congenital defect is linked to the recurrence of an ancestral feature or to the disruption of an embryonic process.

blocks.text: The evolution of organs is studied by **evolutionary morphology** on the basis of data from **comparative anatomy**, **comparative embryology** and **palaeontology**. **Homologous organs** have the same origin and structural plan but may have different functions (the pectoral fin of a fish, the wing of a bird, the human arm). **Analogous organs** have the same function but a different origin (the wings of a butterfly and of a bird).

blocks.label: Figure 15.1
blocks.caption: Homology of the forelimb skeleton of vertebrates: although they perform different functions (walking, flying, swimming, grasping), the bones of the upper arm, forearm and hand are built on one plan (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Rudiments** are vestigial organs that have lost their function in evolution and are retained in all people (the vermiform appendix, the coccygeal vertebrae, the muscles of the auricle, the semilunar fold of the eye). **Atavisms** are the reappearance of features of distant ancestors in individual people (a tail, hair covering the whole body — hypertrichosis, extra nipples — polymastia, cervical fistulae). Most atavisms result from structures present in the embryo failing to be remodelled in time: according to the **biogenetic law** (F. Müller, E. Haeckel), ontogenesis is a brief recapitulation of phylogenesis.

**The biogenetic law** (F. Müller, 1864; E. Haeckel, 1866): ontogeny is a brief and rapid recapitulation of phylogeny. For example, gill arches and pouches, a two-chambered heart, a tail and a head-kidney stage are seen in the human embryo. A.N. Severtsov developed the law and created the theory of **phylembryogeneses**: evolutionary changes are of three kinds depending on the stage of ontogeny at which they arise.

parts.text: Phylogenetically determined defects in humans arise by two mechanisms: 1) **persistence** of an embryonic structure (tail, cervical fistulae, patent ductus arteriosus); 2) **arrest** of organ development at an ancestral stage (three-chambered heart, pelvic kidney, right aortic arch).

sections.title: 2. The integument, skeleton, digestive and respiratory systems

blocks.text: **Integument.** In invertebrates the skin consists of a single-layered epithelium and a cuticle. In vertebrates the skin has two layers: the stratified **epidermis** develops from ectoderm and the **dermis** from mesoderm. Skin derivatives change from class to class: bony and **placoid scales** in fish (their homologue is the teeth of mammals), mucous glands in amphibians, horny scales in reptiles, feathers in birds, and hair, sweat, sebaceous and **mammary glands** in mammals. Anomalies: **ichthyosis** (a hereditary disorder of the horny layer, in which the skin comes to resemble fish scales), hypertrichosis, polymastia (extra nipples along the milk lines).

head: Class

rows: Multicellular mucous and poison glands; the skin takes part in respiration

blocks.text: **Skeleton.** In the lancelet the axial skeleton is the **notochord**; in vertebrates it is replaced by the vertebral column. The skull consists of the braincase and the **visceral skeleton** derived from the gill arches (the auditory ossicles, the hyoid bone and the laryngeal cartilages are derivatives of the gill arches). The five-digit limb arose from the fin of lobe-finned fish. Anomalies: cervical ribs, **spina bifida**, polydactyly, syndactyly, **Sprengel's deformity** (failure of the scapula to descend from its embryonic position in the neck).

**Evolution of teeth.** In fish and reptiles the teeth are all of one shape (**homodont**) and are replaced many times throughout life (**polyphyodont**). In mammals the teeth are specialised into incisors, canines, premolars and molars (**heterodont**) and are replaced only once (**diphyodont** — milk and permanent teeth). In humans the reduction in the number of teeth (failure of the wisdom tooth to erupt, or its absence) continues oligomerisation; extra teeth and cone-shaped teeth are atavistic anomalies.

**Digestive and respiratory systems.** In the evolution of the gut tube we see its division into sections, its lengthening and the appearance of digestive glands. Only mammals form a **secondary palate**; failure of it to close is **cleft palate**. In the embryo the gut tube is temporarily occluded and then reopened (**recanalization**); if this process is disrupted, **atresia and stenosis** of the oesophagus, duodenum or intestine result. The respiratory organs develop from the gill pouches and from an outgrowth of the floor of the pharynx: gills in fish, lungs in land vertebrates, alveolar lungs in mammals. Anomalies: **tracheo-oesophageal fistula**, aplasia of a lung or a lung lobe.

blocks.label: Figure 15.2
blocks.caption: Evolution of the lungs: A — amphibians (sac-like lung with a smooth inner surface); B, C — reptiles (appearance of septa); D — mammals (alveolar lung); 1 — trachea, 2 — bronchi, 3 — septa and alveoli (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The respiratory surface of the lung increases during evolution through internal septa and bronchial branching: the human lung has ≈ 300–500 million alveoli with a total surface of ≈ 70–100 m^2^. In birds the lungs are connected with air sacs and air flows in one direction (“double breathing”). **Meckel's diverticulum** — a remnant of the embryonic vitelline (omphalo-enteric) duct — persists in the small intestine in 2 % of people and can cause inflammation, bleeding or intestinal obstruction.

The line of evolution is the **improvement of the heart** and the **separation of arterial and venous blood**. **The lancelet** has no heart; blood is moved by contractions of the ventral aorta, and there is one circulation. **In fish** the heart has two chambers (atrium and ventricle) and contains only venous blood; there is one circulation. **In amphibians** the heart has three chambers (two atria and one ventricle), there are two circulations, and blood **mixes** in the ventricle. **In reptiles** the ventricle has an incomplete septum (complete in crocodiles), and two aortic arches are retained. **In birds** and **mammals** the heart has four chambers and the blood does not mix: birds retain the **right** aortic arch and mammals the **left**.

parts.text: Congenital defects of the heart and great vessels often resemble ancestral structures: **ventricular or atrial septal defect** (like the amphibian and reptilian heart, with mixing of blood), **patent ductus arteriosus**, **right or double aortic arch**, tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries. When arterial and venous blood mix, cyanosis, breathlessness and delayed physical development are seen.

sections.title: 4. The nervous, excretory and endocrine systems

blocks.text: **Nervous system.** In invertebrates the nervous system evolved from **diffuse** (Hydra) → **ladder-like** (flatworms) → **ventral nerve cord** (annelids, arthropods). In vertebrates the central nervous system forms from the **neural tube**; the brain has five parts: the forebrain, diencephalon, midbrain, cerebellum and medulla oblongata (Figure 15.5). Three brain types are distinguished: **ichthyopsid** (fish, amphibians — the highest integrating centre is the midbrain), **sauropsid** (reptiles, birds — the striate bodies of the forebrain) and **mammalian** (mammals — the **new cortex**, neocortex). Anomalies: anencephaly, microcephaly, hydrocephalus, spinal hernia.

blocks.label: Figure 15.5
blocks.caption: Longitudinal sections of the vertebrate brain: I — bony fish; II — electric fish; III — frog; IV — reptile; V — bird; VI — mammal; 1 — forebrain; 2 — diencephalon; 3 — midbrain; 4 — cerebellum; 5 — medulla oblongata; 6 — pineal gland; 7 — pituitary gland (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 15.6
blocks.caption: Evolution of the inner ear (labyrinth): fish, reptiles, birds and mammals; in mammals the cochlea is coiled into a spiral (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Sense organs.** The inner ear was originally an organ of balance (semicircular canals in fish); the hearing part — the cochlea — develops in land vertebrates and becomes spiral in mammals. The middle-ear ossicles come from the visceral skeleton: amphibians and reptiles have one (the stapes), mammals three (the malleus and incus are derivatives of the jaw-joint bones). In the embryo the auditory tube and middle-ear cavity form from the first pharyngeal pouch, and the external auditory canal from the first pharyngeal cleft.

**Excretory system.** In invertebrates — protonephridia (flatworms), metanephridia (annelids), Malpighian tubules (insects). In vertebrates the kidney is replaced in three stages: the **head kidney (pronephros)** — in cyclostomes and the embryos of all vertebrates; the **trunk (primary) kidney (mesonephros)** — in fish and amphibians; the **pelvic (secondary) kidney (metanephros)** — in reptiles, birds and mammals. All three stages also follow one another in the human embryo. Anomalies: renal aplasia, **horseshoe kidney**, a kidney remaining in the pelvis (dystopia), duplex kidney, polycystic disease.

blocks.label: Figure 15.7
blocks.caption: Evolution of the excretory and genital ducts in vertebrates (I–VI): the head kidney, primary (trunk) kidney and secondary (pelvic) kidney, their ducts and relation to the gonads (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In humans the primary kidney duct (**Wolffian duct**) becomes the vas deferens in men and regresses in women; the paramesonephric (**Müllerian**) ducts form the uterine tubes, the uterus and the upper vagina in women. Incomplete fusion of the Müllerian ducts leads to defects such as a **bicornuate or double uterus** (the normal state in ancient forms of mammals), and failure of the testis to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum leads to **cryptorchidism** (in most vertebrates the testes lie in the abdominal cavity).

**Endocrine system.** Hormonal regulation began with neurosecretion; in vertebrates the hypothalamic-pituitary system takes the central place. The thyroid gland develops from the floor of the pharynx and is homologous with the **endostyle** of the lancelet; the cortex and medulla of the adrenal gland are separate in fish and unite in land vertebrates. Insufficiency of the adrenal cortex is **Addison's disease**: hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes, weight loss and disturbed water-salt metabolism.

sections.title: 5. Ecology. The human as an ecological factor. The biosphere

blocks.text: **Ecology** (the term was introduced by E. Haeckel in 1866) is the science of the relationships of organisms with one another and with their environment. Its branches: autecology (a single species), population ecology, synecology (communities) and **human ecology**. **Ecological factors**: **abiotic** (temperature, light, humidity, ionizing radiation), **biotic** (the influence of other organisms — parasitism, symbiosis, competition) and **anthropogenic** (human activity). An organism lives within a certain **range of tolerance** for each factor; the factor that deviates most from the optimum becomes the **limiting factor**.

**Ecological laws.** **The law of the minimum** (J. Liebig, 1840): the life of an organism is limited by the factor present in the smallest amount (for example, endemic goitre in mountainous areas lacking iodine). **The law of tolerance** (V. Shelford, 1913): both a shortage and an excess of a factor can be limiting; for each species a factor has **optimum** and **pessimum** zones and limits of tolerance. Species with wide tolerance are called **eurybiont**, those with narrow tolerance **stenobiont**; humans are a eurybiont species.

blocks.text: **The biosphere** is the shell of the Earth inhabited by living organisms and transformed by them (the lower atmosphere, the hydrosphere and the upper lithosphere). The doctrine of the biosphere was created by **V.I. Vernadsky**: living matter is the main driving force of the cycling of substances on the planet. Human activity is creating a new state of the biosphere — the **noosphere** (sphere of reason). Current problems: pollution of the air, water and soil, the greenhouse effect, depletion of the ozone layer, desertification and loss of biodiversity; for Uzbekistan — the **Aral Sea** disaster and its effect on public health.

V.I. Vernadsky distinguished the main functions of **living matter** in the biosphere: **energetic** (storing solar energy in photosynthesis), **gas** (maintaining the composition of the atmosphere — O~2~ and CO~2~), **concentrating** (accumulating elements — for example, iron bacteria, calcareous skeletons), **redox** and **destructive** (breaking down dead organic matter). The biological cycle of substances is carried out by producers, consumers and decomposers.

parts.text: **The Aral Sea disaster** is one of the largest ecological catastrophes of the twentieth century: because too much river water was taken for irrigation, the sea level fell sharply, and dust rich in salt and pesticides is blown from the dried sea bed. In the population of the Aral region (Karakalpakstan, Khorezm) **iron-deficiency anaemia**, kidney and liver diseases, tuberculosis, respiratory diseases, thyroid pathology, congenital defects and child mortality have increased. This is a striking example of the effect of ecological factors on health.

**Genetic consequences of environmental pollution:** chemical mutagens (pesticides, heavy metals, benzpyrene), ionizing radiation and some viruses increase the mutation rate — this leads to more hereditary diseases, congenital defects, infertility and tumours. **Genetic monitoring** of the population and control of mutagens are therefore necessary.

blocks.text: **The human as an ecological factor.** Unlike other organisms, humans consciously change their environment. This ability was formed during the long process of **anthropogenesis** (Figure 15.8): dryopithecines → australopithecines → **handy man** (*Homo habilis*, the first tools) → **archanthropes** (Pithecanthropus, Sinanthropus) → **palaeoanthropes** (Neanderthals) → **neoanthropes** (Cro-Magnons, *Homo sapiens*). Alongside the biological factors of anthropogenesis (natural selection, variation), social factors — labour, speech and life in groups — played the decisive role.

Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Human races** are groups within one species (*Homo sapiens*) linked by common origin and territory and differing in external features such as skin colour, hair and facial structure: traditionally the **Europoid**, **Mongoloid**, **Negroid** and **Australoid** great races are distinguished. Racial features formed as adaptations to the environment (for example, dark skin pigmentation protects against ultraviolet light). All races interbreed fully, and most genetic differences lie not between races but **within** each group — so views about “higher” or “lower” races have no scientific basis.
